en: From the *Paribhāṣāvṛtti*.
The first quarter of the first chapter.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.

May this commentary on the Paribhāṣās, which possesses a fresh radiance, shines like the sun, is bold, forcibly subdues defects, encompasses the vast circle of the learned world, and has established beneficial deliberations, be effective for the pacification of the arising of dullness through its cultivation. (1)
The specific understanding [of a term] is derived from its explanation; for it is not because of doubt that something fails to be a defining characteristic. //1//

Through explanation—that is, through the instruction of the traditional lineage of teachers—even when there is doubt, a specific understanding arises; it is not that the definition (or rule) is absent.

Therefore, even when the sixth case [the genitive] is rejected in the rule *sthāne yoga* (Pāṇini 1.1.49), although multiple relations may be possible in the indications of the sixth case, it occurs only through connection with the "place" (*sthāna*). As it has been said: "Specific understanding comes from explanation; for a rule is not rendered invalid by doubt. Thus, we shall explain [the rule] as *sthāne yoga*."
Likewise, there are four occurrences of the term *aṇ* [in Pāṇini’s rules]:
one with the preceding *ṇ*, namely *aṇ aditsu sarvaṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*; and three with the following *ṇ*, namely the occurrences of the term *iṇ*.
In this regard, the logical arguments (*yukti*) are also stated as far as they apply.

Among them, concerning the rule *aṇo dralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ*, it is understood from the force of the mention of *aṇ* that [the lengthening] occurs by the preceding [rule]. For if it were by the subsequent [rule], the mention of *aṇ* would be purposeless.
In this very case, there ought to be [the designation *ac*] for both short and long vowels.
And since this is already established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "and *ac*," what is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*?
This argument can be shown to be fallacious.

And thus, by the inclusion of *aṇ* for both the short (*hrasva*) and long (*dīrgha*) vowels, this is the purpose: so that even for a non-*aṇ* vowel, there may be long and short forms, as in *agīṣkaḥ*, *adhūṣkaḥ*, *śvaliṅkaḥ*, *madhuliṅkaḥ*, and *vaḍhām* / *varḍhum*.
And in this way, regarding what was stated by the author of the *Nyāsa* concerning *laṇ*—"because of the impossibility of *hal* followed by *ke* being an *aṇ*"—and so forth.

Similarly, when the rule *acaśca* is brought into proximity by the rule *tathā dīrghaśrutyā*, one must consider the point that lengthening (*dīrghatva*) must apply only to a vowel (*ac*), and so forth. Regarding this, some reflect as follows:
in examples such as *agīṣkaḥ*, once the visarga and other operations have been performed, there is neither the *aṇ* [vowel] nor the *repha* [the sound 'ra'].
Nor is there the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*),
because [the substitution] is prohibited by the rule *na mune* through a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*).
Furthermore, one need not speak of non-mention (*anabhidhāna*).
Because this has been explained in the commentary on the rule *roḥ supi* within the *Nyāsa* on the *Agnīṣkādigaṇa*.

Furthermore, regarding the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*), it was stated that in cases such as *varḍhā* and *varḍhum*, even the *repha* (the letter *r*) not being a vowel (*anac*) undergoes lengthening because of the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* by means of the subsequent *ṇakāra*.
That is not correct.
If this were the intended purpose, then [the author] would have formed the *pratyāhāra* using the letter *ṭ* in *hayavaraṭ*.
[The objection is: "By the rule *dralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṭi*, [the vowel] preceding the elision of *r* becomes long.

Alternatively, let it be that in forms such as *varḍhā* and *varḍhum*, the vowel *ṛ* itself is long; nevertheless, once that [lengthening] has been applied, by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, a *guṇa* substitute arises from the combination of the vowel *a* and the vowel *ṛ*. Then, when the substitution of *r* for the final element (*raparatvam*) is performed, the resulting form remains exactly the same:
*varḍhā* and *varḍhum*.
Therefore, the inclusion of the term *aṇ* in the rule *ato’ṇ ca* is for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra* with the preceding *ṇ*.

It is not for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra* with the subsequent *ṇ*; for if it were so, the lengthening of the vowel *r* (in *pra-ṇamati*) would be redundant, and one would have to assume that it subverts the application of *āṭ-ṛ-guṇa*.
In this way, there would be two distinct functional capacities [for the rule].

In the rule concerning homogeneous sounds (*savarṇavidhi*), when a *pratyāhāra* is understood by means of the final *ṇakāra*, the inclusion of the *tapara* marker in the rule *ur ṛt* (P. 1.1.50) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

For if, in that case as well, [the *pratyāhāra*] were understood by means of the preceding [ṇakāra], then when a short *ṛ*-vowel mentioned in the rule is prescribed in place of a short vowel mentioned in the rule, there would be no possibility at all for the two-moraic [long vowel] to apply due to the absence of homogeneity;
thus, the *tapara* marker would be purposeless.

Regarding what was stated by the author of the Nyāsa concerning the rule *laṇ*— namely, that even for a long vowel as a substitute, it must be a short vowel exactly as heard in the text, and thus the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (the short *ṛ*) would be purposeless because there is nothing to exclude— the claim made therein that a two-moraic vowel possesses the status of a substitute (*sthānin*) is inconsistent.
Because, like the substitute (*ādeśa*), the original element (*sthānin*) also lacks the status of having two morae (*dvimātra*).
If it is argued that the status of being the original element belongs to the genus (*jāti*) of having two morae, we say no;
for if that were so, the same consequence of having two morae would follow for the substitute as well.
Now, [the view that] the genus (*jāti*) refers to the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the individual (*vyakti*) refers to the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not convincing.

If that is the case, then in the rule *ur ṛd*—where the two vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*) and thus take the neuter singular short vowel ending—the long vowel also possesses the status of a substituendum.
As for the absence of the augment *num*, it is due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the teaching regarding augments.
This, however, is logical:

since the *ṛ*-vowel is not included within the *aṇ* pratyāhāra, the *ṛ*-vowel is not grasped by the *ṛ*-vowel due to their being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*). Consequently, the *ṛ*-vowel does not possess the status of a vowel (*actva*).
Therefore, how could the shortness prescribed for vowels apply to the *ṛ*-vowel?
It is said:

by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*, the shortening of vowels (*ac*) is prescribed. Since the vowel *ṛ* is included in the *ac*-pratyāhāra, and because the universal class (*jāti*) of the sound *ṛ* is relied upon there, even the two-mora (*dvimātrika*) sound *ṝ* must necessarily be treated as short; thus, it is logical that the substitute applies even to a long original base (*sthānin*), and so forth.
And this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) was indicated by the author of the Bhāṣya in the rule *laṇ*.
As it has been said:

"But why is this letter *ṇ*, which is the cause of doubt regarding the production of phonemes, attached again even though it was already attached? Because by means of this [ṇ], there arises a doubt in the case of references to *aṇ* and references to *iṇ*: [does it refer] to the former or to the latter?"
Or rather, in this way the Teacher makes it known that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) exists, [as stated in the principle] "by virtue of the explanation," and so forth.
(1) Now, as for how the sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed in the expression *viśeṣapratipatti*, [one might object]:
since there would have to be a prohibition by the rule *karmaṇi ca*,
and since a sixth-case ending characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix cannot be compounded, this compound cannot be established.
Because the commencement [of the rule] is specifically regarding that object and the action;
it is said:

by the phrase "and in the case of an action" (*karmaṇi ca*), when both [the agent and the object] are eligible [to take the genitive], the prohibition of compounding is understood to apply only to that genitive which is restricted by the rule "in the case of an action."
Regarding this matter, the rule *kartari ca* is the authority.

Otherwise, since the prohibition would already be established by the rule *karmaṇi ca* in cases such as *apāṃ sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters") and *odanasya bhojakaḥ* ("the eater of rice"), the inclusion of *kartari ca* would be purposeless.

Nor can it be argued that this [rule] is intended to prohibit the sixth-case compound with a word ending in the agentive suffix in instances like *praiṣyasya hārayitā* ("one who causes a servant to carry") and *praiṣyasya kārayitā* ("one who causes a servant to do"), on the grounds of the optionality provided by the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām*.
The formation of that [compound] is established by the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* alone.

As for the statement made in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari*—namely, that "the mention of *tṛc* is for the sake of subsequent rules"—that was said with the rule *kartari ca* already established.
Some say that the phrase "for the sake of subsequent rules" was stated with reference to roots ending in *aṇ*.

Furthermore, by the restrictive rule *ubhayaprāptau*, the genitive case [is applied] only where both agent and object are explicitly mentioned, because the term "usage" (*prayoga*) from the rule *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* is understood to carry over; thus, it occurs only in cases such as: "The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful."

For in this case, a marvel is to be established; and that [marvel] occurs when the mention of the agent is obtained through implication (*sāmarthya-prāpta*)—as in the case of cows difficult to milk and a task performed by one who is unskilled and lacks a cowherd—wherein the genitive case is used for the agent, and not otherwise, because there would be no comprehension of the specific distinction.
However, here, since the agent such as the student is incapable of effecting anything, the mention of the agent is not obtained through implication.
This being so, in the rule *antardhau yenādarśanam icchati*, the use of the third case in *yena* is not appropriate, because the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* prescribes the genitive case for the agent.
It is said:
there is no fault, because the third [case-ending] follows from the very statement [of the rule].
But another explains:
Even when the object (*karman*) is merely implied (*gamyamāna*), the restriction (*niyama*) "when both [agent and object] are applicable" (*ubhayaprāptau*) certainly applies.

Thus, regarding the rule *antarddho yenādarśanam icchati*, the author of the *Nyāsa* and Rakṣita have stated that the formulation *antarddho yena* is established because, under the restriction "when both are applicable" (*ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not occur even when the object is merely implied.
However, regarding the statement in the *Nyāsa* concerning the rule *kiṃ tvevam aiuṇ*: "In that [rule], the mention of 'that' (*tasya*) occurs by means of a single [word]," it is not correct.
For even here, since the object (*karman*) is understood as that which is to be grasped, the genitive case should not occur due to the restriction *ubhayaprāptau* (Pāṇini 2.3.66).
This has been explained by the author of the *Nyāsa* in his grammatical treatise (*śabdānuśāsana*).
As for what the author of the *Anunyāsa* stated there out of the boldness of his own intellectual prowess:
"Where both [agent and object] are obtained by implication, that is the domain of the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between the domains of the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* and the rule *ubhayaprāptau*."
And [the claim] that "there is no action without an agent" is due to logical necessity; however, that is incorrect,
because in cases such as "Devadatta is the breaker of forts," where the agent is already expressed, the restriction [in question] would not apply.
To this it is replied:

Although the mention of "usage" (*prayoga*) from the rule *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* continues [into subsequent rules], we have stated that there is no division [of cases] by not accepting it—just as you have stated a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the object (*karman*) when it is understood (*gamyamāna*) by means of the rule *ubhayaprāptau*. In the same way, we have stated the absence of division by not accepting the governing heading (*adhikāra*) *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed").

And this is incorrect; for it must be stated that the prohibition applies to [stems] ending in *k* and *ā*. Wherever a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is set aside by another, the positive injunction (*vidhi*) has already fulfilled its purpose, as in the case of *cikīrṣā-ravi-ālokānām*.

Likewise, in the case of "the mat is to be made for Devadatta" (*kāryaḥ kaṭo devadattasya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applying to the expressed object (*abhihite karmaṇi*). To this it is replied: the genitive in the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* and that in the rule *ubhayaprāptau* are not genitives in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇe*); rather, they are in grammatical coordination with different referents (*vaiyadhikaraṇye*).

The meaning is as follows: there would be no distinction between the domains of the rule *kartari ca* (P. 3.4.67), which is connected with *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, and the rule *karmaṇi ca* (P. 2.3.66), which applies when both [agent and object] are possible. This is the intended point:

if, even when the agent is understood, the restriction *ubhayaprāptau* were to apply to the object, then in cases such as *idhmavraścanaḥ*, where the suffix *lyuṭ* denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*), the prohibition [of the genitive] by the rule *karmaṇi ca* would also apply to the agent-denoting *lyuṭ*.

In the case of *idhmāpravraścanaḥ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta, who cuts the fuel"), since the agent (*devadattena*) is understood from the phrase "by Devadatta himself," the application of both [rules]—the genitive and the sixth case—is indeed unimpeded.

Thus, since the prohibition of compounding for all instances of the sixth case in relation to the object would be established by the rule *karmaṇi ca*, the rule *kartari ca* would not need to be commenced at all. Yet, because it has been commenced, it is rightly said that there would be no distinction between their respective domains.
And this is not so;
for there is no evidence that the word *ātmanā* (by oneself) functions as a designated agent (*kartṛ*).

If that is the case, then just as in examples such as "Devadatta is the breaker of the city," where no restriction [of the instrumental case] occurs because the agent is already expressed, so too here in the expression "instruction in words" (*śabdānuśāsanam*), there is no application of the agent.

In that regard, just as a restriction is stated even when the agent is merely implied— despite the fact that the genitive case for the agent would otherwise apply— so too, even though the agent is explicitly prescribed, the distinction between the scopes [of the two rules] is stated after setting aside the restriction.
And thus, there is no lack of distinction between the scope of the prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) and the restrictive rule (*niyama*).
And this is stated because, when the particles *ā* and *kā* are employed, the injunction has already achieved its purpose and thus does not require further reliance [on other factors]. || 1 ||
For that which is an effect is not accepted as being the cause.
The meaning is that whatever participates in the operation of a grammatical element (*kāryabhāk*) does not itself become the cause (*nimitta*) for that same operation.

Therefore, in forms such as *adhyetā*, *adhyāpakaḥ*, *śayitā*, and *śāyakaḥ*, the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions by the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5) does not apply, because the roots *iṅ* and *śīṅ* are marked with the *ṅ*-sign.
Likewise, in the form *aririṣati*, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if the substitute were the original) by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59) does not apply.
If it were so, then after reduplication has been performed, the form would be *arīṣati*.
And the evidence for this is that in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*, both *dīdhīṅ* and *vevīṅ* are included for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* even after *kṅit* suffixes.
It should not be argued that since the prohibition by the rule *kṅiti ca* applies only to *vṛddhi* characterized by an *ik* vowel,
the inclusion of both *dīdhī* and *vevī* would be necessary only to prohibit *vṛddhi* characterized by an *aj* vowel as well.

Because the inclusion of the term *bhavati* in the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* indicates that a prohibition applies even to a *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by an affix (*aj-lakṣaṇā*), the following objection is raised:

"But surely the *Bhāṣya* has rejected the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* on the grounds that the augment *vuk* is permanent (*nitya*) and that *indh-* is Vedic (*chāndasa*); likewise, it has rejected *dīdhīvevīṭām* as well.
As it says: 'The mention of *dīdhī* and *vevī* is purposeless, because these two are Vedic.'"

Furthermore, because we observe the *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *ādīdhet* and *ādīdhayuḥ*, the inclusion of the term *iṭ* [in the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*] would be purposeless. Since the mention of *iṭ* continues from the rule *neḍvaśi kṛti*, the repetition of *iṭ* in *ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* is for the purpose of preventing any modification of that *iṭ*.
Consequently, due to the absence of the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), the forms *kaṇitā* and *raṇitā* (meaning "he will sound" or "he will roar") are established.
Nor should it be argued that, by this same logic, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would not occur even in cases such as *pipaṭhiṣati* or *apāṭhīt*;
for what is excluded here is specifically the operation of the *aṅga* (the stem), on the basis of its being of the same class [as the examples where the rule applies].
However, in the case of *grahītā*, lengthening does occur because of the formulation of rules such as *graho 'liṭi*.
If it is argued that, in the case of *pipaṭhiṃṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* would not occur, we say no;

for in this instance, the augment *num* itself does not exist, because when *num* is to be applied, the elision of *al* (*allopa*) is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, and thus the word does not end in a consonant (*jhal*). Nor is there a rule stating "that which is elided in *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*."

Kaiyaṭa has explained that the *vārttika* "na sthānivat" applies with respect to what follows a *kvip* suffix; thus, in this case, the *num* augment occurs not after the *kvip*, but rather after the *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending]. Vāmana, however, maintains that the rule applies only when the *kvip* is elided (*lupta*).

And thus, in the rule *maparyantasya*, it has been stated that the inclusion of the word *tena* (by that) is for the purpose of exclusion; therefore, the substitute occurs only where there is something to be excluded. Consequently, in the case of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* followed by the suffix *ṇic*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.

From the root *yuṣmayati* with the suffix *kvip*, the substitutes [of the case endings] do not occur here because there is no [suffix] to be excluded (*varjanīya*). Nor does the elision of the *ṇi* possess the status of being "as if in its original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*), because of the rule stating that what is elided by *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.
Thus, this remains established:
according to the view of the Bhāṣya, there is no evidence for the rule that "it does not apply to that which has an object" (*na hi kāryī*).

However, in the rule *sthaṇḍilācchayitari* (Pāṇini 6.3.120), the mention of *śayitari* is evidence for it; or alternatively, the inclusion of the root *kuṅ* (meaning "to sound") among the *kuṭādi* roots serves as evidence.
Others, however, explain as follows:
the prohibition of *vṛddhi* characterized by the marker *i* occurs only when conditioned by a *kṅit* suffix, and not when conditioned by a *kṅit* root.

Therefore, in forms such as *mṛṣṭaḥ*, *mṛṣṭavān*, *nyanuvīt*, and *nyaghuvīt*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* occurs only when a suffix conditioned by *kṅit* follows; by association with that, the prohibition of *guṇa* is also understood to apply.
In examples such as *bobhūyate*, only a suffix conditioned by *k* or *ṅ* should be applied.
For this very reason, in *adhyetā* and *śayitā*, there should be no application of the prohibition conditioned by a *kṅit* suffix following a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, in *aririṣāti*, the status of being a cause for the substitution of *aj* (as prescribed by *dvirvacane’ci*) is restricted precisely to its non-activity (*akāryitva*). Thus, in connection with the substitution of *aj*, the term *aci* [in Pāṇini’s rule] possesses non-activity; by virtue of its association with that [non-activity], [the same applies to other elements].

Even when a rule for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is prescribed, if the condition *acī* (in the presence of a vowel) were merely a non-agent (*akāryitva*), then the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*) would apply, as in the case of *cakratuḥ*.

However, in *aririṣati*, since the second vowel (*ikāra*) undergoes reduplication, the vowel *i* participates in the reduplication; thus, in the prescription of reduplication, *acī* functions as an agent (*kāryitva*) rather than a non-agent.
Therefore, this paribhāṣā should not be accepted, as it lacks any practical necessity.
And this is logical;

otherwise, in the case of *asyām satyām prorṇunaviṣati*, after the application of *guṇa* and *ādeśa*, there would be no status as a *sthānin* (original element) by virtue of the rule *dvirvacane'ci* [P. 1.1.59], because the entire form ending in the *saN* suffix (*sannanta*) would be the subject of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*).

Likewise, regarding the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, it is stated "when *ac* follows"; however, the counter-examples cited—namely *heghīyate* and *dedhmīyate*—are untenable because they suffer from a deficiency of two constituent factors (*dvyaṅgavaikalyāt*). For just as the *yaṅ* suffix is not preceded by an *ac*-vowel, so too is it not the cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*). In that case, this must be said:
While experiencing its own effect, the effect is resorted to as the cause;
however, in the case of "one smells," the effect is resorted to as the cause without being experienced.
But another [cause] is not resorted to at all.

For instance: in the case of *aririṣati*, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there would be the undesirable consequence of doubling the suffix *iṣ*; therefore, only a *san* beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) can function as both the object of the operation (*kāryitva*) and the cause (*nimittatva*).

However, in the case of *prorṇunaviṣati*, while the *san* beginning with a vowel functions as the cause, it is the verbal root element *nu* itself that functions as the object of the operation, since it is that very element which is prescribed to undergo doubling.
Therefore, since the suffix *san* does not directly possess the status of being the object of the operation (*kāryitva*) here, it is indeed correct to adopt it as the cause (*nimitta*).

Even so, in the case of *śādhī*, regarding the substitution of *dhi* for *śādhī*, the rule of "asiddha" (non-application) with respect to the substitution of *ha* for *hi* would not apply because they share the same basis (*samānāśraya*). This is because the substitute *dhi* is not the cause for the original element (*sthānin*) *hi*; thus, there is an absence of having a common cause.
In this regard, it must be said that this is a general rule; it is applied in specific instances according to the requirements of the subject matter. (2)
Even operations that are mutually dependent are established in the grammatical treatise.

The principle is that effects which depend upon one another do not proceed when they are in opposition. Regarding what was stated—that there is no establishment [of the point] due to mutual dependence—this exception is now commenced.
The word "api" (even/also) is used here in the sense of "in some cases."
This is the meaning:
in some cases, things proceed based on mutual dependence;
for example, the protection of a forest and a lion proceeds through their mutual reliance upon one another.
Likewise, in the grammatical treatise, in examples such as *gārgīya*, the designation *vṛddhi* is applied even to that which has already been brought about by the designation *vṛddhi*.
Otherwise, in cases such as *śālārairaupa*, the designation *vṛddhi*—which finds its scope elsewhere—would not apply due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
And here there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*): in the rule *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, by means of the term *saṃprasāraṇa*, the *ik* vowels are to be understood as replacing the *yaṇ* sounds;
and since the designation *saṃprasāraṇa* applies to those *ik* vowels that occupy the place of *yaṇ*, there is a state of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
How else could this be established?
"If there were no instance of mutual dependence anywhere," so says the author of the Bhāgavṛtti;
"this is merely an explanatory description (anvākhyāna) of eternal words, and therefore the fault of mutual dependence does not apply."

As for what was stated— that all [objections regarding] mutual dependence have been refuted in the Bhāṣya by the words "but it is established because words are eternal"— if it should be argued that "an *ik* vowel is prescribed in place of a *yaṇ*, and since the relationship between the original (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is man-made, the eternality [of the word] is thereby undermined," this is not a fault.

In common worldly usage, terms such as *iṣṭam* (sacrificed) and *yaṣṭā* (sacrificer) are eternal; therein, the root *ij-* is established as correct in the specific sense of the root *yaj-* (to sacrifice). To this extent, the status of being dependent on a person belongs to the root *yaj-* by its very nature. Thus, the establishment of *ij-* occurs in place of *yaj-*, and the augments (*āgama*)—being subordinate to it—are included by the mention of that [root]. || 4 ||

In the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau*, because the words "beginning" (*ādya*) and "end" (*anta*) denote constituent parts (*avayava*), it is extended that the augments marked with *ṭ* and *k* possess the status of being the initial and final parts [of the element they are attached to]. Similarly, in the rule *midaco 'ntyāt paraḥ*, by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "end" (*anta*), an augment marked with *m* also possesses the status of being a final part. It has been stated that parts are included by the mention of the whole; therefore, this maxim is established: "Augments are subordinate to that [to which they are attached]."
And some state that this is also an *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) for the sake of easy comprehension:
in the rule *ṇeraniṭi*, the prohibition regarding "that which does not take the augment *iṭ*" serves as an indicator.

For if an *āgama* (augment) were not included by the mention of *āgama* [in the rule], then in forms such as *kārayitavyam*, the elision of *ṇi* would not apply simply because it is separated by the letter *i*; thus, what would be the purpose of the phrase "provided it does not take *iṭ*"? This is the indicative proof.

Therefore, because *suṭ* is included under the term *sup* in the rule *sarveṣām*, the substitution of *et* (the replacement of the final vowel with *e*) is established when a *sup* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows.
Objection: If this [rule] were present, then in forms such as *cicchidatuḥ* and *cicchiduḥ*, the elision of *tuK* would result from the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*.
Response: It is said that in the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, the perspective of a genus (*jāti*) is adopted for the sake of establishing forms such as *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*.
And in that regard, since this single rule— "sakṛd eva papāṭha" and so forth— effects the removal of the initial consonant (*hal*) from what is beginningless,
it follows that in forms such as *cicchidatuḥ*, the *tuk* augment which occurs after the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* would not undergo removal,
because there is no longer any basis for the rule.
And this must necessarily be so;
otherwise, the example cited by both the author of the Bhāṣya and Maitreya in the rule *ajāder dvitīyasya*—
"oṇer uvoṇiṣati"— would provide an occasion for the second doubling [of the root] to apply.
That would be inconsistent,
because of the undesirable consequence that the *v* would be elided by the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*.

If this were so, then in forms such as *vavṛte*, once the substitution of *u* for *ṝ* (*uradatta*) and the substitution of *ra* for *ṝ* (*raparatva*) have been applied, there would be no elision of the *r*.
It is said:
in the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, the phrase *uraṅ* will be understood as carrying over; thus, when *uraṅ* has been applied, the removal of the *repha* (the letter *r*) will occur.
If that is so, then in the case of *uñcheḥ aiñcicchat* after *tuk* has been applied, its removal would necessarily occur by the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*.
It is said:

although the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is already carried over (*anuvartamāna*) from the rule *che ca*, its repetition here by means of the word *ca* (and) serves as an indicator (*sāmarthya*) that the short vowel itself is accepted as the augment (*āgama*), and not the entire group ending in a short vowel. Consequently, the *tuk* augment is applied only to a part of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). By virtue of this, even a sub-part of a whole is not included under the designation of the "whole" in this context, whereas elsewhere it certainly is.

Therefore, in the case of *śerataḥ*, it was stated that a part of a constituent part becomes a constituent part of the whole; thus, in the rule *śīṅo ruṭ*, it was stated that there is *guṇa* for *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

However, in this way, in the case of *śobhanacchāyaḥ*, there would be the fault that *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) would not occur because the second member (*uttarapada*) is separated by the *tuk* augment. It is replied: [The objection is: "In the case of *śobhanacchāyaḥ*, *puṃvadbhāva* should not take place because the second member [of the compound] is separated by the *tuk* augment. It is said in reply: [The answer is: This is not so. For the *puṃvadbhāva* is prescribed by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34), which states that a feminine word ending in a long vowel, when it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, becomes like the masculine provided the first member is a word expressing a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), or a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Now, in the present case, the word *chāyā* is indeed a feminine word ending in a long vowel, and it is the first member of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Furthermore, it denotes a quality (*guṇa*), as it signifies "shade" or "appearance," which is a quality. Therefore, since all the conditions for *puṃvadbhāva* are met, the transformation into the masculine form *chāya* occurs correctly, and the objection is refuted. Thus, the formation of *śobhanacchāyaḥ* is established.
This [rule] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the short vowel in this context, but it does not apply to the rule *padāntādvā*.

In the case of *dadhi chādayati*, since a consonant is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) when a rule concerning vowels (*svaravidhi*) is to be applied, the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) by the rule *tiṅñatiṅ* could be effected. If this [present rule] were in existence, the purpose of including the mention of *num* in the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* would not be observed.

Bhartṛhari, however, has stated that the mention of *num* was intended for cases where the *nakāra* is not at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in the example *prāhiṇvat*, where there is *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) after *num* following the root *hi* in the *laṅ* tense. Regarding this, he noted that since the governing rule for "the preceding member" (*pūrvapada*) applies only to compounds (*samāsa*), and the technical designations of "prior" and "subsequent" members exist only therein, it was not clarified here how *ṇatva* could occur in this instance. If that were so, then the mention of *num* would indeed be for the sake of forms such as *prahiṇvan*.
It is said:

by the rule *alpāctaram* (the shorter [word] comes first), when the prefixing of *num* was to be applied in rules such as *prātipadikānta*, the fact that he employs the mention of *num* situated between the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the case-ending (*vibhakti*) indicates this:
namely, that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only for that letter *n* of *num* which stands between these two.

In the rule *aṭ-kuh-āṅ-num-vyavāye ’pi*, the author of the Bhāgavṛtti has demonstrated that the absence of *ṇatva* in the word *prenvam*—due to the fact that the *num* augment deviates from its status as a *pūrvānta* (an integral part of the preceding element)—is established either by the indicator (*cihna*) of such deviation or by the rule *kṣubhnādi-gaṇa*. It is similar in that regard. Now, one might object: if *num* is indeed a *pūrvānta* because it is marked with the indicator *mit*, then in the case of *niṣkauśāmvinī kule*, once *num* is applied, the shortening of the neuter vowel (*napuṃsakahrasvatva*) would not apply, because the final vowel would no longer be an *ac* (vowel).
As in the case of *suvāk* [in the compound] *brāhmaṇakulam*.

This is not a fault, because the *num* suffix is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) due to its dependence on a case ending (*vibhakti*), whereas the shortening (*hrasvatva*) is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) since it does not depend on a case ending; therefore, the latter will occur first.
Thus it has been said:
Or rather, it is not so, because [the substitution] is external (bahiraṅga). || 4 ||
These are the substitutes for that which is being specified. || 5 ||

Substitutes occur in place of a whole group or a part thereof that has been specified by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For example, in the rule *pādaḥ pat*, the word *pad* replaces *pādaḥ* precisely where it is specified by the genitive; as in *dvipadaḥ paśya* ("look at the two-footed one"), it does not apply to the whole ending in that [word] due to the technical restriction regarding the governing heading of "stem" (*aṅga-adhikāra-paribhāṣā*).
In the rule *tathā bhavetām*, the substitution of *tām* occurs in place of *tas*, and not of *sayāsuṭ*.

This is like a single part [of a whole]; for example, by the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya*, when a homogeneous vowel with the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇa*) is prescribed for the initial portion of the root *sthā*, it does not apply to the augment *āṭ* in the form *udasthāt*.

Likewise, by the rule "there is vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of *ṣyaṅ*," the absence of vocalization for the *repha* and *vakāra* in the word *vārāhīputra*—where the *ṣyaṅ* suffix has undergone vocalization in part—is explained by this very rule.
This technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is recited for the purpose of [explaining] the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāne yogā* ("the genitive case is used when there is a connection with 'in place of'").
For it is said in the Bhāṣya on that point:

"Even though there are one hundred meanings of the genitive, as many as there are, all of them would apply whenever the genitive is uttered; however, those meanings which consist of proximity, interiority, modification, and so forth..."

But what else could there be for the word other than its place? One might object: "Are not relations such as 'immediacy' (anantara) and so forth also possible for a word? To this we reply: regarding the statement "astebhūrbhavati," there is a doubt as to whether [the substitution] occurs in place (sthāne) or in proximity (samīpe). It cannot be in proximity, because it is impossible for two words with the same meaning to be used in the same location simultaneously.
Furthermore, this is merely a doubt;

for this [principle] applies to all doubts: "A specific understanding arises from an explanation, for there is no non-characteristic due to doubt. We shall explain [the sūtra] as "in the proper place" (*sthāne*).
If that is so, then this rule (*yoga*) need not be stated now.
It must be stated:
what is the purpose of [specifying] the genitive ending so that it may apply in the sense of "in place of"?
It is so that whatever is uttered in the genitive case may be precisely that which is useful for the grammatical operation.
By this, it is established that substitutes (ādeśas) occur for that which is being specified.

This being the case, regarding the rule *śīṅo ruṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.6), what the author of the Nyāsa stated is as follows: "If the augment *ruṭ* were to belong to the phoneme *jha* itself, then the substitute [for *jha*, namely] *ad* would not apply to *jha*; rather, it would apply to that very *ruṭ*, because of the rule *ādeḥ parasya*."

Likewise, regarding what was cited under the rule *maparyantasya*—namely, that *yuvakām* would belong to the form with the *sākacka* [suffix]—this must be resolved by disregarding that [objection]. || 5 ||
The state of having multiple *al* sounds [in a substitute] is not caused by its *anubandha*.
The fact that [the substitute] consists of multiple *al* phonemes due to its suffix (*anubandha*) is not taken into account.
Therefore, in the case of *arvaṇas trasaun añi* (Pāṇini 7.1.95), in forms such as *arvantau* and *arvantaḥ*, the substitution of *tra* occurs only for the final phoneme, not for the entire word.
Some, however, cite *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* as examples.
That is not correct;
for by the rule *diva ut*, only the phoneme *u* is prescribed. To explain:
according to the rule *taparas tatkālasya*, the technical designation *ud* is prescribed specifically for the phoneme *u* alone.
And thus, by this rule *diva ud*, only the phoneme *u* alone is prescribed, not the word *uc*.
This must necessarily be so;
otherwise, what would be the outcome regarding the rule *ato bhisa ais*?
For here, the substitute *at* is not being prescribed; rather, the vowel *a* is indicated as the technical term (*saṃjñin*) by means of the designation *at*.

As for what was stated under the rule *sthāghvoricca*—"and [the substitution of] *i* for which [consonant] is the *t*-ness of the *t*?"—this was said by accepting that parts of the expository statement (*pratipādaka*) possess the status of being parts of the thing to be explained (*pratipādya*). It is precisely according to that view that the *bhāṣya* states regarding the rule *titsvaritam*: "In the expression *tid*, there is the inclusion of the suffix.

However, in the rule *taparastatkālasya*, it is stated that the phoneme (*varṇa*) alone is the technical name-bearer (*saṃjñin*), and not the entire complex (*samudāya*) consisting of the *ta* and the *para*.
And this is logical;
otherwise, by the continued application of the term *svam* (itself) in the rule *taparas tatkālasya*, the substitution *ais* would also occur in the word *bhavadbhiḥ*.
Furthermore, this paribhāṣā applies under the view that "the *anubandhas* are constituent parts."

And the proof for this is the inclusion of the term *śit* in the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya*. If being "multi-alphabetic" (*anekāltva*) were to apply even by virtue of an *anubandha*, then in forms such as *sarve*, the substitution of *jasaḥ* for *śī* would already be established as a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*) simply because it is multi-alphabetic; thus, the mention of *śit* would be redundant. One might object: "In the rule *dhvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca*, it is stated that 'the elision (*lopa*) must be declared as *śit*'. If that *śit* is accepted there, then the mention of *śit* [in the *anekāl-śit* rule] would indeed be for the sake of total replacement. [For example, in the case of *dehi* and *dhehi*, the elision applies to the whole. [Response: No, because the elision there is not a substitute (*ādeśa*). Furthermore, the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) is not a substitute at all. Moreover, since the elision of *dhva* and *s* is taught as *śit*, it follows that the elision of the reduplicated syllable is also intended to be *śit*. Consequently, the mention of *śit* in the *anekāl-śit* rule is not for the purpose of total replacement. Rather, it is for the purpose of excluding the elision of the reduplicated syllable from being a substitute. For if it were a substitute, it would have to be a total replacement, and the elision of the reduplicated syllable would not occur. Therefore, the mention of *śit* serves to indicate that the elision of the reduplicated syllable is not a substitute. Thus, the mention of *śit* in the *anekāl-śit* rule is indeed a proof [that an *anubandha* does not cause a form to be considered multi-alphabetic].
An elision occurs. It is said:
by the very force of the fact that this elision is marked with the ŚIT indicator, it will become a substitute for the whole.
Alternatively, it is unnecessary to state that "the elision of the *śit* [augment] must be prescribed.

By the rule "when [an operation] is meaningless, the substitution does not apply to the final letter," the elision will occur for the entire [root]. As for what is said—that "in that case, [the rule applies] except in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable"—that is not universal, as it depends on the specific nature of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).
Objection: If this technical rule (paribhāṣā) applies, then when there is the suffix *ṇal*, a substitution for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*) would not be obtained.
Response: It is said: this is established by the sequential order [of the rules].
For instance:

when there is a universal substitution (*sarvādeśa*), the letter *ṇ* in the substitute *ṇal* possesses the status of being the beginning of an affix (*pratyayāditva*) due to its being taught [as such]; consequently, by the rule *cuṭū*, it receives the technical designation *it*; and from that, it acquires the status of a marker (*anubandhatva*). Thus, this status of being a marker—which is preceded by the universal substitution—is unable to obstruct the status of being a universal substitute, because the status of being a universal substitute has already been established prior to it. || 6 ||
In a rule based on phonetic form (*varṇāśraya*), the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of a suffix as present) does not apply.

Consequently, in the examples *gave hitam* → *gohitam* and *rāyaḥ kulam* → *raikulam*, the substitutions *ava* and *āya*—which would otherwise be triggered by the condition "after a vowel" (*aci*) due to the presence of the suffix—are not applied.

In the example *lavaṇā yavāgūḥ*, when the suffix *ṭhak* is elided by the rule *lavaṇālluk*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which would otherwise be triggered by the condition "after a stem ending in *ṭhak*" according to the rule *ṭhaṅantāt ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*—does not occur.

The vowel *a* is reiterated there so that the suffix *ṅīp* may be understood as depending solely on the phoneme [itself]. Thus, it is qualified by the markers *ṭ*, *i*, and so forth, but the markers *ṭ*, *i*, and so forth are not qualified by the vowel *a*. For this very reason, the genitive case is employed in the rule *kvarap-khyunām* (Pāṇini 4.2.91).
And this point is established by the second mention of the word *pratyaya* in the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*.
For it is stated there:

although one could simply say *tallakṣaṇam* ("characterized by that"), the fact that *pratyayalakṣaṇam* is said again—whereby the word *pratyaya* is repeated—is so that an operation dependent specifically on a suffix (*pratyaya*) may occur by virtue of the suffix being the defining characteristic, as in the case of *suptiṅantam*.
Regarding the word *pada*, it is stated so that [the rule] should not depend merely on the phonemes *a* and *c*.
And the evidence (*jñāpaka*) for this here is the mention of *śravaṇā* in the rule *śravaṇā-kārttikī-caitrībhyaḥ*, where *śravaṇā* is cited with the suffix *ṭap*.

Objection: If the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the status of being treated as a suffix) does not apply when it depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*), then in the form *atṛṇeḍ*, the augment *im* prescribed by the rule *tṛṇahaim* would not occur, because the introduction of the augment *im* depends upon a consonant (*hal*) and a phoneme (*varṇa*).

Response: This [augment] does not depend on a phoneme; rather, since the context of the *aṅga* (stem) governs the implication of a suffix, it depends on a suffix that begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi-pratyaya*).

This is what is meant: with respect to a suffix (*pratyaya*), there are two kinds of operations—those caused by the suffix itself and those not caused by the suffix. Among these, that which is caused by the suffix should occur precisely through the characteristic of the suffix even when the suffix is elided; it is for this purpose that the second mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is made in the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam*. By this, [the substitution of] *ay*, *av*, and *āv* in the rule *aicoyavāyāvaḥ* is set aside by the paribhāṣā because it depends on the phonemes (*varṇa*). However, as for the augment *im*, since it is caused solely by the suffix—and because the suffix is implied within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the stem (*aṅga*)—what contradiction could there be in its occurrence?
Nor should one suspect the application of *iyaṅ* in the case of *śriyai* (dative singular) or *śryartham* (purpose), where the suffix begins with a vowel;
for there is a prohibition by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*.

As for the fact that the author of the *Nyāsa*, while stating that this [prohibition] is generally applicable (*prāyikatva*) in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, remarked that the augment *im* occurs even when depending on a phoneme—as in *atṛṇeḍ*—[this is merely an observation of usage].
That is another means.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in examples such as *go-hitam*, the rule prescribes *luk* (elision) and not *lopa* (deletion)? If so, there would be no occasion at all for the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an element as if it were present despite its elision); why then resort to this *paribhāṣā*? [Reply: It is said: even when *luk* occurs, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* still applies, because *lopa* has the meaning of "non-appearance" (*adarśana*). Thus, although the suffix is elided by *luk*, it is treated as if it were present for the purposes of grammatical operations.
And the authority for this is the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 1.1.63]: "There is no [substitution] when an element (aṅga) has been elided by 'lu'."
In some cases, even a single part persists.
By the force of the *svarita* accent, sometimes a portion of a sūtra or even a portion of a word is carried over (*anuvartate*).

Therefore, in the rule *dāmahāyanāntācca*, only the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth from the preceding rule *saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ* is carried over. Similarly, in the rule *jhontaḥ*, although the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) from the rule *āyan-nādī-sūtra* has ceased, the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is carried over.

And here there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*): in the rule "tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (P. 1.1.66), since the word *iti* is already present from the preceding sūtra, the word *iti* is used again in "tasmādityuttarasya" (P. 1.1.67).
For if the recurrence of the words were simultaneous [in both rules], then the word *iti*, like the term *nirdiṣṭa*, would have recurred from the previous sūtra;
so what would be the purpose of this [redundant] use?
By doing this, the Teacher makes it known that in some instances even a single portion [of a rule] continues to apply.
For if this were the case, then only the mention of "nirdiṣṭa" (specified) would continue to apply, and not the particle "iti."
When there is the apprehension of meaning, that which is meaningless [is not apprehended].
In the investigation of meaningful versus meaningless [elements], only a word that possesses meaning is to be understood, not one that is meaningless.
Therefore, by the rule *vano ra ca*, the substitution of *r* for the final vowel of *van* occurs only when *van* and *vaniP* are meaningful through their sense of "agent" (*kartṛ*).
Thus, we have *dhīvarī* and *pīvarī*.
Not [the root] *han* when it is meaningless;
for example, in *atiśunī* and *atiyūnī*.
Likewise, in rules such as *inhanpūṣāryamṇām*, there is the inclusion of *han* only when it is meaningful and ends in *kvip*.
Therefore, even in the case of *plīhānau* and *plīhānaḥ*, the long vowel is not excluded by that rule.

Now, one might ask: how can the word *van* be said to be meaningless in examples such as *atiśunī*, given that it possesses meaningfulness both in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*) and through its meaning (*arthena*), just as was stated regarding [the technical term] *vṛddhi* in the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*?

Because the word *vṛddhi* possesses meaning both in its own form and in its referent prior to its connection with the notion (*saṃjñā*) and the object of that notion (*saṃjñin*), it has the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus they have said:
"When a certain word is uttered, whatever meaning is perceived..."
"It is for the sake of bringing that [word] forward that this is the definition of a word, and not something other than the meaning.
For when a word is employed with its own form as its primary object, its own form alone is its meaning, because it is directed toward that [form].
And in cases such as *atiśunī*, the groups of phonemes such as "van" and so on are not directed toward their own forms.

Because they are uttered for the purpose of bringing about a collection such as *atiśūnya*, they possess meaning; for this very reason, it was stated in the *Sūtra* that in examples such as *vanaṃ* and *dhanaṃ*, the final limit (*anta*) consisting of the letter *n* is not meaningless.
However, when words like *vana* in *atiśūnya* and so forth refer to their own phonetic forms (*svarūpa*), then they indeed possess meaning.

In the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, however, there is the inclusion of both types of *iṭ*: the meaningless augment and the meaningful suffix. Regarding the *ṭ* in *iṭo't*, its purpose is to ensure that the term *iṭ* is understood in a general sense in the rules *āto lopa iṭi ca* and *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere*; this was stated by Rakṣita as an explanation of the Bhāṣya commentary on those two rules.
However, in this way, even in the case of *iṭ* (the augment *iṭ*), there would result the inclusion of both the *āgama* (augment) and the *pratyaya* (suffix).

Likewise, in the case of *iṭ-vahi-mahiṅ*, when another phoneme is to be formed for the sake of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference), the employment of the letter *ṅ* would serve not only for the purpose of the *ṅit*-operation, but [would also imply the inclusion of the suffix];
and thus, in the case of *sasraṁsimahi*, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) prescribed by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* would undesirably apply.
This must be resolved.
Puruṣottamadeva, however, has stated that in the rule *dādhāghvadāp*, there is no inclusion of the two meaningless words *dā* and *dhā* which are parts of the verbal roots *dā* and *dhā*;
likewise, in the rule *śe*, there is no inclusion of the meaningless part of a word, namely *kāśe* and *kuśe*.
Others do not accept this [position].

For instance, in the case of *praṇidadāti* and *praṇidhāvati*, even though the designation *ghu* applies, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur by the rule *nergadanada...* because the designation *upasarga* does not apply to the prefix *ni-* with respect to the verbal roots *dā* and *dhā*.
And so says the Bhāṣya:
"And these two [roots] *dā* and *dhā* do not have a connection with an action [when preceded by *ni-*]."
In cases such as *sanimīmāṃsu*, because the term *ghoḥ* refers to the stem (*aṅga*) and because [the suffix] does not begin with the letter *s*, there is no fault in forms such as *didāśiṣati*.

The fact that the designation *pragṛhya* does not apply to the word *śe* in the phrase *kāśe kuśe śe*—because it is a technical term (*lākṣaṇika*)—has been explained by the author of the *Nyāsa* specifically regarding the word *śe*.
Furthermore, this paribhāṣā concerns the domain of rules prescribing a specific form (*svarūpavidhi*).

Because of the inclusion of the term *arthavat* (meaning-bearing) in the rule *arthavad adhātuḥ*, the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) by the rule *āpsupaḥ* is established even for the meaningless prefix *pra-* in the word *pralambate*. This is because meaninglessness, indeclinability (*avyayatva*), and the status of a preposition (*upasargatva*) belong to particles (*nipāta*); and according to the statement that "the operations prescribed for meaning-bearing items apply to meaningless particles as well."

And here, the rule *adhiparī anarthakau* (Pāṇini 1.4.93) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This rule prescribes the designation of "karmapravacanīya" for the particles *adhi* and *pari* when they are meaningless, for the purpose of removing their designation as "upasarga.
For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya—"it must be stated that a particle which is meaningless receives the designation of *prātipadika*"—has been rejected.

If this is so, then since [the word] possesses the status of a particle (*nipāta*), its indeclinability (*avyayatva*) is established by that very force, and consequently, the elision of case-endings (*subluk*) is also accomplished.
This is not so;
for the status of the word as a particle (*nipāta*) is justified merely by its function regarding accentuation.
As for the meaninglessness of the prefix *pra*, that is refuted because its sense of "intensity" (*prakarṣa*) is understood from the context and other factors.

In this case, the absence of case endings due to meaninglessness is not raised as a prima facie objection (pūrvapakṣa), because of the inclusion of the term "nominal stem" (prātipadika) in the rule *prātipadikārtha-*. For that [inclusion] has this purpose: so that the nominative case may occur even from a mere nominal stem that is devoid of meaning.
And this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) was indicated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *svaṃ rūpam*.
For it is stated there: "The mention of *rūpa* (form) need not be made.
If it were simply said *svaṃ śabdasya* (the [thing] belonging to the word itself), although both the form and the meaning of the word would be 'its own' (*svam*)."
Nevertheless, it is the form alone that is apprehended, not the object;
for when a word is uttered, there is first the cognition of its form, and from that, the cognition of the object.
Likewise, at the time of imitation, the word abandons its meaning but not its form.

Thus, because the word is so closely proximate to the intellect, and because it is eternally connected as something not to be discarded, it is the form (*rūpa*) alone of the word that is to be grasped, and not the meaning, for the opposite is the case.

Therefore, since the grasping of the form is already established by the very mention of "its own" (*svam*), it follows that in the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), the meaning is accepted just like the form.
Alternatively, the mention of *bhrāj* in the rule *vraścādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its existence [as a meaningful element].

For if there were a mention of even that which is meaningless, then since the mention of *rāj* alone would suffice for the inclusion of even a portion of *bhrāj*, he would not have mentioned *bhrāj* in the form *rājabhrāj*.
Since it has been mentioned, this serves as an indicator that only that which possesses meaning is included, and not that which is meaningless. 9.
Not in the case of the perceptions of color. || 10 ||
This is a refutation of the previous [position].
The "phonemes" (varṇa) are [those beginning with] the letter 'a' and so forth.
When these are being apprehended, the paribhāṣā regarding meaning and form does not apply.

Just as by the rule *yatheko yaṇ aci*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs for the meaningless *ik* even when followed by a meaningless vowel— as in *bhavaty atra bhavatu*— otherwise, the *yaṇ* would occur for the meaningful *ik* related to suffixes such as *ṅīp* only when followed by a meaningful vowel, as in *kumāryau* and *aśvaśvau*. Similarly, by the rule *asya ghu au*, it occurs even for the meaningless [stem] *as*.

In the rule *śklīkaroti*, otherwise there would be [the application of] the letter *ā* which denotes Viṣṇu only when it possesses meaning. Regarding the inquiry as to whether this collection of letters *ig* in the rule *iko jhal* should be understood as a meaningful pratyāhāra or as a meaningless verbal root (*dhātu*), it was rightly stated by Rakṣita that the pratyāhāra is to be accepted by means of the *arthavat-paribhāṣā*.
For when withdrawal is established, the apprehension of phonemes occurs at a subsequent time, and not from the very beginning.

Now, if the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* does not apply to the perception of individual phonemes (*varṇa*), how then can the author of the Nyāsa raise the doubt regarding the inclusion of the meaningful *iṭ* in the rule *vija iṭ*? Likewise, how can the inclusion of the meaningful *iṭ* be asserted in the rule *iṭota*?
Furthermore, once the augment *sīyuṭ* has been applied, how can the mere *iṭ* possess meaning, given that only the *iṭ* together with *sīyuṭ* is meaningful?
Just as it was stated that [the rule] "they might split" (*bhindyuḥ*) is purposeless here,

how can the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a meaningful element is significant) be invoked regarding the mention of *iṭ*, when it has been stated under the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* that the addition of the marker *ṭ* in *iḍ-vahimahiṅ* is for the sake of including both suffixes and augments when the marker *ṭ* is to be applied?
Thus, it must be by means of the apprehension of the universal alone.
It is said: as for what was stated—that this is the apprehension of the phoneme (varṇa)—[it is not so].
That is not so;
for where a grammatical operation is prescribed after pronouncing an *anubandha* (indicatory letter), there the prohibition based on the phoneme (*varṇa*) does not apply.

And here, in the rule *graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ*, when the augment *īṭ*—which is an exception to *iṭ*—is to be applied in the form *agrahīt*, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) was made for the purpose of deleting the suffix *sic* by the rule *iṭa īṭi*. This [mention of "long"] is performed by means of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
This [rule] is a general indicator (*sāmānyajñāpaka*).

Therefore, where there is the employment of an *anubandha* (indicatory letter), this rule does not apply to the inclusion of phonemes (*varṇagrahaṇa*). If that is so, then in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* as well, because of the employment of an *anubandha*, this [general indicator] should not apply.
This is not the case;

because the letters beginning with *ka* function as markers for the entire group (*samudāya-anubandha*), there is no inclusion of the letters beginning with *i* along with their respective markers (*sānubandha*).
It is not accepted that markers belonging to a whole group can simultaneously function as markers for its individual parts.

By including the letter *ṅ* in the rule *karmaṇi iṅ*, a *saṅ* abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) is formed; thus, although one might have stated "roots ending in *saṅ*," the statement "roots ending in *san* and so forth" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, in the form *na sasraṃsimahi*, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) occurs. However, in the case of *kurute*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) arises because of the *ñit* designation. Furthermore, regarding the rule *anuparābhyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.78), which follows immediately after the rule on *gandhana* and so forth, the fact that it is formulated as *anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ*—rather than simply *anuparābhyām*—is intended to indicate that the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* (Pāṇini 1.3.72) also applies here.
This is for the purpose of making it known that a prohibition occurs.
Thus, although the *ñ* of *kṛñ* is a marker (*anubandha*) of the entire complex, it is also a marker of its constituent part.

As for the objection raised regarding the rule *svādibhyaḥ*—that when *auḍas* is applied, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) would occur due to the presence of the marker *ḍ*, resulting in a fault—that [objection] is addressed as follows.
This should be understood by accepting that the rule *so'nuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ* serves as a general indicator (*sāmānyajñāpaka*).
Furthermore, as for what was said— that only the form with the augment (*sāgamaka*) possesses meaning while the mere root *iṇ* is meaningless—
that too is not correct.

This is because it is accepted that the *āgamas* (augmentative elements), being subordinate to those [roots or stems] to which they belong, are included by the mention of those very roots or stems according to the order of grammatical derivation (*prakriyākrama*).
However, in the context of the *Bhindyuḥ* rule, it is accepted that for those [bases] which lack an *āgama*, substitutes (*ādeśas*) that possess an *āgama* occur.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—that when a *ṭh*-ending suffix is to be applied, there is a general inclusion due to its *ṭit*-character, and so forth—[that too is addressed].
That too is not correct;
for it is stated that the mention of suffixes and augments [occurs] by virtue of an indicator (jñāpaka) only when there is a purpose [for doing so].
In the rule *vija iṭ*, there is no purpose whatsoever for the indicatory letter *ṅ* (*ṅittva*) in the augment.
Because the *guṇa* vowel does not have that [the augment] as its cause;
and since in the rule "iṭot" (Pāṇini 7.2.35), the substitution of *ad* is prescribed for the *iṭ* that is topical to the context, how could there be any suspicion of the application of an augment?
And the evidence for this is the rule *uñaḥ*.

If the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a grammatical operation applies only to meaningful elements) were to apply even in the case of the mention of a phoneme (*varṇa*), then in the example *u iti*, where the *it* sound in the word *iti* is meaningless, the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur by virtue of the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* alone; thus, the designation of *pragṛhya* for *uñaḥ* would not have been formulated.
And because it has been done, this serves as an indicator.
Alternatively, the rule "mixing with food" (Pāṇini 2.1.34) serves as an indicator (jñāpaka) for this [interpretation]. 10.
When it is being pronounced, the short vowel *a* does not include its homogeneous counterparts.
An *aṇ* vowel being prescribed as a substitute does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*).
Consequently, in the case of *itidam*, the rule *iś* does not result in a three-moraic substitute for the three-moraic original (*sthānin*), due to the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*).
Likewise, in *he anaḍvan*, the rule *aṃ-sambuddhau* does not result in a long vowel.

Regarding the form *lavitā* in the expression *lavitum*, they say that because the rule *vṛto vā* prescribes the optional lengthening of the augment *iṭ*, this *iṭ* does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*sarvarṇagrahaṇa*).
And this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is stated as the very meaning of the term *apratyaya* in the rule *aṇuditsarvasya cāpratyayaḥ*.
For it is thus:
that which is made known, enjoined, or brought about is a *pratyaya*; that which is not a *pratyaya* is an *apratyaya*.

The meaning is "not being taught" (*abhāvyamāna*). In this context, the rule that the suffix *aṇ* includes all homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*) stands clearly established as: "an *aṇ* being taught does not include its homogeneous counterparts."
Some state that even an indicator (*jñāpaka*) exists for the sake of easy comprehension:
namely, the prescription of the long *ī* in the rule *ī haly-aghoh*. Otherwise, in place of the long vowel, by virtue of being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*), only a long vowel would have occurred.
This technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) is not eternal;
therefore, in the rule *amū* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), the long vowel *o* (which consists of two morae) becomes the long vowel *u* (also consisting of two morae).
Regarding this point, the inclusion of the *tapara* marker in the rule *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

If an *aṇ* vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) were never to include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), then in the case of *dyubhyām*, even after applying the rule *chroḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* to change the *ū* to *ūṭh*, a short vowel would be established in place of the long one;
what then would be the purpose of employing the *tapara* (the *a* with the *p* marker)?
Its employment indicates that in certain instances, an *aṇ* vowel being taught does include its homogeneous counterparts.
Alternatively, the use of the long vowel marker *ā* (tapara) in the rule *śāsa idaṅ haloḥ* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). || 11 ||
When a rule is prescribed concerning a specific element, that element is understood to include its initial portion as well.
In a rule where a vowel (*al*) is mentioned in the locative case, that operation applies to a group beginning with that [vowel], not to one ending with it.

Therefore, in the case of *pibate* and *apape*, the substitution of *piba-* [for *pā-*] does not occur by virtue of the rule *pā-ghrā-dhā-pā-jighra-dhamati-dheg-hi-jakṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.78). Likewise, by the rule *aci* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occur before vowel-initial suffixes, as in *śriyo* and *luluvatu-luluvuḥ*.
In the case of *śriyau luluvaḥ* as well, this is because of the treatment as if it possessed a designation (*vyapadeśavadbhāvāt*).

For if there were the rule of extension to that which ends in such [a suffix] (*tadantavidhi*) here, then in *śriyo luluvatuḥ*, it would not apply, because [the stem] ends in a consonant (*halantatvāt*).

And this is the meaning: since a rule in the Sūtra that prescribes [an element] after something (tadanta-vidhi) is supplemented by a rule prescribing it before that (tadādi-vidhi) in the form of a metarule (paribhāṣā), it is established as such.
According to Vāmana, however, this [vṛddhi] is described on account of the inclusion of the term *apṛkta* in the rule *guṇo'pṛktaḥ*.
As it has been said:

while the rule *uto vṛddhir luki halī* continues to apply, when a *guṇa* would otherwise be required before a consonant-initial suffix, the inclusion of the term *apṛkta*—being made for the purpose that it should occur only before a simple consonant (*hal-mātra*) and not before a consonant-cluster (*hal-ādi*)—indicates that this [vṛddhi] exists.
The metarule states: "A rule [applies] where [a condition] is specified," and so forth.

By this, if the term *hal* were continued [from a previous sūtra], the operation would apply only when preceded by a consonant (*hal*). However, because of the inclusion of the term *apṛkta*, it occurs even before a mere phoneme (*varṇa*), as in *praurṇot*.

If this were so, then the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution would occur only when a suffix beginning with *k* or *ṅ* follows— as in *gṛhītaḥ* and *gṛhītiḥ*— but it would not occur when a suffix beginning with *ya* follows, as in *gṛhyate*. To this, it is replied:

The rule "before *kṅit*" does not refer to individual phonemes (*varṇa*), because by the bahuvrīhi compound "*kṅitau yasya*" ("that which has *k* and *ṅ* as its [final] elements"), a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamudāya*) is understood.
When the three—vidhi, vidhāna, and vidhibhāj—are present together, the rule of "ending with that" (tadantavidhi) applies. || 13 ||
By that [rule], *erac*—meaning the suffix *at* occurs after a word ending in the vowel *i*—is established.
This is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) by which the meaning obtained through the very force (*sāmarthya*) of a rule (*vidhisūtra*) is expressed.
For instance:
The instrumental case in *yena* denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). Since there can be no instrument without an agent (*kartṛ*), an agent is also implied.
Furthermore, because it is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*) used here with the word *anta*, which signifies a part (*avayava*), it is understood as the whole (*samudāya*).
And that agent is brought into proximity in three ways.

In some cases, it is due to explicit mention (*nirdeśa*); for example, in the rule *īdūdeddvivacanam*, the dual number (*dvivacanam*) is mentioned as the agent (*kartṛ*), which then prescribes the designation *pragṛhya* by means of the instruments (*karaṇa*) consisting of *ī*, *ū*, and *e*. In other cases, it is due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Just as in the rule *erac*, because of the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the term "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), the verbal root is brought to mind as the agent (*kartṛ*); that [root] prescribes the suffix *ac* by means of the letter *i* as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
In some cases, this occurs through semantic implication (*sāmarthya*).

For example, in the rule *iko jhal*, since the suffix *san* is prescribed only after a verbal root, the verbal root is brought to mind as the agent by virtue of that implication; then, by means of the letter *i* as the instrument, it prescribes the *kit*-status of *san*.

Thus, in rules such as *īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, since there exists a possibility of a *karman* (the object) being prescribed by the rule that ordains the *pragṛhya* designation, a *karaṇa* (the instrument) consisting of the vowels *ī*, *ū*, and *e*, and a *kartṛ* (the agent) consisting of the "dual ending" (*dvivacana*) which possesses the rule,
the *tadantavidhi* (the principle that a grammatical operation applies to that which ends with the specified element) is established by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*.

Consequently, this very meaning of the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya* is that when these three— the rule (*vidhi*), the prescription (*vidhāna*), and the possessor of the prescription (*vidhibhāj*)— are in proximity, the *tadantavidhi* occurs.
In rules such as *eco'yavāyāvaḥ*, [the rule] does not apply because that which is subject to the operation (*vidhibhāj*) is impossible.

Now, one might object: since this is a treatise on the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*), the word-form itself must be the agent (*kartṛ*) subject to the operation; so how can it be said that there is an absence of an agent? It is replied:

Rakṣita has explained in his commentary on the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* that the form of the word (*śabdarūpa*) is not accepted as the agent [of substitution] because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Consequently, in rules such as *aicoyavāyāvaḥ*, since the form of the word is not accepted, the status of being the substitute (*sthānitva*) belongs to the mere vowel (*ac*) alone, and the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) belongs to the mere consonant (*aj*) alone; thus, the condition is "when a vowel beginning with *a* follows a stem ending in *ai*, *o*, or *au*.

If that [form of the word] were the agent of substitution, then in examples such as *vṛkṣāv atra*, the substitutes *āva* and so forth would be replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), because they consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāltvāt*).

"Is it not the case that substitutes occur for what is being specifically indicated (*nirddiśyamāna*), so that the substitute must apply only to the locative form ending in *-e*, and not to the one ending in *-ai*?
True, this is so with respect to the individual instance (*vyakti*); however, there is a fault with respect to the universal (*jāti*).
But another says:"
There would be no rule for individual phonemes (*varṇavidhi*) among the rules concerning phonemes (*alvidhi*).
Thus, as stated by the author of the *Bhāgavṛtti* regarding the rule *iko yaṇ aci*:

since the whole (*samudāya*) is brought to mind by means of its parts—the *ik* and the vowel (*ac*)—the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply to that which ends in an *ik* when followed by a vowel-initial [suffix], and thus there would be no rule for individual phonemes at all. Let [this matter] rest; eat curd! (*tiṣṭhatu dadhyaśāna tvam*).

Regarding the example "śākena": however, when a substitution of *yaṇ* occurs for a stem ending in a vowel before an initial vowel, it certainly does not constitute a *pada-vidhi* (a rule concerning words), because operations such as the substitution of *ṣatva* are prescribed by means of the non-enunciation of [the technical term] *pada*, such as in the rules *padāt* and *sup-supā*.
