For those things taught as being in a single yoga, there is either simultaneous occurrence or simultaneous cessation.
For words taught as being in a single connection, their application or their cessation must occur simultaneously;
it is not the case that one is applied while the other is ceased.
Therefore, in the rule "uca," everything from "liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu" is understood to apply.
Thus, the meaning is this:
the affixes *liṅ* and *sic* following a verbal root ending in an *ṛ*-vowel become *kit* when the *ātmanepada* endings are used.
For in that context, the root ending in the vowel *ṛ* is intended by the term *ṛ*, and not the root *ṛ* in the sense of "to go.
Regarding this, the author of the Nyāsa states the reason:
it is the style of the Teacher that wherever he intends to include this particular root, he invariably provides its citation with the suffix *śtip*.
As in the rule *yathā’rttipiparttyīśca sarttiśāstyarttibhyaśca*.
And here, in the Nyāsa commentary, the phrase "for the purpose of resolving doubt" (*sandehavicchedāya*) is to be supplied.
By this, the meaning is as follows:
Where he intends to include this verbal root (dhātu), he necessarily provides an indication by means of the *śtip* affix (*ti*) for the purpose of eliminating doubt;
where there is no doubt, he may or may not provide such an indication.
Thus, in the rule *smi-pūṅ-rañja-aśāṃ sani*, even though there is the inclusion of the root *ṛ* meaning "to go," there is no indication by means of *śtip*.
For in that regard, in the rule *kiraśca pañcabhyaḥ*, there is no doubt because of the inclusion of *dṛṅ* and *dhṛṅ*;

otherwise, since the augment *iṭ* would already be established for forms such as *didiriṣate* and *didhariṣate* by the rule *smipūṅrañjaśāṃ sani*, the inclusion of *dṛṅ* and *dhṛṅ* would be purposeless.
As for what was stated there by Rakṣita:
The phrase "for the purpose of resolving doubt" (*saṃdehavicchedāya*) is to be supplied here;
consequently, there is no contradiction with the rule *śmi-pūṅ-rañja-vaśāṃ sani*.
Furthermore, in the rule *kiraśca pañcabhyaḥ*, the very inclusion of the root *kṛ* (as opposed to *kṛi*) is the cause for the exclusion [of the augment *iṭ*].
That is incorrect;

for since the phrase "or after *vṛ*" is carried over [from the previous rule], and since an augment *iṭ* would already be optionally applicable by the rule "an *iṭ* is optional after *san*," the mention of *kṛ* and *gṝ* would be intended to prescribe the *iṭ* as mandatory.
It is replied:

If the inclusion of *kṝ* and *gṝ* were intended for the purpose of prescribing [the augment *iṭ*] as a permanent rule, then one would not have formulated the rule *kiraśca pañcabhyaḥ*, but rather would have formulated it as *smipūṅrañjvaśkṛgṛpracchāṃ sani*.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that the mention of "five" (*pañcabhyaḥ*) serves no purpose in the subsequent rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*;
for in that case, a *vṛt*-marking (a boundary marker) must be made to include the five roots beginning with *rud*, and from that alone the restriction will be established.

Alternatively, this term *kṛgṛsvīkāra* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is the acceptance (*svīkāra*) of *kṛ* and *gṛ*. The phrase *kiraśca pañcabhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.75) is included within that very rule *kṛgṛsvīkāraḥ*; the inclusion of *dṛṅ* and *dhṛñ* therein is the cause for the interruption [of the application of the rule].

Or else, in the rule *smipūṅrañjaśāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 7.2.74), the mention of *ṛ* does not serve the purpose of including roots ending in a short vowel, because *dṛṅ* and *dhṛṅ* are specifically mentioned [therein].

If there were an option for the augment *iṭ* even after a long vowel by the rule "iṭ sani vā," then [the mention of the root] *dīrgha* would be unnecessary, because a constant rule (*nitya*) and an optional rule (*vikalpa*) are mutually contradictory. Thus, the mention of *ṛ* [in the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ*] would be purposeless; therefore, in the rule "iṭ sani vā," the mention of *ṛ* does not carry over, but only *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* do. The option for *iṭ* applies only to *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, whereas for roots ending in *ṛ* (such as *smi*, *pūṅ*, *añj*, and *vaś*), the *iṭ* is established as constant by the rule "sani. Consequently, the mention of *kṛ* and *gṛ* alone is the cause for the interruption [of the previous context].
And the evidence for this here is the mention of *sij* in the rule *hanaḥ sic*.

If it were the case that only one [term] from among two words specified in a single sūtra is carried forward (anuvartate) and not the other, then the mention of *liṅ* would not be carried forward from the rule *liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu*, and only the mention of *sij* would be carried forward;
consequently, the mention of *sij* would be purposeless.
And this meaning, obtained through the force of the svarita accent, is recited in the form of a paribhāṣā.
For this very reason, although the term *it* is carried over from the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsika it* to the rule *laśakvataddhite*, the term *anunāsika* is not carried over.
There is indeed a dispute between Rakṣita and Anunyāsakāra regarding the acceptance and adherence to the oral instruction (*upadeśa*). To illustrate:

in the *gāṅkuṭādi* rule, the author of the *Anunyāsa* stated that the mention of *it* (the marker *it*) is redundant under the theory of substitution (*ādeśapakṣa*), because the designation *it* is already established for the initial [element] by the rule *laśakvataddhite*. And so forth.

Rakṣita, however, has stated that since the term *upadeśa* (original enunciation) is understood to carry over into the rule *laśakvataddhite*, the fact that the letter *ṅ* is the first [of the pratyāhāra] does not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the absence of the substitution of *im* in the case of *asati* (the feminine suffix *ṭāp*), because [in that context] it would not be designated by the technical term *it*.
In this regard, Rakṣita’s intention is as follows:
if the governing heading *upadeśa* were absent in the rule *laśakvataddhite*, then in the formation of the locative plural of *niś*—namely *nicchu*—the letter *ś* would incur the designation *it*.
If [the rule] were not to be considered asiddha when the designation *it* is to be applied,
then— given that the *u* in *sasajuṣo ruḥ* has the force of a formal declaration (*pratijñāna*) regarding the nasal quality (*anunāsikya*) of the *r*,
and given the citation *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*— it would have been made known that the status of being *asiddha* does not apply generally when the designation *it* is to be applied.

Likewise, in the case of *bhiyaḥ kruklukanau* (Pāṇini 3.2.174), where *bholuka* is derived from *klukana* after the elision of the letter *k*, the letter *l* would [otherwise] receive the designation *it*.
This is not so;
because there is no purpose for it, the designation *it* does not apply.

But accent (*svara*) is not the purpose [of the rule], because that is already established by the fact of its being marked with an *n* (*nittva*). If that is so, then accent is the purpose in cases such as *bebhīluka* in the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*);
for instance: [text continues].
"Because it has the designation *lit*, the vowel *e* becomes acute; because it has the designation *lit*, the vowel *ī* would [also] occur.
This is the intention of the author of the *Anunyāsa*:
that in the rule *nicśvi*, the designation *it* will not apply because [the preceding rule] is considered as if unestablished (*asiddha*).

As for what was stated— that because of the commitment to the nasal quality (*anunāsikatva*) of the letter *roru* and because of the technical designation (*nirdeśa*) as *liṅkṣu*, there is no status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*)—

that [non-establishment] does not occur precisely when the two rules, "the nasal [consonant] in the *upadeśa* is *it*" (*upadeśe 'janunāsika it*) and "the final [consonant] is *it*" (*halantyam*), are to be applied, since it is only in that context that the possibility of such a proof exists.
In other cases, however, there would simply be the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*).
Regarding the form *bebīluka*, since the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*), the designation *it* will not apply to the *l*.

Alternatively, if the *l* were designated as *it*, then after the substitution of *yaṇ*, the form would be *bebhyuka*; since this contains only a single *aj* vowel, where would the accent (*lit-svara*) apply?

By the rule *nicśviti*, the letter *ja* replaces the letter *śa* due to *jaś*-hood (*jaśtva*), and the letter *śa* replaces the letter *sa* due to *ścutva*. Furthermore, by the rule *svari ca*, the letter *ca* replaces the letter *ja* due to *cartva*.

Now, one might object: in the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*, it was stated by Rakṣita that the letter *śa* does not possess *jaś*-hood, because of the technical indication (*nirdeśa*) in the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*.

For this very reason, in the rule *masjinaśorjhali*, the letter *da* replaces the letter *sa* by *jaś*-hood for the sake of deriving the form *majjati*; and since there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*) due to the technical indication *bhṛjjati*, the letter *ja* is substituted by *ścutva* in the *Nyāsa*.
It has been stated:

otherwise, if the *sakāra* were changed to *śakāra* by the rule for *ścutva*, and then that *śakāra* were changed to *jakāra* by the rule for *jaśtva*, the resulting form would be established as *bhṛjjati*. In that case, it would be improper to argue that [the change] does not apply because [the former rule] is not yet established (*asiddha*). And so, how could the *śakāra* here be changed to *jakāra* by the rule for *jaśtva*?
It is said:

since in the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* there is no substitution of a *jaś* sound for the letter *ś* when followed by a *ca*-class consonant, and because of the homogeneity [of the cases], there is likewise no substitution of a *jaś* sound for a *ś* followed by a *ca*-class consonant elsewhere; thus, that which is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) applies only in that specific instance and not everywhere. Or, [it may be argued] that it is established by an indicator in some way, but not universally.
The *uṇādi* suffixes form underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
They say that this point is established as true because the Sūtra was composed with purpose;

otherwise, since all *uṇādi* derivatives are formed from verbal roots and thus possess the designation of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) by virtue of being *kṛt*-suffix formations, he would not have formulated that rule.
Others, however, maintain that these [words] are included because the term *kaṃsa* is mentioned in the rule *ataḥ kṛkami*, following the inclusion of the root *kam*.

By the rule *tena kṛgṛkuṭividibhidibhyaśca iḥ kit*, the suffix *i* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *gṛ*, *kuṭi*, *vidi*, and *bhid*. Thus, for the words *kiri* and *giri* ending in the suffix *i*, when the *yaṇ* substitution occurs in the nominative case (*osi*), the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *dhali ca* does not take place because they no longer possess the status of verbal roots (dhātu). This results in the forms *kiryoh* and *giryoh*.
However, this is not correct.

Because of the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the preceding element is treated as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), and thus the occurrence of lengthening is not applicable. Nor is there a case where [the *sthānivadbhāva*] does not apply with respect to the prescription of lengthening;

for there is the specific statement: "In the cases of vowel-change (*svara*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), a substitute for an elided letter (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as if it were the original."
As in the example *pratidīvna*.

If that is the case, then from the root *jṛ* (to age), by applying the suffix *krin* according to the rule *jīryater dhātoḥ jīryateḥ krin raśca vaḥ*, and after the substitution of *it* and the replacement of the vowel with *ra* (*raparatva*), when the letter *ra* is changed to *va*, the form becomes *jivri*. Since this is no longer a verbal root (*dhātu*), the long vowel [of the penultimate] does not apply;
for every *dvandva* compound is optionally singular. 16.

Therefore, the forms *bābhravāś ca śālaṅkāyanāś ca* (the Bābhravas and the Śālaṅkāyanas) and *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanam* (the Bābhrava-Śālaṅkāyana group), as well as *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanāḥ*, are justified through both the singular and the plural.

If this were the case, then even in a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*), the dual would result in forms such as *vāktvacam* (speech and skin) or *śrīsrajam* (fortune and garland); likewise, in the alternative case of a copulative compound (*itaretarayogadvandva*), the singular would also occur.
To this it is replied:

By the rule *sarvo dvandvaḥ*, both the collective (*samāhāra*) dvandva and the distributive (*itaretara-yoga*) dvandva are not prescribed as optional singulars (*vibhāṣaikavat*) for the first time; rather, what is already established by logic is restated.

For instance, by the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ*, a dvandva is formed in the sense of *ca* ("and"); and since the sense of *ca* is distributive conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*), when that [conjunction] possesses a predominance of distinct members, then, following those distinct members, dual and plural endings occur.

When, however, the parts are already established as accomplished and there is an intention to express them as concealed—meaning that the collection (*saṃhati*) is primary—then it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*). In that case, because the collection is primary, the singular number is used.
Thus, it is recited as a metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "In the sense of *ca*, every *dvandva* optionally becomes a singular.
Now, one might object: the meaning of *ca* is conjunction (*samuccaya*), not mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*).
Because when the word "ca" (and) is employed, only conjunction (samuccaya) is perceived.
This is true;
however, mutual connection (itaretarayoga) is merely a specific variety of that [conjunction], and not [the same as] conjunction and the others.
For instance: when there is a collection (*samuccaya*) of words that denote objects simultaneously and which are mutually dependent, then a *dvandva* compound is formed.
It is by this much alone that the meaning of "mutual conjunction" (*itaretarayoga*) is said to be the very sense of the particle *ca*.

Now, if this entire category of *dvandva* compounds and so forth indeed has such a meaning, for what purpose then does the author of the *Nyāsa* state that the inclusion of the plural number in the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ* is for the sake of an *jñāpaka* (indicatory hint)? [He says:
"Tiṣya is one and Punarvasū are two; because of this plurality, the plural form is already established. There is no possibility at all for the singular number.
Since the dual will occur whenever there is the possibility of the plural, what is the use of this mention of the plural?"
This indicates that it has been established:
this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) beginning with "every *dvandva* compound," and so forth, exists. It is replied:
It makes known and brings about understanding; it is a "maker known" (*jñāpaka*) and a "bringer of understanding" (*bodhaka*).
Of what is it the bringer of understanding?
Of the intended rule.
Where is the intended restriction?

It is in the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām*, where it is understood that for members of living beings, musical instruments, and armies, the compound is only a collective (*samāhāra*). For if the reverse restriction were applied—that only members of living beings and so forth form a collective compound and not others—then the *dvandva* compound of Tiṣya and Punarvasu would always be only an associative (*itaretarayoga*) compound and never a collective one.

And thus, since there would be the contingency of only the plural number (rather than the dual), the mention of the plural (*bahuvacana*) would be purposeless. Furthermore, this has been explained by the commentator Rakṣita in the passage beginning with "because of the mention of the plural in the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvornakṣatradvandve bahuvacanasya*," [showing that] in the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇitūrya*, a contrary restriction— that the collective compound (*samāhāra*) applies only to parts of living beings and so forth— is not accepted.
But surely, in that case, the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇitūrya* would be purposeless;
for by that rule, the singular form is prescribed only for a collective compound (*samāhāra*).
In that instance, since the collective dual-compound (*samāhāradvandva*) is already singular, the use of the singular number is already established.
It is said:
the purpose of the rule is that for members of animal bodies and the like, the *dvandva* compound should be only a collective (*samāhāra*) and not a copulative (*itaretarayoga*).
Now, one might ask: for what reason is the singular number applied to the collective, rather than applying the singular form directly to the copulative itself?

In this way, the inclusion of a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) would not need to be established through special effort, and the rule would operate solely by way of a positive injunction (*vidhi*).
It is replied:

if there were a single-remainder formation (*ekavadbhāva*) only for the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), then in the case of *asthitvacam*, the suffix *ṭac*—which is the characteristic mark of a collective compound according to the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in *cu*, *ṣ*, or *ha*, [the suffix *ṭac* is added] when it denotes a collection"—would have to apply.
But even so, according to the method previously stated, the singular number occurs only for a collective compound (*samāhāra*), and the collective compound itself is indeed one.
And thus, the suffix *-vat* in the term *ekavad* (as if one) is not justified, for that which is already one cannot be "as if one.
It is replied:
The suffix *vat* will occur by superimposing multiplicity upon [the object] through the intellect (*buddhi*).
And it has been said:
"For the Blessed Intellect produces differentiation even where there is no difference."
As in the expression "the head of Rāhu.
Alternatively, this is not the suffix *vat*; rather, it is the suffix *vijant* (from the root *vad*), which functions as a singular. [Objection:
Even so, since singularity is not prescribed for every *dvandva*, the meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) would be untenable.
It is said:
what is the meaning of "every dvandva"? The meaning is that it consists of either *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) or *samāhāra* (aggregation).
[Objection: Even so, the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛgādi* (Pāṇini 2.4.12) would be redundant;
for by this very paribhāṣā, forms such as *plakṣanyagrodham*, *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ*—just like *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanam*, *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanāḥ*—would already be established.
[Reply: It is said in response:

Since the status of being a singular entity for *vṛkṣa* and so forth has already been established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*), the present rule prescribing optionality (*vibhāṣā*) serves to exclude confusion; it ensures that a *dvandva* compound of these words occurs as a singular only with members of the same class (*sajātīya*), and not with those of different classes (*vijātīya*).
Consequently, a *dvandva* of *paśu* and so forth with members of different classes does not become a singular; rather, such a *dvandva* is one of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
And so says Bhaṭṭi:
"Of men, monkeys, and rakṣasas. (16)
Thus ends the second pāda, concerning the roots *gāṅ* and those beginning with *kuṭ*, in the commentary on the Paribhāṣās composed by the Great Professor Sīradeva.
An *ūdit* [vowel] includes its homogeneous counterparts, but not every homogeneous sound.

The rule *udidvarṇo’ṇuditsavarṇasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.69) indicates that [an *aṇ* vowel] grasps only that which is its *savarṇa* as qualified by both place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*), not merely anything that is a *savarṇa*.
Consequently, in the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30), the mention of *ku* does not include the letter *ha*.
And the indicator (*jñāpaka*) here is the inclusion of the letter *s* [in Pāṇini’s rule], made by including the term *tu* in the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*.
This meaning is indeed established by logic alone; it is stated by means of an indicator merely for the sake of easy comprehension.
To explain:

Since the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneity) is prescribed based on similarity in both place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*), and since there is no homogeneity between the dental stop *t* and the sibilant *s* precisely because of a difference in their efforts, how can that [the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam*] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?
For it is precisely because homogeneity arises from similarity in both place and effort that the author of the *Vṛtti* stated regarding the sūtra *aiuṇ*:
"The short *a*-sound is contracted (*saṃvṛta*) in actual usage."
However, the long and protracted vowels possess a wide articulation (*vivṛtatva*).
It is declared that in this treatise, the vowel *a* is here asserted to be wide-open for the sake of establishing their homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*).
Regarding this, the author of the Nyāsa has stated:

It should be understood that [the vowel *a*] is asserted to be more open (*vivṛtatara*). However, it has been stated by the author of the *Anunyāsa* that it should be understood as being asserted to be most open (*vivṛtatama*).
Otherwise, because the vowel *ā* is most open, there would be no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) even if the vowel *a* were asserted to be merely more open.
Because their efforts [of articulation] are unequal;
for there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) at all among those whose efforts are unequal.
Thus, in the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the author of the Bhāṣya stated that the letter *ś* lacks the status of being a vowel (*actva*) precisely because of its lack of homogeneity with other vowels.

The articulatory effort (*karaṇa*) for the consonants (*sparśa*) is *spṛṣṭa* (contact); for the semivowels (*antasthā*), it is *īṣatspṛṣṭa* (slight contact); and for the sibilants (*uṣman*), the articulatory effort is *vivṛta* (open).
The word "īṣat" (slightly) is understood [from the previous rule]; "of vowels" (*svarāṇām*) is also [understood]; "openly" (*vivṛtam*) is understood; and "slightly" (*īṣat*) is excluded.

By this, it is stated that there is an absence of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between the vowels *e* and *ai* and the consonants *ś* and *ṣ*, because the former are *vivṛta* (open) while the latter are *īṣadvivṛta* (slightly open).
And thus, the purpose of the rule *nāj-jhalau* ("a vowel and a consonant cannot coalesce") is also not observed;
for in examples such as *dadhi śītam*, there is an absence of *sāvarṇya* precisely because of the difference in their qualities (*guṇa*), namely, being deficient or excessive [in openness].
Furthermore, the absence of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between vowels possessing fewer or more constituent elements must necessarily be admitted.
Otherwise, in rules such as *eṅaḥ padāntādati*, because of the homogeneity between *e* and *ai*, or *o* and *au*, there would be the inclusion of *aikāra* and *aukāra* as well.
However, Rakṣita has stated that in the rule *eṅaḥ*, the absence of homogeneity is established by the force of employing the *praśleṣa* (insertion of an extra letter) with the *ṅ* in *eoṅ*.

Otherwise, if the inclusion of *ai* and *au* were intended, he would have used the letter *c* in the term *eca* to form a *pratyāhāra*. However, if it were so, there would be homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the actual phonetic forms of *ai* and *au* wherever they are employed as such— for instance, in the rule *īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*.
In this context, if the long *ai* were included by the short *e*, then due to the absence of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), the designation of *pragṛhya* would also apply in cases such as *karavāvahāyi*.
Nor can it be argued that homogeneity is excluded here because of the inclusion of the *t* (as in *eta*),
since the purpose of including the *t* has been explained in the *Vṛtti* and *Nyāsa* as being merely for the sake of providing a specific instruction, as there is no other purpose for it.

If this is so, how is it that in the rule *iṇkoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.57), the author of the *Nyāsa* stated that in the word *dāsyati*, the substitution of *ṣ* would apply due to the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *ā* and the consonant *h*— despite their having fewer and more qualities respectively— and then explained the restriction [against such application] by citing the formative usage *vayasyāsu*?
For indeed, the *h* sound possesses the quality of being *vivṛta* (uncovered).
The letter *ā* possesses the quality of being most open (*vivṛtatamatva*).
As the author of the *Śikṣā* stated:
"The articulatory organ (*karaṇa*) of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels (*svara*) is open."
Among those, *e* and *o* are more open; *ai* and *au* are more open than those; and the vowel *ā* is even more open than those.

On this point, they say: although it should have been formulated as a single compound word, *vivṛtaṃ karaṇam ūṣmasvarāṇām*, the fact that it is made into separate words— *vivṛtaṃ karaṇam ūṣmaṇām* and *svarāṇām*— indicates that the term *svarāṇām* alone is to be connected with the subsequent sūtra.

Therefore, the extreme openness (*vivṛtatama*) of the vowel *ā* is relative only to other vowels and not to sibilants (*ūṣman*); thus, because *ā* and *ha* possess equal effort (*prayatna*), the absence of the substitution of the retroflex *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) in the word *dāsyati* is correctly stated by the citation [of the rule].
However, Rakṣita has stated in the rule *iṇkoḥ* that there is homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) even between those possessing lesser or greater qualities.

Now, one might object: since *ā* and *ha* in *dāsyati* and similar forms are respectively vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*), the prohibition of homogeneity by the rule *nājjhalau* already precludes the occurrence of the retroflex; so why is a specific determination made by means of this citation?
It is said:

because of the statement that "the prohibition [of the rule] *nājjhalau* must be stated for those vowels whose homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) have not been grasped," whereas the vowel *ā* does indeed grasp its homogeneous counterparts.
What, then, is the purpose of this prohibition here?

One might ask: for what reason is a prohibition stated specifically regarding those vowels that do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), rather than let the prohibition apply generally? By such a general rule, the absence of homogeneity in cases like *dāsyati* would be established simply by the prohibition "na-aj-jhalau" (Pāṇini 1.1.10).

Likewise, in examples such as *khaṭvā-hastaḥ* and *kumārī śete*, the term *ac* (vowel) need not be supplied [from Pāṇini 6.1.102] in order to prevent the lengthening of a vowel before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*).
It is replied:

if the prohibition *nājjhalau* were to apply even to those vowels that have been grasped as homogeneous, then in the case of *niṃssaḥ*, the elision of the *s*—which occurs under the option of Pāṇini 8.4.65, *jharo jhari savarṇe*—would not take place.

Because the letter *s* is included within the category of *ac* by virtue of its being a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound with the vowel *ṛ*, and because it is taught as an *ac* in the *upadeśa*, it possesses the status of a *hal*. Consequently, the rule "there is no *ac* or *hal* among *ac* and *hal*" (Pāṇini 1.1.10) prohibits [the application of the term *ac* to it].

Furthermore, it is impossible to apply the prohibition of the *savarṇa* designation via the rule "there is no *ac* or *hal* among *ac* and *hal*" (Pāṇini 1.1.10) to the pair consisting of the vowel *ḷ* and the consonant *s*; for there is a logical contradiction in an entity acting upon itself.
For instance:
because the prohibition "lṛ and ś are not [included in] ac and hal" (Pāṇini 1.1.10) excludes the status of *ac* from the letter *ś*,
the prohibition "lṛ and ś are not [included in] ac and hal" would otherwise be untenable.

In this way, a negation would be made by the self of the self itself. Furthermore, regarding the negation of vowels that do not have corresponding *savarṇa* counterparts—in the rule *nājjhalau*, which prohibits the designation of *savarṇa*—the designation of *savarṇa* has not yet come into existence; consequently, the teaching-rule (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) [which depends upon that designation] has likewise not come into existence.
For it has been stated previously: "The exceptions (*apavāda*) operate first, and subsequently the general rules (*utsarga*). (17)
An imitation follows the nature of that which is being imitated. || 18 ||
Regarding this, someone says, "He recites twice," and another person imitates him by saying, "He said, 'He recites twice.

In that case, because the status of being a word (pada) is maintained through the principle of *prakṛtivadbhāva* (the imitation of the original form), the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) is established by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.
In the absence of being a word (*padatva*), that [rule] would not apply;
likewise, in the case of *vṛṣaṇvasu* and *aśva*, the absence of *na*-elision and the substitution of *ṇ* occur.

And the proof for this is found in the rule *parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ* and others; for even though the technical designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is accepted for the sake of generating case endings for the word *kriya-*—which is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *kṛ* and so on—the substitution *iyaṅ* and others, which depend upon its status as a verbal root (*dhātu*), is nevertheless applied.
If this is so, how is the grammatical instruction *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.19) and others to be explained?

Nor can it be argued here that even though the substitution of *iyaṅ* exists, it is superseded by the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111) due to its being later in the order of rules.

For Rakṣita has explained that, because of the specific mention of *kṣiyaḥ* (in Pāṇini 6.4.59), *iyaṅ* alone occurs even setting aside the subsequent *guṇa*, by means of a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior supersession).
And thus, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule *kṣiyo dīrghāt* is justified.

Otherwise, since the inclusion of the long vowel would already be established by the very mention of *kṣiyaḥ* with the *iy-aṅ* substitution, the explicit mention of "long" would be purposeless. It is replied:
Imitation is of two kinds:
that of a meaningful word and that of a meaningless word-form alone.
Thus, in examples such as *kriya*, there is an imitation of the meaningful word *krī* itself, which has already received the designation of a verbal root (*dhātu*).
In that regard, since *iyaṅ* exists as part of the function of a verbal root (*dhātu*), it occurs even in the case of an imitation (*anukaraṇa*).

However, in rules such as *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*, there is an imitation of a mere collection of phonemes devoid of meaning; and because there is an absence of any referent in the form of an action (*kriyārūpa*) therein, the designation "verbal root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) does not apply at all.
Thus, since the designation "verbal root" is absent in the original item being imitated (*anukārya*) itself, the substitution of *iyaṅ* does not occur; what then can be said regarding its imitation?
Thus, this twofold imitation is determined by the performance or non-performance of the *iyaṅ* substitution;
for this very reason, they recite:
"In the case of an imitation of a meaningful form, the imitation behaves like the original."
Objection: If *jer* is an imitation of a meaningless sound, how then is the ātmanepada understood to belong to the verbal root *ji*?
It is replied: because the general form is used to convey the specific, the verbal root is also thereby indicated.

Objection: If *iyaṅ* is a stem-operation (*dhātukārya*) by virtue of being like the base form (*prakṛtivadbhāva*), then the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would be precluded because it is not a verbal root (*adhātu*). Response: It is said: the term *adhātu* is not a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) meaning "it does not belong to a verbal root"; rather, it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

"It occurs other than as a verbal root (*dhātu*). Words such as *krī* and others are not verbal roots because they are imitations (*anukaraṇa*), yet they are considered verbal roots by virtue of their being original forms (*prakṛti*). Thus, because they possess the status of both verbal root and non-verbal root, they occur precisely as "other than a verbal root. Accordingly, in the rule *kṣiyo dīrghāt*, it has been explained in the *Nyāsa* that the nominal stem designation (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) will apply to *kṣi* by virtue of its own inherent nature.

Alternatively, if *nañ* is used in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the rule "not a root" (*adhātuḥ*) does not trigger this technical grammatical operation; therefore, there is no extended application (*atideśa*) stating that "in its performance, it is not like the original form.

This point regarding *nañ* in the sense of exclusion was stated by Rakṣita in the rules "a meaningful element that is neither a root nor an affix is a nominal stem" (*arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam*) and "after a long vowel, [the substitute] *kṣi* [is applied]" (*kṣiye dīrghāt*).
[Objection: Even so, because an imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) is devoid of meaning, the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) would not apply to it.
Nor is the object merely a mental after-image,
for there is no difference [between them].
For it is only when a difference exists that the relationship between the signified and the signifier can occur.
Furthermore, no difference whatsoever is perceived between the imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) and the word being imitated (*anukārya-śabda*).
Nevertheless, there may be a conceptual difference.
Even so, since the object of imitation—the signified—is of the nature of sound (*śabdātmaka*), it is not logical for the imitation—the signifier—to have that as its denotation.
For one word is not the denotable object of another word; rather, it is only the referent [the meaning] that is so.
This is not the case;
for even a word is seen to be the denotable object of another word.
Just as the word *bhū* and so forth [are included] within the word *dhātu*.
But is that not reasonable?
Because the Teacher has established this technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
In that case, it is logical that even an imitation is expressive of that which is imitated,
because the Teacher has treated them as such;
for in the relationship between the signified and the signifier, linguistic usage alone is the basis.
But even if this is so, and although the words possess meaning, the case ending does not apply to the imitation [of a word], because that [ending] is prescribed with respect to number.
Furthermore, in the case of the words being imitated, number—which inheres in substances—is impossible;
for since those [imitated words] consist of sound (śabdātmaka), they are qualities of the air (avaraguṇa) and thus lack substantiality (adravyatva).
Since number is also a quality (*guṇa*), it does not exist therein [in a quality], because of the statement that "qualities are devoid of qualities. It is replied:
its status as a substance (*dravyatva*) is accepted because it is capable of being referred to by pronouns such as "this" or "that" in relation to a word.
Therefore, the case-ending arises from a word that is an imitation of an established form.
The restrictive rule is stronger than the suffixal modifications. || 19 ||

First, there exist restrictive rules (niyama-śāstra) such as "anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam" [Pāṇini 1.3.12], which apply prior to the introduction of the *vikaraṇa* suffixes; only thereafter do the *vikaraṇas* occur. Consequently, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule "nerviśaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.3.17] and others, the statement that the augment *aṭ* is a part of the root and is therefore included by the mention of that root becomes logically justified. To explain further: [The text continues: "In the case of *niviśate*, the augment *aṭ* is added to the beginning of the root *viś*. Since the augment is a part of the root, it is included within the term 'root' (*dhātu-grahaṇena gṛhyate*). Therefore, the rule 'nerviśaḥ' applies. Thus, the inclusion of the augment is established. Similarly, in the case of *parivyayate*, the augment *aṭ* is added to the beginning of the root *vyen*. Because it is a part of the root, it is included by the mention of the root, and thus the rule "parivyaveḥ saṃvaraṇe" [Pāṇini 1.3.19] applies. Likewise, in the case of *samava-syante*, the augment *aṭ* is added to the beginning of the root *syam*. Being a part of the root, it is included by the mention of the root, and thus the rule "samavasambibhyaḥ sthaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.3.24] applies. Furthermore, in the case of *parivyayate*, the augment *aṭ* is added to the beginning of the root *vyen*. Because it is a part of the root, it is included by the mention of the root, and thus the rule "veḥ skanderaniṣṭhāyām" [Pāṇini 8.3.73] applies. In this manner, all such examples are to be understood accordingly. However, one might raise the following objection: "If the augment *aṭ* is indeed a part of the root, then in the case of *niviśate*, the rule 'nerviśaḥ' would apply even when the augment is present. But since the rule 'nerviśaḥ' is stated with the root *viś* ending in a short vowel (*hrasva*), the augment *aṭ*—being a part of the root—would cause the root to appear as having a long vowel (*dīrgha*), and thus the rule would not apply. Similarly, in the case of *parivyayate*, the rule 'parivyaveḥ saṃvaraṇe' would not apply because the root would have a long vowel. Likewise, in the case of *samava-syante*, the rule 'samavasambibhyaḥ sthaḥ' would not apply because the root would have a long vowel. Furthermore, in the case of *parivyayate*, the rule 'veḥ skanderaniṣṭhāyām' would not apply because the root would have a long vowel. How then can these be explained? To this, we reply: There is no fault here. For the augment *aṭ* is not merely a part of the root; rather, it is a part of the entire verbal form (*pada*). It is said: "The augment *aṭ* is a part of the word (*pada-bhakta*). Since it is a part of the word, it does not affect the status of the root's vowel length. Therefore, the rules apply as intended. This is the correct view. However, some maintain that the augment *aṭ* is indeed a part of the root. According to them, the mention of the root in the rules includes its parts, and thus the rules apply despite the presence of the augment. Both views are supported by tradition, and both are accepted by the learned. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Thus, the inclusion of the augment *aṭ* is established through the mention of the root. Furthermore, in the case of *parivyayate*, the augment *aṭ* is added to the beginning of the root *vyen*. Because it is a part of the root, it is included by the mention of the root, and thus the rule "parivyaveḥ saṃvaraṇe" applies. Because it is a part of the root, it is included by the mention of the root, and thus the rule "veḥ skanderaniṣṭhāyām" applies. In this manner, all such examples are to be understood accordingly. A restriction must be applied even to a subsequent suffix that is obligatory due to its *vikaraṇa* status.

And at the time of the application of this restriction, the augment *aṭ* itself is what presents itself; it is not the case that this *aṭ* augment is set aside by the restriction, because the restriction is stronger than the *vikaraṇa*.
Nor can it be set aside by the *vikaraṇa*, because at the time the restriction is operative, the *vikaraṇa* does not yet exist.

Thus, when both the restrictive rule (*niyama*) and the augment *aṭ* apply simultaneously, the augment *aṭ* takes precedence due to its posteriority; therefore, it is correctly stated that the augment *aṭ* belongs to that [verbal base] and is included by the mention of it. Now, one might object: since the restrictive rule operates, would not the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) be superseded? At the time when the augment *aṭ*—which supersedes it—is about to operate, why does the eternal (*nitya*) suffix not occur prior to the augment *aṭ*?
It is replied:
If the augment *iṭ* were to subvert the *vikaraṇa*, then why would the rule—which stands without opposition—not itself subvert the *vikaraṇa*?

Likewise, in forms such as *edhiṣyate* and *aidhiṣṭa*, the rule "from roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or *ṅ*, only the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs, not the active voice (*parasmaipada*)" would apply;

otherwise, since the *vikaraṇas* are applied later and are obligatory, once they have been added, the suffixes *sy-* and so on would be separated from the root by them, and the restriction that "middle voice occurs after roots with low-pitched vowels or *ṅ*, and active voice occurs after the remainder" would not hold.
And thus, *tiP* and the other affixes would apply generally;

however, the restriction [of these affixes] is already fulfilled in cases such as *āste* and *śete*. If this were so, the production of the affixes *sy-* and the others would not occur in the state of the *lā* suffix.

But when the substitution of *l* has been made, in the form *edhiṣyate*, two suffixes would apply: the suffix *yak* and the suffix *syap*. In that case, because it is subsequent, only *yak* should occur. It is replied: when *śap* is applicable for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix denoting the agent, the suffixes *syap* and others, which are prescribed for the impersonal (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*) voices along with *yak*, become sublaters (*bādhaka*) of all [other rules] by virtue of being general exceptions.

And this meaning is indicated by the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* through the prescription of the *parasmaipada* endings; otherwise, since there would be no restriction—given that for roots such as *vṛtu* (to turn) and others, the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam* does not apply when combined with *syen*—both forms would be established by the general prescription of the *tiṅ* suffixes, namely *vartsyati* and *vartiṣyate*. What, then, would be the purpose of this specific prescription? It serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this very point.

Others, however, on the basis of this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), state the following *paribhāṣā*: "The restriction (*niyama*) operates even when the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) has already been applied.
According to this view, in the form *edhiṣyate*, the suffix *syap* must occur at the very stage of the *lā* (the common designation for *laṭ*), because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal).
Likewise, according to this same view, in the forms *auṣyata* and *auhyata*, the augment *āṭ* occurs by the rule *āḍajādīnām* because they begin with a vowel (*aj-ādi*).

Otherwise, since a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is stronger than an exception (*vikaraṇa*), when there is a conflict between a restrictive rule and an augment (*āgama*), the augment would have to apply by virtue of its posteriority. Furthermore, at the time the augment *aṭ* is to be applied, the permanent (*nitya*) suffix cannot be made to operate,
because it has already been set aside by the restrictive rule.
Since the augment *āṭ* must necessarily remain and cannot be removed, it follows that, by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), it indeed becomes an exception (*bādhaka*).

Thus, when the augment *aṭ* has been applied because the root begins with a consonant, the rule *āṭaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.90) prevents the *vṛddhi* substitution; consequently, forms such as *auhyata* would not be established.
Furthermore, in this very view, there is the inclusion of the root *ṛcch* in its non-substituted form.

Since the result is already established by the rule *atyārdeśasya caṅi* alone, the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the sūtra *samo gamy-ādiṣu* is justified. For, if the restriction (*niyama*) were stronger than the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), then when the suffix *śa* is prescribed, the substitution of *ṛccha* would occur even before the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Likewise, according to this very view, the augment *āṭ* for that [suffix] is stated in the sūtra *nergadādiṣu* after the verbal suffix has been applied.

Otherwise, if the rule of restriction (*niyama*) were stronger than the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*), then since the augment *aṭ* would apply even further out [after the suffix], how could the augment *aṭ* be justified for that which ends in a suffix? Now, regarding the mention "after the suffixes" (*vikaraṇebhyaḥ*), once the *s* of the ablative case ending (*bhyas*) has been changed to *r*, the *it*-designation for the *u* of *ru* does not apply because of the rule "that which is established earlier is treated as non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*). To this, it is replied: [The answer is: It is said that the *it*-designation applies because the rule "the nasalized vowel is an *it*" (*ajanunāsika it*) is taught before the rule "that which is established earlier is treated as non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*). Thus, the *it*-designation is established first, and subsequently, by the rule "in place of *r*, there is *u*" (*ro ri*), the *r* is replaced by *u*. Furthermore, the *it*-designation is not lost; rather, it remains as if it were still present. Therefore, the *it*-designation is indeed applicable. Consequently, the *it*-designation is established, and thus the elision of the *s* occurs. This is the intended meaning. Alternatively, one may say that the *it*-designation is established by the rule "the nasalized vowel is an *it*" (*ajanunāsika it*) while the rule "that which is established earlier is treated as non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) is not yet operative. Therefore, the *it*-designation is established. And since the *it*-designation is established, the elision of the *s* occurs. This is the intended meaning. Due to the force of the formal declaration (*pratijñāna*) that the *roru* [the *ru* substitute for *sasajuṣ*] is nasal (*anunāsika*), it does not possess the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*).

Thus, in the rule *upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ*, it was stated by Rakṣita that there is no non-establishment regarding the *it*-designation; for in the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*, the force of the declaration that the *u* sound is nasal serves the purpose of assigning the *it*-designation to it.
To this it is replied:
In the rule *haśi ca*, the vowel *u* of the word *ruḥ* must be declared nasalized (*anunāsika*) so that the term *ruḥ* may be understood as qualified by nasality.
Consequently, in the example *tarūvanam*, the substitution of *u* (as prescribed by *haśi ca*) does not occur.
How then is that capacity designated by the technical name *it*?
Nor should it be argued that, according to the maxim of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*), the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* alone should take precedence over this [rule],
and not [the rule] concerning *taru* and so forth.
For when both the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtaka*) are possible, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the artificial applies. To illustrate:
in the rule for *utva* (*sasajuṣo ruḥ*), because [the substitution of *ru*] is treated as *asiddha*, only the occurrence of *taru-vanasya* is possible, and not the other.
In that case, let it be asserted that the *repha* itself possesses nasality (*anunāsikatva*), just as its *svarita* accent is asserted.
And thus, when the substitution of *u* (*utva*) is prescribed for a *repha* qualified by nasality, how could the substitution of *u* apply again in words such as *punar*?
Therefore, since the nasality of the *repha* must be asserted in this way, the assertion regarding the vowel *u* will, by virtue of that [assertion], receive the technical designation *it*.
This too is not correct.

For if the treatise remained as it stands, the vowel *u* would be a redundant marker (*anubandha*), since the desired result could be achieved by the method just mentioned without even performing the substitution of *ru* for *ra*.
If that is the case, then its efficacy must be based on the principle that the individual word-meaning (*vyakti-padārtha*) is the referent.
And this was demonstrated by Maitreya, who stated that the nasalization of the vowel *u* in the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* is prescribed for the purpose of assigning it the technical designation *it*.
Another, however, says:
even the substitution of *ru* for *ra* when it is qualified by a nasalized vowel would not be possible without the application of the principle of "asiddha" (non-validity).
The same applies to the designation *it*.

In that regard, just as [the rule for] *utva* operates by setting aside its own lack of established status (*asiddhatva*) and proceeding on the basis of the declaration of the *anunāsika*, so too does it proceed on the basis of the designation *it*.
Nor does *utva* operate [merely] because of the statement "it is established by virtue of its substratum" (*āśrayāt siddham*).
Because there is an absence of valid cognition regarding the opposite case. || 19 ||
Thus ends the third section, "The King's Foot," in the Paribhāṣāvṛtti.
When there is a conflict between two rules that apply simultaneously, that which is sublated remains sublated.
Furthermore, it is established through the cognition of recurrence. || 21 ||

These two statements are recited in the form of a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) as the resulting consequence of the two positions—the individual (*vyakti*) and the class (*jāti*)—in the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra. To explain:
when the word-meaning is the individual, because the operation of the grammatical rule differs for each specific instance (*pratilakṣya*), both rules would apply alternatively (*paryāyeṇa*).
Just as food is eaten by Devadatta and Yajñadatta one after another in a single vessel,
so too, in the case of a conflict (vipratiṣedha), the rule "in a conflict, the latter [prevails]" (Pāṇini 1.4.2) restricts the scope of that conflict:
in a conflict, only the latter applies, not the former.
And by this, the previous statement does not become purposeless,
because its non-existence is established by the Sūtra on Contradiction (Vipratiṣedha). This is what is being said:
"In the case of a conflict regarding simultaneous application, that which is once set aside remains set aside.
This is its meaning:
that which is set aside once, at a single instance, remains set aside.
In the case of a conflict regarding application,
by that very rule, since *asuk* is applied by the rule *aj-jas-er-asuk* due to its higher priority, the substitution of *śī* does not occur again;
as in the example *ye pūrvāsaḥ*.

In the case of *tathā stāt tvam*, the substitution of *s* for *t* (the *dvirbhāva*) does not occur because the substitute *tāt* is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, by the rule *ghvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca*, the *s* is changed to *e*.
This has been explained in the Bhāṣya on the *sthānivat* sūtra.
When the category (jāti) is the object, the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) applies only once;
and since both [characteristics] have fulfilled their purpose regarding different objects, it follows that neither should apply in a case of conflict.
This is just as when there is a single servant for two masters of equal power, he does not proceed to perform the work of either due to the contradiction.

In that case, regarding the rule "when there is a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails," since the subsequent rule has already functioned, the preceding one has ceased to operate and thus no longer functions.
Now, an objection is raised: "But the cessation of the preceding rule was already stated previously; so how can it be prescribed now?
It is replied:
It was stated that there is no application [of the rule] due to simultaneous contradiction;
however, when the subsequent rule has been applied because of its priority, there is no longer a contradiction, and thus the prior rule is indeed applicable.
This is what is being said:
It is established by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*).
Therefore, in the case of *bhinddhi akī*, once the doubling (*dhibhāva*) has been applied due to its higher priority, *akac* is applied again.
In the case of *ījatuḥ*, once the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) has been applied due to its higher priority, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is applied again.
The maxim of "once gone" (*sakṛdgatiparibhāṣā*) applies where the earlier operation, as it proceeds, precludes the later one;
however, where the earlier operation does not preclude the later one, some hold the view that the result is established by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punaḥprasaṅga*).
That is incorrect.
For in this way, in the case of *akṣī*, since the rule *ī ca dvivacane* applies later, once the vowel *ī* has been substituted, the *num* augment would indeed have to occur again.
Therefore, the settlement of these two [rules] depends solely on the actual state of the linguistic forms (*lakṣyasthiti*).
Now, regarding the mention in the rule *punaḥprasaṅgavijñānāt*, how can there be a *visarjanīya* based on the status of a word (*padatva*) in the word *punaḥ*?
Since there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the suffixes *su* and so forth must occur after the objects (*karman*) and other factors when they are in the singular and so on.
Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is an indeclinable (*avyaya*);
and indeclinables are devoid of gender and number.
It is said:
in the system of five case-endings (*pañcaka-pakṣa*), the suffixes *su* and so forth are prescribed generally.

Then, by the rule "the plural is used for many," which restricts the meaning such that the plural suffix occurs only when there are many referents, the suffixes remain unrestricted; therefore, the case-endings beginning with *su* certainly exist even after indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Furthermore, even if there is a restriction on suffixes such that the plural suffix occurs only when there are many objects, nevertheless, since this restriction depends upon similar classes of things, it must apply only where a number exists and another number is to be excluded. And thus, due to the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), there is an absence of all case-endings (*sub*) and so forth in the following cases: from numeral words; from the *dvandva* compound "Devadatta-Yajñadatta"; and in expressions such as "at the front of the forest" (*agrevaṇam*) and "mango trees to the east of the village" (*prācīnam grāmād āmrāḥ*).
This must be stated.
For this very reason, the author of the Nyāsa will state under the rule *svādi* that even in the view of the *trika* (the three-number system), there is a syntactic connection with multiple rules;
he says: "By the rule *bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, a syntactic connection with multiple rules is also indicated here."
Now, when there is the position that the triad constitutes a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*), how can there be [grammatical operations] such as *svādi*? And why should they not exist?
Because of the absence of singularity (*ekatva*) and the other [number categories].

If this is so, then [the case endings] would not be obtained even from words such as *vṛkṣa* (tree); for in that regard, just as by the rule "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) and so forth, numbers and the like—which do not actually exist [in the objects themselves]—are expressed by the suffixes beginning with *su*, so too they will be expressed by indeclinables (*avyaya*).
This is not so.

By virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), where number and so forth are not already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, it is precisely within the meaning of that stem that number and so forth are denoted by the case-endings (*svādi*), and not elsewhere.
For example, according to the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*, the suffix *ṭāp* is prescribed when the feminine gender is to be expressed; however, it does not apply to words such as *vṛkṣa*.

In that case, by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *avyayādāpsupaḥ*, case-endings do indeed occur even after indeclinables (*avyaya*), which are devoid of number, object, and other such categories.

And likewise, regarding the use of the plural number, the author of the Nyāsa has stated: "By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*, it is understood that from indeclinables (*avyaya*) which possess inherent numbers (*nitsaṃkhya*), the case-endings beginning with *su* (the nominative) prescribed by general rules do indeed exist.
Regarding this, Rakṣita has stated:
"The indicator in *avyayād āpsupaḥ* applies to the individual instance (*vyakti*)."
Indeed, there certainly exists its scope; for there is room [for its application] in cases such as *pralambate svaḥ*.

For in the case of *pralambate svaḥ*, with respect to the action of hanging down (*pralambana-kriyā*), the word *svaḥ* must necessarily take the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). Therefore, how could that [prescription of the fifth case] be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending?
In that case, it is the rule made for the sake of indeclinables (*avyaya*) such as *nīcaiḥ*—which are devoid of gender and number when expressed—that serves as the indicator.

But surely, even here, by the rule beginning with *prātipadikārtha* [Pāṇini 2.3.46], the nominative case prescribed for the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) would serve the purpose of elision (*lup*). How, then, can that be an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?
It is said in reply:
The fact that [the rule] was formulated for the sake of the second case and so forth serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
However, this is incorrect; for there is no purpose whatsoever in prescribing the second case and subsequent cases after an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
If it is argued that the purpose is the optional application of the suffix *temayādi* by the rule "after a first case preceded by something else, there is optionally [the suffix]," we say no.
Because, according to the position that [the suffix] *prathamā* is prescribed, those [suffixes] necessarily exist [therein].
If it is argued that, in that case, the purpose [of the rule] is the formation of compounds such as *dvitīyā-samāsa* for words ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth—
this too is not correct.
Because, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) whose cause is [the word] *śrita* and so forth is compounded there;

likewise, in the case of "the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so on, since the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "noun with noun" (*sup-supā*) applies, the case ending (*vibhakti*) which has that as its cause must be understood.
It is said:

In the *prātipadikārtha* sūtra, the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of the fact that the nominative case occurs after indeclinables], provided it is not intended [to restrict the application of the rule]. If it were intended, there would be no purpose for the indicator,
because the occurrence of the first case (*prathamā*) after indeclinables is already established by the very inclusion of the word *artha*.
For this very reason, Rakṣita [states] in the *Prātipadikārtha* sūtra:
"The mention of 'meaning' (*artha*) is for the sake of including that which lacks gender;
and that [which lacks gender] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*)."

For this very reason, it has been stated in detail that the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) establishing that the nominative case occurs even after words devoid of number. || 21 ||
Between the internal and the external, the internal is stronger.
This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is recited in the *Bhāṣya* on the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra and in the *Nyāsa*.

Consequently, in cases such as *dyaukāmiḥ* and *sautthitiḥ*, according to the view that analyzes the derivation by successive stages (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*), the internal substitutions of *yaṇ* and *ekādeśa* take effect because the external *vṛddhi* is weaker.
This example is merely illustrative.

Because of the mention of the term *samartha* (semantically connected) in the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) must be formed from that which has all its operations completed; thus, the *yaṇ* and *ekādeśa* substitutions are established.

However, this example—such as *vṛkṣā iha*—is governed by the principle that an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) prevails over an external one (*bahiraṅga*), namely that the *guṇa* substitution takes precedence over the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*).
Nor is this established merely by the metarule stating that "an external [operation] is as if not accomplished when an internal one applies."
The designation "external" (*bahiṣṭva*) applies to the *acor* [substitution] and not to the *ajānantarya* [substitution], because the latter is prohibited.

Now, one might argue: "Even if the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) is applied here, the form *vṛkṣa iha* is established by *āṅguṇa* (P. 6.1.87), since the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies by the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (P. 1.1.57).
This is not so.

Because the substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included by the mention of the "preceding" element (*pūrva*), its status as a *sthānivadbhūta* (acting like the original) is prohibited by the fact that it is a rule concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*).
However, the mention of the "following" element (*parādighaṇa*) need not be stated;

for it is improper to apply the rules of the *sūtra* regarding the beginning or end of a word to something that is neither a word-initial nor a word-final due to its being treated as following [the preceding element].
Indeed, the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā would also not apply,
precisely because of the prohibition in the rule *nājānantarye*.
For just as the *asiddha* paribhāṣā renders the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* meaningless, so too does the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā.
It is said:
The rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* is not rendered meaningless by the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā,
because the application of *tuṅ* occurs precisely due to its being *antaraṅga*.
Because the long vowel is permanent (*nitya*),
the long vowel alone would apply there by virtue of its priority (*paratva*).
As for the statement that "the internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger than even the permanent," that is merely the result of priority, not something previously unestablished.
Alternatively, let the *tuk* augment apply because it is internal (*antaraṅga*).
Once the lengthening has been applied, its disappearance would indeed occur by the rule regarding the removal of a cause (*nimittāpāyaparibhāṣā*).
Thus, it is precisely by the rule concerning external elements (*bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*) that the sūtra "the substitution of *ṣatva* and *tuk* is not established" becomes redundant.

Therefore, there is a prohibition stating that for that [substitution] alone, there is no "immediate sequence" (*nājānantarya*). Furthermore, if there were a prohibition of the *antaraṅga* maxim in this context, then the *antaraṅga* maxim would become devoid of scope.
Moreover, since all grammatical operations are accomplished by the *bahiraṅga* maxim itself, this [maxim] is not accepted by the author of the Bhāgavṛtti.
In that view, although the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* does not apply to cases such as *vṛkṣa iha* where there is no immediate sequence of vowels (*acorānantarya*),
nevertheless, the refutation of the objection must be explained according to the *padasaṃskārapakṣa*.
As they say:
"The wise grasp the sentence after having thoroughly investigated the meaning of the words.
This is indeed logical;

otherwise, in the case of *vṛkṣaiḥ* and *iha*, during the formation of the sentence, the rule for the lengthening of all vowels (*sarvaṇadīrghatva*) would prevail, overriding the internal *ādguṇa* (the substitution of a single vowel) by means of the paribhāṣā "that which depends on more [elements] is stronger" (*śabdaparavipratiṣedha*).

Just as in *diva ut* and *divokaso devāḥ*, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *u* is protected by [the rule] *utkaḥ*. Nor can it be argued that, by virtue of the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*, forms such as *vṛkṣaiḥ* and *iha* must necessarily result from the *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *i* + *e*];
for if that were so, the *yaṇ* substitution for the vowel *i* would likewise occur in *divokasaḥ*.

Now, another example of this is *ṛtviya*. Here, after the substitution of *ghas* [for *ṛtu*] and the replacement of that with *iy*, the designation *pada*— which is applied by the rule *siti ca* because it is internal (*antaraṅga*)— subverts the designation *bha*, which is applied to bases beginning with vowels by the rule *yaci bham* and is thus external (*bahiraṅga*).
But there is no simultaneous occurrence [of two cognitions],
because of the governing rule of "a single cognition.
And this [position] is incorrect.

And because the fact that [the present rule] sublates the technical designation *bha* is established by the very commencement of the sūtra "siti ca," for this reason the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "one technical designation" (*eka-saṃjñā*) does not apply to this purpose.
To explain:

Since the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designation *bha*— by the rule *yaci bham*— with the designation *pada*— by the rule *svādiṣu...*— is already established, if the rule *siti ca* were [merely] restating this, then *siti ca* would indeed be redundant.
Now, one might argue as follows:

In the rule *yaci bham*, because of the acceptance of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "one designation" (*eka-saṃjñā*), there is no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *bha* and *pada*.
And thus, in the case of *siti ca*, since the heading of "one designation" does not apply, there would indeed be a co-occurrence of the designations *bha* and *pada* in the word *ṛtviya*.
[Objection: Even so, the rule *siti ca* would be purposeless.
For this is its purpose:
in the word *ṛtviya*, because [the suffix] has the marker *s*, it is treated as a *pada*; thus, let there not be the substitution of *guṇa* for *au*.
However, if there were an overlap with the technical designation *bha*, then the substitution of *guṇa* for *au* would indeed occur.
And thus, regarding what was stated by the author of the *Anunyāsa* under the rule *evaṃ cākaḍārāt*:
"This [rule] is stated for the sake of that which has no other occasion;
in the case of *ayaṃ te yonir ṛtviyaḥ*, the designation *pada* subverts the designation *bha*."
That is incorrect; it is not incorrect, because the status of being a word (padatva) serves the purpose of the avagraha. || 22 ||
When there is a mention of both [the ablative and the genitive], the mention of the ablative is stronger. || 23 ||

Where there is both a mention in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) and a mention in the locative case (*saptamī-nirdeśa*), whether explicitly stated or understood through *anuvṛtti*, the mention in the ablative is stronger; therefore, the rule "from that [ablative], for what follows" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*) applies.

Consequently, in the rule *ami sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* ("*suṭ* is added after a pronominal ending in *ām*"), although *at* is understood from the previous context, this ablative mention—meaning "after a pronominal ending in the vowel *a*"—transforms the locative mention *āmī* into a genitive sense, so that the augment *suṭ* occurs specifically before the ending *ām*.
And this rule, "In case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails," is recited as a *paribhāṣā* (metarule). To illustrate:

the rule "In the presence of that which is specified by the locative case, an operation applies to what precedes it" (Pāṇini 1.1.66), as exemplified by "iko yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77) in cases such as *dadhy atra* and *madhv atra*, has its scope of application elsewhere.
Therefore, the ablative case designation in *tasmādityuttarasya* has already served its purpose in the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ*.
Regarding the word *āstīrṇam*:

however, where both the locative designation and the ablative designation have already served their respective purposes, when both would apply simultaneously, the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* prevails due to its posteriority in the sequence of rules.
For instance:
in the rule *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ*, the ablative *āt* has fulfilled its purpose in the prescription of *asuk* in the rule *ājjaserasuk*;
likewise, the locative *amī* has fulfilled its purpose in the rule *trestrayaḥ*.
When two rules of equal strength conflict, the subsequent rule (the fifth case) effects the transformation of the seventh case into a sixth case.
However, where the seventh case is *anavakāśā* (without scope/irreducible), there the very mention of the seventh case effects the transformation of the fifth case into a sixth case.

For example, in the rule *āne muk*, the seventh case *āni* is *anavakāśā*; therefore, it effects the transformation of the fifth case *ataḥ*—which has already fulfilled its purpose in the rule *yeyaḥ*—into a sixth case.
Consequently, in the subsequent rule, *muk* is applied only to a stem (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *a*.
If this is so, then how can the augment *dhuṭ* be added to what follows an initial *s*, as in the rule *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*?
For the locative case *si* (in *ḍaḥ si*) has no other purposeful application anywhere.
It is said:
just as this locative case ending *sī* (in *sīti*) is without scope, so too is this ablative case ending *ḍa* (in *ḍa iti*).
And thus, when both are without scope, it is indeed proper that the latter takes precedence.
Nor should one suspect a simultaneous assumption of mutual genitive relations,
nor even a sequential one;
for in the rule "one [suffix] after what precedes and follows" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*), the mention of "what precedes and follows" (*pūrvapara*) is made.
As it has been said:
"And there is no simultaneous apprehension of both [aspects], because of the prior and posterior grasping.
Nor, therefore, is the mention of the locative case (saptamī) purposeless.
This is for the sake of brevity; for if one were to specify "sa" (the letter *s*), there would be prolixity. And this has been stated in the *Nyāsa* commentary on the rule *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*.
In this context, however, regarding the rule *dīrghāt padāntād vā*, although the locative case in *cha* has already served its purpose, nevertheless—

because that [locative] would otherwise have no scope for application here due to its connection with the svarita accent— it causes the ablative *dīrghāt* to be interpreted as a genitive. The ablative, having established a relationship of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*), then withdraws once its purpose is fulfilled.
Therefore, this is the meaning:

when the letter *cha* follows a long vowel, the augment *tuK* is applied to that very preceding long vowel; in that case, this [rule] has no application. Thus, in the rule *tasmād uttarasya*, there is a *nyāsa* (commentary).
However, regarding the rule *dīrghāt*, the author of the *Nyāsa* states that in the rule *tasmād uttarasya*, a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made by reading *tasmāt*.
The term *pūrvasya* ("of the preceding") is carried over from the previous sūtra.

Therefore, it has been stated that even when there is a specification in the ablative case, as in the rule *dīrghāt* ("after a long vowel"), the grammatical operation applies only to the preceding element. || 23 ||
All ritual injunctions are subject to option in the Vedic language.
In the case of *dhuri dakṣiṇāyām*, since the locative case is optional in this sense and the genitive is prescribed for the remaining cases (*śeṣe*), the form *dhuri dakṣiṇāyāḥ* is established.

Similarly, in the expression *ye yūpāya takṣanti*, the singular number is used for the plural sense of "those who carve. This meaning is justified by a word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *ṣaṣṭhīyuktaś chandasi vā*.
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is merely an elaboration of the rule "there is much transposition" (*vyatyayo bahulam*). || 24 ||
When a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element after which it is prescribed and ends with the suffix itself.
When a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that very portion from which it is prescribed as well as that which ends with that suffix.
The purpose [of this rule] applies to verbal roots (*dhātu*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), nominal stems (*prātipadika*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*āḍhya*).
According to the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots," the designation "verbal root" applies only to that which begins from where it is prescribed and ends with that suffix.
Regarding the form *cikīrṣati*:
it does not belong to the compound [verb stem].
As in *prācikīrṣat*.

By the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāś ca*, that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and this applies only to that which begins with it and ends with it— such as *kārakaḥ* and *gārgyaḥ*—
but not to the entire aggregate.
"A brahmin is the agent; [the name] Gārgya is a brahmin.
[From this,] by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, one forms *putrīyati* from *putram icchati*.
It does not arise from a compound (*saṃghāta*).
Regarding the expression "he desires a great son" (*mahāntam putram icchati*),

in the rule for the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita-vidhi*), because of the mention of the suffixes *ya* and *yañ* in the rule *yañiñoś ca*, the suffix *phak* occurs only after that [stem] from which those two [suffixes] were prescribed, and not after the beginning of the entire word.
"Gārgyāyaṇa"—it does not occur after a compound. For example:
"vipra gārgyāyaṇa."

The term *sup-supā* refers to a compound (*samāsa*), not to a mere collection of words, as in the example "the king's prosperous servant" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). Furthermore, this meaning has been established by means of a formal division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) within the sūtra that prescribes suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*).
For instance:
because the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*) is analyzed as "that which begins with [the element] when a suffix follows" (*tadādi pratyaye*),
and the word "being grasped" (*gṛhyamāṇe*) must be supplied.

When a suffix (*pratyaya*) is being apprehended, that which precedes it is what is grasped as the base, and not the entire complex ending with the suffix. For this very reason, in the *Aṅgādhikāra* (the section on bases), having established the rule "from which [a suffix is prescribed] as the beginning" (*yasmād ādi*), the rule "of the base" (*aṅgasya*) is not annulled.
Now, one might object: even there, the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is established through a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).
The [rule for] *satya* is established;
however, because of the prohibition "not when there is a feminine suffix and no secondary derivative (*anuparjana*)," the second case ending is not established.
To explain:
In this context, following the rule *neyaṅuvaṅsthānāvastrī*, the term *astrī* (not feminine) is understood to carry over.

Due to the force of that carry-over, there is the inclusion of a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Furthermore, because the grammatical operation applies to the primary element, it is understood that the rule "not when [the suffix] is a feminine suffix that is not a subordinate member" (*anupasarjane*) is intended.
In that case, let this very section be composed within the *Aṅgapāda*.

Nor should it be argued that, in a word such as *atatakṣat*, there would be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the light (*laghu*) designation and the heavy (*guru*) designation; for that would result in the uselessness (*vaiyarthya*) of formulating the light designation.
Otherwise, he would have simply used the term *hrasva* (short) in the rule concerning light syllables (*laghupradeśa*).
It is said in reply: because from the initial sūtra, the phrase "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) into the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam*.
This treatise is for that purpose.

Therefore, according to the view that "doubling" (*dvirvacana*) means a double application, the designation of "word" (*pada*)—defined as "that which ends in a *sup* or a *tiṅ* suffix"—is established for the entire aggregate *pacasi-pacasī*, because of the inclusion of the initial element (*tadādi*). To explain: ... [the rule] *suptiṅantaṃ padam* applies to the whole. Thus it is established.

Because the meaning and form are identical, that very same *pac* is the same as the *tiṅ* prescribed after the preceding [element], and that which is prescribed after the subsequent [element] is also the same as that prescribed before; thus, by virtue of the inclusion of "that beginning" (*tadādi*), the entire aggregate constitutes a word (*pada*). And since that is a word, in the case of *āṃ pacasi pacasi devadattā*, the status of being separated by one interval (*ekāntaratā*) is established by the rule: "An vocative (*āmantrita*) separated by one [word] from another vocative is not considered 'near' (*anantika*)."
And this explanation of the commentary on the rule *sarvasya dve* was stated by Rakṣita.
To this it is replied:
"But surely, since a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is prescribed here even after each individual [word], there would not be multiple words."
It is said that the completion of a sentence occurs through a collection; thus, the collection possesses the status of a word (*pada*).

Just as when both the collection and its constituent parts consist of a single vowel, reduplication applies to the collection and not to the parts—as in *papāca*—so too here, the collection possesses the status of a word.
In this way, the rule concerning the aggregate is upheld.
However, if the designation "word" (*pada*) were applied to the two constituent parts alone, the aggregate would be excluded, and consequently, the rule pertaining to it would be rendered nullified.
Furthermore, the continued application of the phrase "beginning with that" (*tad-ādi*) would likewise become meaningless.
However, in this view, in cases such as *andho 'ndho duḥkhī*, since each individual word lacks the status of being a "word" (*pada*), the grammatical operations pertaining to words would not apply.
To prevent this, one must consider that the status of being a word applies there through the completion of the sentence with respect to each [constituent], and thus the word-operations follow.
Another, however, says that in the case of *gaurībhyām*, if the designation "heavy" (*guru*) were applied, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would occur by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ*.

However, while the governing rule *ekasaṃjñādhikāra* (the principle that only one designation applies) remains in force, it is the designation *nadī* alone that prevails because it is an exception (*apavāda*), and not the designation *guru*.
