But surely, even if the *ekasaṃjñādhikāra* remains in force, there can be no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between the designations *guru* and *nadī*,
because they pertain to different domains (*bhinnaviṣayatvāt*).
For instance: the designation *guru* applies to a mere vowel, whereas the designation *nadī* applies to that which ends in the vowel *ī*.
It is replied:
In the opinion of some, the designation *nadī* applies to the vowel alone.
Nor should it be argued that under this view, the designation *nadī* would not apply to words such as *lakṣmī* because of the absence of femininity [in the vowel];
for the designation *nadī* is prescribed by superimposing upon the constituent part the femininity that resides in the whole.
And here, the prohibition "neṅavaṅsthānāvastrī" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this].

Likewise, regarding the rule *acchīnadyornum*, it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) that [the augment *num* occurs] when *śī* and *nadī* follow; thus, there is a fault in the view that [the term *nadī*] refers to the phonemes.
Therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation (*yathānyāsam*).
But this [position] is without scriptural authority. || 25 ||
Nor [is there substitution] when the suffix denotes a female and is not a subordinate member (anupasarjana). || 26 ||
This paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) does not apply when the suffix is a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) that is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*).

Consequently, when a suffix is mentioned within the governing rule for feminine forms (*stryadhikāra*), the entire complex (*saṃghāta*) is included; however, the meaning of the sentence is not that only that which begins with the element from which the feminine suffix arises is to be understood.
Therefore, by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*, since the suffix *aṇ* applies [to the word *kāra*], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added to the word *kāra* ending in that [suffix].
The suffix *ḍhak* does not apply to that which begins with it or only to that which ends with it; rather, it is applied to the entire compound itself, as in *kaumbhakāreya*.
Otherwise, the suffix *vṛddhi* and the accent would apply to the constituent member [of the compound].

Now, one might object: since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed after bases ending in *aṇ*, it will apply to the word *kumbhakāra* itself by virtue of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of *kṛt* suffixes. To this it is replied:
In the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the term *aṇ* does not refer exclusively to a *kṛt*-suffix;
rather, it refers to both *kṛt* and *akṛt* suffixes.

Now, one might object: since the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the inclusion of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) is absent here, just as the suffix *ḍhak* prescribed after words ending in feminine suffixes occurs after the composite word *kumbhakārī*, would it not likewise occur after the word *kāra* alone?
It might be thought so;
but this is not the case,
because the operation proceeds from the aggregate itself due to its predominance.
Likewise, in the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, because *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed under the heading of "feminine" (*stryadhikāra*), it possesses femininity;
and by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it possesses the nature of an affix (*pratyayatva*).

Therefore, since the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) is prohibited when that [substitute] is mentioned, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the entire *ṣyaṅ* itself, as in the example *paramakārīṣagandhīputraḥ*.

Because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *anupasarjane*, the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*) certainly applies when a feminine suffix occurs as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).
Consequently, in forms such as *atikārīṣagandhyaputraḥ* and *atikārīṣagandhyapatiḥ*, vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) does not take place.

Now, even so, since grammatical operations pertain to the principal element (*pradhāna*), the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix should apply only when the suffix itself is the principal element.
And thus, in the case of *atikārīṣagandhyāputra*, there would indeed be *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization).
It is said [in response]: if there were *saṃprasāraṇa* here, then the prohibition regarding what is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*) would be purposeless.

[Objection: Even so, in the case of *ardhapippalī*, the elision of the suffix *su* by the rule *halṅyādibhyaḥ* would not apply, because of the maxim concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).
[Objection: Because that which ends in a feminine suffix is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

[Response: It is said: in the rule *ekavibhakti ca apūrvanipāte*, because the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) which recurs from the previous rule is understood as a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option), the absence of the designation *upasarjana* is established.
Therefore, the prohibition of the restriction regarding "that which begins with it" and "that which ends with it"—namely, that there is no feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*)—indeed remains in force.

Now, let it be granted that this does not apply to a technical (*śāstrīya*) designation of "subordinate element" (*upasarjana*). However, when a worldly (*laukika*) subordinate element is present, the rule "there is no feminine suffix" cannot possibly take effect.

Because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *anupasarjana*, there must indeed be an application of the restriction that a term beginning with that [which is specified] applies (the *tadādinīyama*), according to the maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).
By the mention of the word *upasarjana*, it is precisely the worldly (*laukika*) *upasarjana* that is understood.

For instance, in the case of *pañcakhaṭvī*, according to the view that the aggregate (*samudāya*) is distinct from its constituent parts (*samudāyin*), even though the technical designation of "subordinate element" (*upasarjana*) does not apply, the shortening [of the final vowel] is prescribed by the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya*; and then, relying on the worldly sense of "subordinate element," the suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed by the rule *dvigoḥ*.
It is said:

because of the understanding that the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally), which recurs in the rule *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte*, refers to a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), as in the case of *ardhapippalī*, the shortening [of the final vowel] does not occur; for here, in the absence of a technical (*śāstrīya*) upasarjana, the shortening—which would otherwise depend on a worldly (*laukika*) upasarjana—is not applied.
Likewise, the prohibition [of elision] by the rule *anupasarjanāt* does not apply either.

Alternatively, because the word "long" (*dīrgha*) is mentioned in the rule *hal-ṅy-āp-...*, they say that in certain cases—even when a feminine suffix occurs as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*)—the term "feminine suffix" (*strī-pratyaya*) here is understood to function [as a general term for such suffixes].
By this, the elision of the final vowel and consonant (*hal-ṅy-āp-...*) is established in the case of *ardhapippalī*.
But how can this be an indicator (*jñapaka*)?
For, in order that there be no elision of the *su* suffix in the counter-examples "he amba" and "he nadi," the mention of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) ought to have been made.
[Objection: But surely, in these cases, there must indeed be elision of the *su* suffix by the rule "after a vocative ending in *eṅ* or a short vowel" (*eṅhrasvātsaṃbuddheḥ*).
Nor should it be said that because of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), [the elision] must not occur;

for otherwise, in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), one could have composed the rule as *hrasvaiṅoraṅyāpaḥ saṃbuddheḥ* without including the mention of "long" or the rule *eṅhrasvāt*. Consequently, in cases such as *he amba* and *he nadi*, the elision of the nominative suffix (*su*) would not occur.

[Objection: Even so, in the case of *badaryāḥ phalam* ("the fruit of the jujube tree"), when the sense is "a derivative (*vikāra*) of that," the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anudāttādeśca*. Then, by the rule *phale luk*, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix; and by the rule *taddhitaluki*, there is also elision of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Since [the long vowel] has not been mentioned [in the rule], the elision of the case-ending *su* would occur in the word *badaram* by virtue of the mention of the "suffix" [in the rule]; [therefore] the mention of the long vowel is purposeful, so that this [undesired elision] does not take place. [Reply: It is said:
Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the elision of *am* after a neuter [stem] in this case must be considered as superseding [the elision of *su*];
or rather, it is stated thus because the individual instance (*vyakti*) is taken as the referent of the word-meaning. || 26 ||
In a rule prescribing a technical name (saṃjñā-vidhi), when a suffix (pratyaya) is mentioned, there is no extension of the designation to that which ends with it (tadantavidhi).

By the rule *tena taraptamapaughaḥ*, the suffix *tara* alone receives the designation *gha*; consequently, when the rule *gharūpakalpa* prescribes a short vowel for a *gha*-designated suffix, it applies to *tara* as well. However, it does not apply when *tara* is at the end of a compound, as in *gaurī brāhmaṇitarā*.
Likewise, by the rule *ktaktavatū niṣṭhā*, only the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* receive the technical designation *niṣṭhā*,

and not words ending in them. Consequently, in the case of *dṛṣattīrṇā*, there is no substitution of *na* for the letter following the *da* of *dṛṣad*, nor is there the substitution of *da* for the preceding letter.

Objection: Let it be granted that the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*) does not apply in the case of a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*). However, in a rule prescribing a short vowel (*hrasva-vidhi*), the shortening should occur only when the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*) ends in a *gh* sound.
Response: It is said:

In the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu*, by including the mention of *aṇ* and then specifically mentioning *lekha*, it is shown that even in a rule prescribing a short vowel (*hrasva*), there is no application of the "specification of that which ends in [the mentioned element]" (*tadantavidhi*). Similarly, in the rule *radābhyām*, although there is the mention of *na* (for the prescription of *natva*), there is no understanding of *tadantavidhi* precisely because of the prohibition of *tadantavidhi* in rules prescribing technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*). Now, one might object: since the purpose of prohibiting *tadantavidhi* in a rule prescribing a short vowel has already been served [by the previous example], the argument based on "logical necessity" (*sāmarthya*) is inappropriate.
It is said:

if the prohibition of *tadantavidhi* (the rule that an operation concerning a suffix applies to what ends with that suffix) in the case of a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*) has its purpose solely in the prescription of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, then one could simply have formulated [the rule] as "the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha* when they are followed by *pit*"— without including the word "ending" (*anta*) in the rule "a word (*pada*) consists of that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*"), and without teaching that in the case of a technical designation, there is no *tadantavidhi* when a suffix is mentioned.

And this is the meaning: in the rule *pitau taraptamapau ghasaṃjñau bhavataḥ*, because of the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*), the domain of the suffix *an* is also included under the heading "in the formulation of a technical designation" (*saṃjñāvidhau*). Alternatively, the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix does not apply in a rule prescribing the substitution of *na*; for in that case, the word *niṣṭhā* is employed as a qualifier of the letter *t*.

In the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*, by the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita*, the designation applies only to that which ends with them, not to the two themselves. For, although the prohibition [of being a nominal stem] would have applied by the rule *apratyayaḥ*, the designation for *kṛt* and *taddhita* is commenced. Furthermore, it has been stated that the phrase *apratyayaḥ* constitutes a prohibition of that which ends in a suffix.
Since that [suffix] would be prohibited at the end of such a form, the technical designation (saṃjñā) being introduced applies specifically to that which ends in it.
This is also evident from the inclusion of the term *sāt* in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*.

For if the designation were to apply only to the primary suffix (*taddhita*) itself and not to what ends in it, then because *sāti* would be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the prohibition of the retroflex *ṣ* would already be established by its status as the beginning of a word (*pada*) when followed by a case-ending (*sup*); thus, the inclusion of *sāt* in the rule would be purposeless.
It might be so;
however, in rules such as *supi sthaḥ*, an effort must be made regarding the mention of *sub* (nominal suffixes) to ensure that the term *upapada* applies to the word ending in that suffix.
The indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) in the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam*.

Since *suP* and *tiṅ* are suffixes (*pratyaya*), their status as being "ending in" those suffixes would be established by the very paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix; therefore, the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) here would be purposeless.
Thus ends the fourth section, the Kāraka-pāda, in the Paribhāṣāvṛtti.
Thus ends the first chapter. || 1 ||
When a nominal stem (prātipadika) is mentioned [in a grammatical rule], that which is qualified by gender is also included.
Wherever a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, there the inclusion of that which is qualified by gender—that is, feminine stems ending in *ṅī* and *āp*—also occurs.
Here, by the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*), the suffixes such as *aṣṭan* and others, which are the causes for the manifestation of gender, are understood;
this is because the term for the designation is applied metaphorically to the designated object.
Therefore, just as here [in Pāṇini’s grammar] *kyaṣ* occurs after roots such as *lohita-*— as in *lohitāyate*— so too here [in this context] we have *lohinīyate*.
Just as [the rule] "after a pronoun, the third case ending may also be used" results in *bhavatā hetunā* here, so it is here as well.
So it is here as well with the word "hetunā. Some say that just as the collection of male elephants is called *hāstika*,
so too they say the collection of female elephants is *hāstika*.
And that is incorrect;

because even prior to the application of the suffix *ṭhak*, the rule "for a *bha* stem ending in a vowel before a non-ṭhita suffix" (*bhasyāḍhe taddhite*) would cause the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Nor is there a prohibition of the masculine form by the rule "and [in the case] of a genus" (*jāteśca*), since that prohibition does not apply to what is added as a supplementary rule (*aupasaṅkhyānika*).

Furthermore, in the case of the form *pravāhaṇeyī-bhārya*, although the prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule *jāteśca* would already have been established, the rule *vṛddhinimittasya ca taddhitasyāraktavikāre* was stated again to prohibit the masculine treatment.

The specific prescription of the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the final syllable of the second member in the word *pravāhaṇa*— namely, that it ends in the suffix *ḍha*— serves to indicate that the rule *jāteśca* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

Therefore, it has been explained in the *Nyāsa* that the prohibition [of the *puṃvadbhāva*] prescribed by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) "and after a word denoting genus" (*jāteśca*) does not apply here;
and this is indeed necessary.

Otherwise, even in the case of *hāstikam*, where the suffix *ṭhak* is added according to Pāṇini 4.2.51 (*bhasyāḍhaḥ*), the *puṃvadbhāva* would not occur because of the prohibition by the rule "and after a word denoting genus" (Pāṇini 6.3.41).

If it is argued that in the rule *bhasyāḍhe* (Pāṇini 1.4.18), the locative case is a *taddhita*-locative (denoting the condition for the application of a suffix) rather than a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*), we say no;
for in the rule *bhikṣādibhyo’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.38), it has already been explained as a locative of scope.

Indeed, it was stated there that the inclusion of the word *yuvati* [in the *bhikṣādi* list] is for the purpose of prohibiting the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel follows, as in the example *yauvatam*.
Otherwise, since the word *yuvati* ends in the suffix *tip* and begins with an unaccented vowel, the rule *anudāttāder añ* would apply; thus, [the present rule] would serve to block that *añ*.
Furthermore, Rākṣita has stated that in the rule *aṇiñoranārṣayoḥ*, this [locative case] functions as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).
To this, it is replied:

Those who maintain that the word *yuvati* is included in the *bhikṣādi* group in the rule *bhikṣādibhyo ṇaḥ* solely for the purpose of preventing the application of the suffix *añ*—which would otherwise apply by the rule *anudāttādeśca*—should be understood according to this view.
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāgavṛtti states: "A collection of young women is *yauvana*."
And it is seen thus: "The life of that merit-maker is fruitful, for whom there is a servant endowed with beauty and charm, skilled in the arts, and in the prime of youth."
In this very view, Rakṣita has stated in the *ṅyāpprātipadika* sūtra that "a collection of female elephants is *hāstikam*" is an example of this paribhāṣā.

Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that the prescription of a compound for "yuvan" and "jaratī" in the rule *yuvā khalatipalitavalinajaradbhiḥ*—which falls under the heading of *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality)—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this paribhāṣā.
Otherwise, if this [paribhāṣā] did not exist, a compound would be impossible because grammatical coreferentiality between these two [terms] would be untenable.
To this it is replied:
But surely, even though the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) exists, the compound is indeed untenable because "young woman" (*yuvati*) and "old woman" (*jaratī*) have different meanings. To explain:
A young woman is one in her second stage of life;
an old woman, however, is designated as "vṛddhā" (an aged woman).
It is said:
A young woman is like an old woman due to the absence of fickleness;
or an old woman is like a young woman due to fickleness—thus there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "young woman" and "old woman.
If it is so, then a young man is like an old woman because of his swollen breasts.
And because of the absence of a beard [in the case of the old woman].
Likewise, just as a young man [is called] "old" due to boldness, so too here there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); how then is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) made known?
It is said:

in the case of *yuvajaratī*, when a compound is formed between "youth" (*yuvan*) and "old woman" (*jaratī*), that metaphorical grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not perceived due to its inherent nature;
just as the meaning of "he has eaten with five" is expressed by the word *pañcabhukta*.
And this is inferred from the otherwise inexplicability (*anyathānupapatti*) of the maxim regarding that which is qualified by gender as described by the author of the Bhāṣya and others.
Now, if the communication of the maxim is due to the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
then why is the opposite meaning not communicated?
"When there is the mention of a word qualified by its gender, there is also the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
The purpose [of this rule] is as follows: in the rule *revatījagatīhaviṣyābhyaḥ praśasye*, by the mention of *jagatī*, there is also the mention of *jagat*;
likewise, in the rule *eṇyā ḍhañ*, by the mention of *ṇī*, there is also the mention of *ṇa*.
It is said:

if the contrary meaning were intended, then in the expression "the youth [is accompanied] by ascetics and so forth" (*kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ*), the mention of the feminine forms of "ascetics and so forth" (*śramaṇādīnām*) would be purposeless.
[Objection: Even so, when a compound with *jaratī* (an old woman) is being taught, it would not apply to *jarat* (an old man), as in the case of *yuvajarant*.
This is not so;
in another recension, *jaradbhiḥ* is read.
For the Teacher has instructed his disciples in both ways, and thus both are established; this is the analysis (*nyāsa*) regarding the form *yuvakhalati*.

This is a general technical rule (paribhāṣā) concerning both the domain of prescriptions regarding the essential form (svarūpa-vidhi) and the domain of prescriptions regarding what is not the essential form (asvarūpa-vidhi).
They also cite a *jñāpaka* [for its existence]:
namely, the word "roṇī."
This designation "ku" is improper because it ends in the nominative case;
in the formulation of a grammatical suffix, the ablative case is required.
In that context, just as the topical (prākaraṇikī) ablative is bypassed [in favor of the one required by the rule], so too should this be understood.
Likewise, there is also this statement: "There is no *tadantavidhi* (the rule of extension to what ends with a stem) when a nominal base (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix.
By this, just as the suffix *aṇ* occurs in *rauṇa*, so too does it occur in *ajakarauṇa*.
Now, one might object: "The statement that 'there is no *tadantavidhi* when a nominal base is accompanied by a suffix' prohibits *tadantavidhi* [altogether]."

This base *roṇī* is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because it ends in a feminine suffix. If that is the case, then this [usage] indicates that a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) operates even in cases where a rule does not prescribe its own form.

By means of this, the frequentative form *kumārayati*—derived from *kumārīm ācaṣṭe* ("he describes a young girl")—is established without resorting to excessive strain on the rule regarding the word *bahula*.
And this [suffix] is *anitya* (non-obligatory). That non-obligatoriness is indicated by the inclusion of the word "ghaṭī" in the rule *śaktilāṅgalāṅkuśayaṣṭitomaraghaṭaghaṭī*.
Consequently, by the rule *tenānmahataḥ*, the substitution of *āt* does not occur in the case of *mahatī-priya*.

Regarding the rule *dviṣatparayos tāpeḥ*, the author of the Vṛtti explains that in the case of *dviṣatīṃ tāpayati*, the suffix *khac* does not occur because of the mention of two *t* sounds (*dvitakāraka*). Furthermore, regarding the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*, the absence of the suffix *ṭac* in the word *mahārājñī* is stated in the Vṛtti because the word *rājan* has been placed first [in the compound].

In the rule concerning the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-grahaṇe*), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) occurs; and this arises from the application of the paribhāṣā: "A rule concerning words applies only when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*).

The meaning of this technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is as follows: "An operation (*vidhi*) on words occurs when they possess semantic competency (*samartha*). Furthermore, in this context, the word *vidhi* is derived in the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*).
That which is enjoined is an injunction (*vidhi*). It is not an injunction in the sense of an action-noun (*bhāva-sādhana*), such as "the act of enjoining" (*vidhānam*);
nor is it an injunction in the sense of a locative-noun (*adhikaraṇa-sādhana*), such as "that in which words are enjoined" (*padāni vidhīyante 'smin*) called a *pada-vidhi*.

In the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*, the suffix *ki* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *lyuṭ*. In that context, the employment of the long technical term "upapada" in the rule *tatra upapadaṃ saptamīstham* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the inclusion of the definition of the object (*karman*).

For this long technical term "upapada" is a descriptive designation (*anvartha-saṃjñā*); thus, because the maxim regarding semantic competency (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) is brought into play by it, the suffix *aṇ* [which would otherwise apply] in the sense of an object does not occur in the case of *mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti*, since there is a lack of semantic competency due to the dependence [of the word *mahāntam* on another].

It does not occur; and this very point is established by the people [of the tradition] thus: that here there is the inclusion of the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*) as the means of action (*karmasādhana*), and not otherwise.
As for that which is stated there by Maitreya— "vidhi" is prescribed [as a masculine noun]—
by this he indicates that the suffix *ki* occurs after the verbal root *vidh*.
For the suffix *lyuṭ* (which forms "vidhāna") would otherwise supersede the suffix *ki* when it denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, the rule of optional non-identity of suffixes (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply there, because of the statement: "The rule of optional non-identity of suffixes does not apply in the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and suffixes having the sense of *khala*.

Moreover, since the roots *dhā* preceded by *ni-* and *ava-* and the root *dā* preceded by *vi-* have the meaning of "to do" (*karoti*), they function as [verbs of] giving (*saṃpradāna*) and taking away (*apādāna*).
Although a derivation based on the sense of "action" (*bhāva-sādhana*) is possible, it has been rejected by the author of the *Nyāsa*.

Regarding that which was stated—that there is no *kip* suffix in that locative context—that is incorrect; for when the word *pada* is used as the object (*karman*) in composition, there is indeed a *kip* suffix as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *lyuṭ* suffix, according to the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*. Thus it is said.

Just as [the rule] was stated by Nyāsakāra beginning with a purely injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*), there is no fault because Maitreya has likewise formulated it in that manner. For instance, since there is an absence of a verbal object (*karman*) as a subordinate element (*upapada*) there, the application of the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca* does not occur.

[Objection: Even so, since the word *pada* is subsequently connected with the object (*karman*), this [word] falls within the scope of the suffix *kip*; thus, having set aside the scope of the exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*) cannot apply the suffix *lyuṭ*, according to the principle that "the general rule applies after the scope of the exception has been excluded.
[Reply: It is said:

On the view that the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied first, because it is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned), it cannot be sublated by the *kip* suffix, just as the *lṛṭ* suffix is not sublated by the *luṭ* suffix in the expression "he will do tomorrow" (*śvaḥ kariṣyati*).
However, this is incorrect;
in the case of "he will do tomorrow," the sublation of *luṭ* by *lṛṭ* is indeed appropriate.
They say that because the *luṭ* suffix is not prescribed in connection with a subordinate word (*upapada*),
whereas the *kvip* suffix is prescribed in connection with an object as a subordinate word, the refinement of the sentence (*vākya-saṃskāra*) alone is always appropriate.
In the context of a case ending, there is the inclusion of that which is qualified by gender.

The *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender) does not apply to grammatical operations that depend on case-endings (*vibhakti*). Consequently, in the case of *gomatī*, the augment *num* prescribed by the rule *ugidacām* does not occur; likewise, in the case of *supuṃsī*, the substitute *asuṅ* prescribed for the word *puṃs-* does not occur.
In the example *yuvatīḥ paśya*, the semi-vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) does not occur because of the rule *śvayuvamaghonām ataddhite*.

Others, however, say that because of the word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *allopo 'naḥ* into *al* and *lopaḥ anaḥ*, and because of its connection with the mention of *aṅga* [in the preceding rule], there is semi-vowel substitution for *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* when they end in the suffix *an*.
And this is correct.

Otherwise, if by this *paribhāṣā* the absence of *saṃprasāraṇa* were understood, then when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *yuvan* according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*, the form *yuvatī* would necessarily undergo *saṃprasāraṇa*. Furthermore, this *paribhāṣā* is cited in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *yuvoranākau*, and it is explained by the author of the *Nyāsa* on the rule *matuvasoru*.
The authority [of this] is established by this much alone. || 29 ||
Thus ends the section on *samartha* (syntactic connection) in the *Paribhāṣāvṛtti* composed by Sīradeva.
In the Sūtra, gender and number are not restrictive.

In the rule "by that action, [he gives] to whomsoever he intends," the use of the masculine gender (*yam*) and the singular number (*ekavacanena*) is not restrictive; therefore, the designation applies even when there is a different gender or a different number. For example:
*brāhmaṇyai dadāti* ("he gives to a Brāhmaṇī") and *brāhmaṇebhyo dadāti* ("he gives to Brāhmaṇas").
This point is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*).

In the Sūtra, gender and number are employed according to the analogy of grain and its husk. Furthermore, there is an indicator (jñāpaka) for this: the inclusion of the word "one" (*eka*) in the rule *ā kaḍārād ekā saṃjñā*, as well as the inclusion of the word "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) in the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*.

However, in the rule *dyadbhyo luṅi*, although a singular form should have been used for the reference, the fact that a plural is employed indicates by its very force (*sāmarthya*) that this [rule] does not apply here.
That which is connected with a negative particle (nañ) denotes something else similar [to that which it negates], because such is the meaning. 30.

Therefore, in the rule *añceś chandasy asarvanāmasthānam*, the term *asarvanāmasthāna* is understood to refer to a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that resembles a *sarvanāmasthāna*. The meaning of this has been explained in the Bhāṣya: "That which is joined with *nañ* or *iva* applies to something else that is similar."
And it should be understood that *evaṃ cānyat* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) resembling a word ending in the nominative case, used in the sense of "in another [instance].
Furthermore, another says:
"A word-form joined with *nañ* or *iva* functions in reference to something similar."
Why?
Because it means that the form of the word is other than the form of the word expressing the primary meaning.
Thus, by means of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the word "as it were" (*iva*), [the secondary meaning] is distinguished from the primary meaning.
The word is established according to its object;
that is to say,
"object" means that exactly such an object is cognized.
By this, he demonstrates that the understanding of this meaning is established through common experience;
and this very understanding has been made manifest by the Teacher while composing the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*).
For it is as follows:
The word *abrāhmaṇa* is a compound formed by the negative particle *nañ* with the word *brāhmaṇa*, which is used here in the sense of a *kṣatriya*.
Precisely for this reason, by means of the negative particle, [the referent] is excluded from its primary meaning and established in a secondary sense.

This is just as in the case of *nīlotpalam* ("blue lotus"), where the compound "that which is blue and that which is a lotus" excludes the lotus from qualities other than blue, thereby establishing the lotus as possessing the quality of being blue.
However, this is the distinction:
when this word "brāhmaṇa" is used alone, it conveys its primary meaning due to conventional usage;
but it conveys a secondary meaning through its proximity to the negative particle (nañ).
In that case, because the meaning of "kṣatriya" is expressed through metaphorical usage (upacara),
the negative particle (nañ) is thus explained as functioning by way of exclusion (paryudāsa).
And in this way, the predominance of the meaning of the final member (uttarapada-pradhānatā) is established for the *tatpuruṣa* compound "abrāhmaṇa."
And when that [negation] exists, the use of the singular number in the word "aneka" (not-one) is established.
For instance,

it is observed in common usage that when a meaning such as duality is understood through the force of error, and a single object is figuratively attributed to it, that [single object] is perceived upon the presence of the negative particle *nañ*.
Likewise, when a word such as "one" (*eka*) is employed to denote an object to which unity has been superimposed, it is used in its own inherent number.
For example, in the figurative expression "Sāṃkāśya is four *yojanas*," the singular number is appropriate.

However, when duality or another number is superimposed upon an object that lacks duality and so forth, and the distinction between those [superimposed] numbers is relied upon, then there is a corresponding difference in the grammatical number of the word denoting it.

Just as [the rule] "after roots ending in *dyu* and after *vṛt* etc., in the *luṅ* tense, and after [roots] beginning with *vṛt*, before *syas* and *san*" [is applied], so too, by adopting this view, usages such as *aneka* and others are established. They state that the mention of *nañ* here, when the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, is merely illustrative (*prāyikatva*).

Because of the inclusion of the term *kāraka* in the rule *akartari ca kārake*, if this [term *kāraka*] were not present, the understanding of a *kāraka* would occur solely through the similarity with the agent (*kartṛ*) when joined with the negative particle *nañ*. Therefore, the negative particle *nañ* is established even in the case of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

"The king’s wives are not to see the sun"—thus, by the power of such expression, negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) like *adharma* and others are seen to signify meanings contrary [to their literal components].
Now, one might object: "In the rule for forming negative compounds, the letter *ñ* need not be used, for there is no other word 'na' that must be excluded; why then is the letter *ñ* employed?"
On this point, it has been explained by Rakṣita in the *Pūrvapakṣa*:
"Even here, there is a purpose [for the rule], namely that when it is said 'not' (*na*), this might not be taken as a prohibitive sūtra.
This is not so.
Because it would result in the futility of injunctive statements,
nor should one postulate an alternation between injunction and prohibition,
since an option is already established by the Mahāvibhāṣā.

Alternatively, if the letter *ñ* were not present in the negative particle *nañ*, its status as a non-indeclinable (*avyaya*) would be established by its own phonetic form; thus, the very hearing of case-endings would preclude its being a prohibitive statement.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of this [term] being taken as the genitive plural form *asmat* (the substitute for *mad*), because a compound ending in a genitive case is already established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* itself.
On this point, they say:

But how can the compound of the word *nañ* ending in the genitive case be designated by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* alone? For, according to the statement that "the elision (*luk*), being a bahiraṅga operation, overrides even antaraṅga rules," the elision of the case-ending would occur prior to the substitution of *nañ* for *na*. Once the elision of the case-ending has taken place, there is an absence of the genitive ending; therefore, the substitution of *nañ* [for *na*] would not apply.
It does not obtain;
nor is there an operation characterized by the sixth case (genitive) ending by means of the characteristic of a condition (*pratyaya*).

This is because, according to the principle that "when there is an extension of a general property, specific properties are not extended," there is no extension of a specific operation belonging to the sixth case.

Furthermore, because the word *vidhi* (rule) is included in the rule *analvidhau*, even a specific [operation] is indeed extended; nevertheless, since the substitute *naṭ* occurs only when there is a case-ending (*vibhakti*)—as indicated by the mention of the word *sthā* [in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*]—there is no substitution of *naṭ* in the absence of a case-ending.

Moreover, if the rule were formulated as *naḥ* instead of *nas*, the *paribhāṣā* "operations that are *antaraṅga* [take effect first]" would not apply, because the substitution of *naṭ* is conditioned by the technical rules governing compound formation (*samāsa-śāstra*).
Therefore, this is to be reflected upon and protected. On this point, some reflect as follows: "The final conclusion (siddhānta) here is exactly the same as the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)."

For just as you suspected that the word *naṣ* [in the rule *naṣ-ṭādau kṛt-i*] might be understood as the genitive plural due to the statement "even internal [elements]," so too have I stated that the compound is established by the very rule "the sixth case [is compounded] with a sixth case. 31.
The rule regarding the compounding of words denoting direction (*gati*), case-roles (*kāraka*), and upapadas with *kṛt*-derived nouns applies prior to the addition of nominal suffixes (*sup*).

Even though the governing rule *sup-supā* (a word ending in a case-suffix is compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix) is in force, the rules *kugatiprādayaḥ*, *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, and *upapadamatiṅ* indicate that this compounding of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* must be understood as occurring prior to the derivation of the case-ending (*sub*). Consequently, in the word *praṣṭhī*, the *gati*-named prefix *pra-* is compounded with the word *stha-*— which is not yet a nominal stem (*asubanta*)— by means of the suffix *ka* added according to *ataścopasargaḥ*, resulting in the compound *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

If, however, there were a compound with a word ending in a *sup* suffix, then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would apply before the *sup* suffixes because it is *antaraṅga*. Consequently, due to the absence of a final long vowel (*ā*), the suffix *ṅīṣ*—prescribed by the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*—would not occur.

Likewise, in the case of the words *aśva* and *dhana*, which have already acquired the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*), the compound is formed with the word *krīta* (which ends in a *kṛt* suffix) according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.

Likewise, because the words *aśvakrīta* and *dhanakrīta* end in the vowel *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies according to the rule *krītāt karaṇapūrvāt*. Similarly, there is a compound of the word *kaccha* with the word *paśabda*, which ends in the suffix *kap*, according to the rule *upapadam atiṅ*.
And thus, because the word *kacchapa* ends in the vowel *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies according to the rule *jāteḥ*, resulting in the form *kacchapī*.

Many other purposes as well have been set forth in the Bhāṣya. Now, one might ask: why is the feminine suffix taught after forming a compound with words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, when it could be established even earlier? For immediately after the production of the *kṛt* suffix, the case-ending (*sup*) arises from the compound and its cause; and since the feminine suffix is more "internal" (*antaraṅga*) than that, it would be applied first by rules such as *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*, thereby correctly deriving forms like *praṣṭhī* and *aśvakrītī*.
Do not say so.

For in that case, since the aggregate beginning with *praṣṭha* would lack the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) due to its ending in a non-kṛt suffix, it would be impossible to form a feminine suffix from that aggregate.
To this, it is replied:

Regarding the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*, one might argue that by the inclusion of the term *kṛt* (primary suffix), and by the paribhāṣā stating "when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included," the entire complex [consisting of the prefix, root, and suffix] indeed possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
This is not so;

for in the rule *arthavadadhāturapratyayaḥ prātipadikam*, the mention of the term *apratyayaḥ* (not being a suffix) would, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix, result in the designation of a nominal stem not applying to that which ends in a suffix.

For this very reason, by the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule], the designation applies to that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix, but not to that which is preceded by a *gati* or *kāraka* even by virtue of the *paribhāṣā* concerning the mention of *kṛt*.

If it were so, then in the sentence *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*, even in the alternative case where there is no compound—by the rule *tṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyatarasyām*—there would have to be elision (*luk*) of the third case ending. Nor should it be argued that, in such a case, the statement regarding optional compounding would be rendered purposeless.

Because the purpose is for the sake of the accent. [The rule] "A kṛt-derivative following a verb root, a kāraka, or an upapada [takes the udātta accent on its final syllable]"— this accent based on a tatpuruṣa compound must not occur.

Furthermore, if the feminine suffix were to occur prior to the compound, then in the case of *prabhāvinī* and *prabhaviṇī*, the final letter of the subsequent member ending in a *ṅī*-suffix would not be the letter *n*. Consequently, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) would not occur according to the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca*.
Although it has been stated here in general terms that [the suffix occurs] "prior to the production of the nominal suffixes (*sup*)," [this specific objection applies].
Nevertheless, a compound occurs only when the *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada* elements are themselves *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix).

Consequently, in the case of *carmakrī* and *carmakārī*, because they end in a case-suffix, the elision of the *n* (in the root *krī*) based on their status as a word (*pada*) is established. Furthermore, in the case of *vaiyākaraṇa*, because it possesses the status of a word (*padatva*), the augment *ai* is applied.
And the authority here is the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, which prescribes the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending.
In this view, because [the word] *abhiprayaṇa* and so forth belong to the *śakandhu*-class, the compound is formed, thereby establishing its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).
Now, one might object: if the case-ending does not remain in the final member of the compound, then that member would lack the status of being a "word" (*pada*).

Furthermore, because the designation "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) would not apply, the non-elision (*aluk*) prescribed when a subsequent member follows would not occur in the case of *sarasijam*.
It is replied:
the designation "subsequent member" is accepted for the subsequent portion of the compound by virtue of its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
This is understood from the governing rule concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*).
And this is necessarily so;

otherwise, even though there is a compound of words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), the status of being a subsequent member would never occur anywhere, because of the statement: "and when it is the subsequent member, [the rules] regarding what is not the beginning of a word apply."
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) has been made known by the author of the *Bhāṣya* through the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* in the rule *upapadam atiṅ*.
As it has been said:
"Since there is the governing rule *sup supā*, there is no possibility of a compound with a verbal form (*tiṅanta*); so what is the purpose of including *atiṅ*?"
Furthermore, that [formation] indicates that the rule *sup-supā* (a noun with a noun) does not apply to these two types of compounds.

Consequently, it is established that the prescription for the compounding of prefixes (*gati*), objects (*kāraka*), and adjuncts (*upapada*) with primary derivatives (*kṛt*) occurs prior to the addition of nominal suffixes (*sub*).

Now, one might object: if the compounding of prefixes and the like with another word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) occurs before the addition of the nominal suffix, then this would also apply to the entire collection consisting of a verbal root and its prefix (*dhātu-upasarga-samudāya*).
And in this way, the case-ending would arise from the combination of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the prefix (*upasarga*).
It is said:
under the view that "the verbal root is first joined with the suffix" (*sādhana*), this [objection] must be resolved.
This [sūtra] has two meanings,
as explained by the author of the Nyāsa regarding the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*:

one meaning is that the compounding of prefixes (*gati*), agents (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) occurs only with *kṛt*-suffixal stems, and that this takes place prior to the addition of case-endings (*sup*).
The second [view] holds that the compounding of *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada* occurs without distinction with *kṛt*-affixes, but before the production of case-endings (*sup*).
In that second view, there would be compounding even in the case of *prapacatitarām*.
However, some maintain that the compounding of *gati* and the others with *kṛt*-affixes occurs only with that which already possesses a case-ending (*subanta*).
And likewise, it was stated by Rakṣita in the rule *upapadaṃ tiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19):

"Just as there is a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) in the example *dhanakrītā*, so too there is one in *uraḥkeṇa*. Consequently, the substitution of *s* [for *t*] prescribed by the rule *so 'padādau* (Pāṇini 8.3.38) does not occur."

It is argued that when the word *uraḥ* is compounded with a word ending in a *su*-affix that itself ends in the suffix *kap*, the *s*-substitution prescribed by the rule *so'padādau* does not occur because the *k* is at the beginning of a *pada*.
This, however, is incorrect.
For even though there is a compound with a word ending in a *su*-affix, the *s*-substitution must nevertheless take place.

Because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule regarding the application of suffixes when there is an "uttarapada" (subsequent member) and in rules concerning what is not the beginning of a word (*apadādi*),
the word *ka-* lacks the status of a *pada* since it ends in the suffix *am*. To this, it is replied:

Regarding the rule *uttarapadatve cāpadādividhau* (P. 1.4.16), this prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of suffixal rules) does not operate when the prohibition *so'padādau* (P. 8.3.38) is to be applied. That the rule *gatikārakopapadānām* (P. 6.2.139) is merely occasional (*prāyika*) and that the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* does not apply in the case of *so'padādau*, is understood from the fact that the substitution of *satva* (the change of *s* to *ś*) is specifically prescribed (*nipātana*) in the word *bhāskārānta*. To explain: * **The occasional nature of P. 6.2.139:** This is established because if the rule were universal, the form *kāraka* (where the prefix *pra-* is elided by P. 2.2.18) would require the substitution of *śatva* for the initial *s* of *kāraka* by P. 8.3.38, since *pra-* is a *gati* and *kāraka* is its object (*upapada*). However, the form *kāraka* appears without *śatva* in the Veda (e.g., *kārakam*), which shows that P. 6.2.139 is not universally applicable. * **The non-application of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* in P. 8.3.38:** This is established by the specific prescription of *satva* in *bhāskārānta*. If the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* did not apply here, the *s* of *anta* would have been changed to *ś* by P. 8.3.38 (since *anta* begins with *a*, which is not a *pada*), making the specific prescription of *satva* redundant. Its necessity proves that the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* prohibition does indeed apply to prevent such a change. Thus, the rule *uttarapadatve...* prevents the application of suffixal rules when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is involved, provided that the operation in question is not one that applies to the beginning of a word (*apadādau*). Since the prohibition in *so'padādau* is an operation on the beginning of a word, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule remains active there. This is why the *satva* is prescribed in *bhāskārānta*; otherwise, the *s* would have been changed to *ś* by the general rule of *so'padādau*. Therefore, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* prohibition does not operate in the context of *so'padādau*.

If the compound occurs before the case-ending (*sup*) on the basis of the rule *gatikārakopapadānām*, then in the word *bhāskaraḥ*, the substitution of *s* (by *so’padādau*) is established precisely because of the absence of being an "uttermost member" (*uttarapada*).

Alternatively, since this paribhāṣā is only generally applicable (*prāyika*), the compound in *bhāskaraḥ* may consist of two items ending in case-endings; even so, by the prohibition of the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*) in the rule *uttarapadatve cāpadādividhau*, there is an absence of *pada*-status, and thus [the rule] *so’padādau* applies.
Thus, existence would be established;
it serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the meaning already stated. This is the purpose of the indicator.
In examples such as *uraḥkeṇa*, there is an absence of *satva* (the substitution of *s*) by the rule *so 'padādau*.

Now, one might object: "If the compound occurs prior to the case-ending (*sup*), then since the letter *k* would not be at the beginning of a word (*apadādi*), the rule *so 'padādau* would apply, and *satva* would occur in the form *ayaḥkrītī*. It is replied: [this is not so].
One might think that a living being (*satva*) must necessarily exist here;
or else, because of the enumeration [of suffixes] in the rule *pāśakalpakakāmyeṣu* under the heading *so 'padādau*, [the substitution] does not occur.
If this is the case, then let the enumeration *pāśakalpakakāmyeṣu* not be made at all.

Regarding the inclusion of the term *satva* in the rule for *bhāskārānta*, let it simply be understood that by its own force (*sāmarthya*), the substitution of *satva* does not occur in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

Consequently, since the absence of *satva* in forms such as *ayaḥkrītī* is established by that very principle, the explicit enumeration [of these cases] in the rule *pāśakalpakakāmyeṣu* is indeed purposeless. || 35 ||
Thus ends the second quarter in the commentary on the Paribhāṣās.
In some cases, even regarding the domain of an exception, a general rule still applies.
Therefore, in the case of *kāñcanī vāsayaṣṭiḥ*, the suffix *añ* occurs by the rule *anudattādeśca* within the scope of the suffix *mayaṭ* prescribed by the rule *nityaṃ vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ*.
Likewise, in the phrase *pradīyatāṃ dāśarathāya maithilī*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs by the rule *prāg dīvyato’ṇ* within the scope of the rule *ata iñ*.
However, another says:

Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "of capable [bases], the first two," the form *dāśarathāya* is established by the suffix *aṇ* [applied by the rule] "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) in the alternative where the suffix *iñ* is absent.
However, this is incorrect;
for where a general rule (*utsarga*) is optional (*vibhāṣā*), the general rule does not apply to a domain that is exempted by the exceptional rule (*apavāda*).
This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *pīlāyā vā*.
However, the inclusion of the word *vā* (or) serves the purpose of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

Regarding the compound meaning such as "the offspring of Daśaratha" (*daśarathāpatyam*), the author of the *Nyāsa* has stated that the recurrence of the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) from the rule *daivayajñi-śaucivṛkṣi-sātyamugri-kāṇḍeviddhibhyo 'nyatarasyām* applies here as well.

And here there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*): in the example *kaṭaṃ kārako vrajati*, the prohibition of the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*) when used with a future passive participle ending in *-aka-*—by the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadadhamaṛṇyayoḥ*—is established.
For that [prohibition] is only logical if, in the domain of the exception *aṇ karmaṇi ca*, the general rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* applies; otherwise, it would not be so.
Now, one might object: by the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), the suffix *-ṇvul* is indeed already established even in the domain of the exception *aṇ karmaṇi ca*.
Whence, then, is there proof?
It is said:
when a verb is used as an upapada (governing word) for the sake of another action, the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*asarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply.

Since the suffix *ṇvul* is already established by the rule *ṇvultṛcau*, the fact that *tumun* and *ṇvul* are prescribed again by the rules *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām* and *lṛṭ śeṣe ca* in this specific domain indicates [the following].
Otherwise, since *ṇvul* would have been established in the domain of *lṛṭ* by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vā'sarūpa*) alone, he would not have prescribed it again.
Since he has done so, it is understood that in this domain, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not apply by virtue of the rule of non-identity of form.
But surely, if there were no purpose, it would not be an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

And there is indeed a purpose for [the rule] *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyām*: namely, that the suffix *ṇvul* should apply in the sense of future time. Consequently, in the rule *akenoḥ bhaviṣyad-adharmaṇyayoḥ*, because the *akan* suffix prescribed under the heading of "future" (*bhaviṣyat*) is understood, there is a prohibition of the genitive case in examples such as *varṣaśatasya pūrakaḥ* ("filler of a hundred years") and *putrapautrāṇāṃ darśakaḥ* ("beholder of sons and grandsons").
It does not occur. It is said:
the intention of those who maintain that this is an *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) is that there is no fault here, because the suffix *ak* prescribed for the future tense is included therein.
For instance,
in the expression "the completer of a hundred years," the word "completer" does not refer to a future time;
for by the very context, general rules (utsarga) operate everywhere except in cases where they are set aside by exceptions (apavāda).
For this very reason, in the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyā-caturthyau ceṣṭāyāmanadhvani*, the mention of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is made;
otherwise, it would have been stated simply as *caturthī ca*.
By the force of including the word "and" (*ca*), the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix will not occur, as in *grāmaṃ gantā* or *grāmāya gantā*.
In the Bhāṣya, however, the sūtra itself is rejected.
As it has been said: "For what purpose is this stated?"
So that the fourth case may occur:
although the second case is established by the rule "karmaṇi" alone,
and the fourth case is also established by the rule "saṃpradāne" alone, [the desired application] is not established.
That which one intends through an action is called the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). And here, one does not intend the village by means of an object (*karman*), but rather by means of an activity.
By what activity? By the activity of going.
"And the mention of 'action' (kriyā) is extended there as well.
Regarding this, it was stated by Rakṣita in the Bhāṣya:
"Just as the sūtra has been rejected in the Bhāṣya..."
Likewise, in the expression "he goes to a beautiful village" (*śobhanaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati*), the adverbial modifier would not possess the status of an object (*karman*).

Furthermore, in the expression "it is gone to the village" (*grāmāya gamyate*), because the verb would be intransitive (*akarmaka*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) would have to appear in the impersonal passive sense (*bhāve*).
To this, it is replied:
Now, what kind of verbal artifice is this? Since the rule beginning with "gaty-artha" (Pāṇini 1.4.52) exists, that which qualifies an action is treated as an object;
thus, the expression "he goes to a beautiful village" (*śobhanaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati*) is established.

Since the *gaty-arthādi* sūtra exists, the action of going (*gati-kriyā*)—which has become the object through various actions such as praying or resolving—is qualified [by the word *śobhana*]. Consequently, because the rule "the inclusion of the action [as the qualifier] must be stated so that the object may be beautiful" does not apply universally, the form *śobhanaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to a beautiful village") occurs.

Likewise, because the village is pervaded by the action of going, it possesses the status of an object (*karman*); and since the object is expressed by the *L*-suffix in the case of the object (*karmaṇi lakāre*), only the form *grāmo gamyate* ("the village is being gone to") occurs.
Because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *lakāra* suffix is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), resulting in the form *grāmāya gamyate*.

However, in the absence of the rule "tatprayojaka... (Pāṇini 1.4.55), one must state that the status of recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) is to be expressed by the inclusion of the word "action" (*kriyāgrahaṇam*) in order to establish the form *grāmāya gacchati*.
The meaning of this [inclusion] is: "that which one intends to reach through the action, namely the object (*karman*), becomes the recipient."

In this context, regarding the expression "he goes to the village" (*grāmāya gacchati*), the action of going possesses the status of an object (*karman*) because it is pervaded by actions such as praying for or resolving upon [the destination].
To illustrate: someone desiring a result perceives that result, thinking, "this is the fruit of this [action]."
Having seen [the object], one desires it;
thereafter, one resolves to act upon it.

Since the action of intending is the cause and the motive for the action, even though the actions of desiring and resolving are themselves being understood [as objects], the action of going possesses the status of an object (*karman*).
And thus, because the village is connected with the action of going—which has become an object—the status of *saṃpradāna* (recipient) arises.

For this very reason, it was stated regarding this alternative that in the sentence "he goes to the village for the sake of protection" (*rakṣitena grāmāya gamyate*), the *lakāra* suffix would appear in the impersonal (*bhāva*) voice due to the verb being intransitive.

Furthermore, in the case of "he goes to a beautiful village" (*śobhanaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati*), one must explain the distinction between actions such as "requesting" (*prārthanā*) in accordance with the use of the accusative case for the object.

Furthermore, since the action of going (*gati*) lacks the status of being an object (*karman*), how could its qualifier possess the status of an object? Thus it was rightly stated that a qualifier of an action cannot have the status of an object, as in the case of "he goes to a beautiful village" (*śobhanaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati*).

[Objection: But even when one intends to express a distinction between actions such as requesting and so forth, since the village is pervaded by the action of going, it acquires the status of an object according to the rule "that which is most desired by the agent is the object" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*). Moreover, because the word "action" (*kriyā*) must be explicitly mentioned [in the definition], there would also be the status of recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

In that case, because it is established by the technical designation *karman* (object) due to its higher priority, in the expression "he goes to a beautiful village" (*śobhanaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati*), even though the verbal root itself is transitive, the *lakāra* suffix will not occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*).

It is argued: if this were so, then in the expression "he goes for a beautiful village" (*śobhanaṃ grāmāya gacchati*), the dative case would also not occur, because the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) would be sublated by the status of the object (*karman*).
How, then, was the Sūtra rejected in the Bhāṣya? It is said:
in the case of *grāmāya gacchati* ("he goes to the village"), by means of the prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), it receives only the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

Similarly, in the case of "the village is gone to" (*grāmo gamyate*), where the meaning of the *l*-suffix denotes the object (*karman*), because there is no distinction in actions such as requesting and so forth, the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is that in the sentence "he goes to a beautiful village" (*śobhanaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati*), the word "beautiful" (*śobhanam*) must be explained as having a distinct relation of being the object (*karmatva*), whereas for the word "village" (*grāmam*), there is indeed non-distinction (*abheda*). // 33 //
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Unexpressed," in the commentary on the Paribhāṣās.
The suffix *lyap*, being external (*bahiraṅga*), supersedes even internal (*antaraṅga*) grammatical operations.
Since a compound is based on two words, it is *bahiraṅga* (external) and thus overrides *antaraṅga* (internal) rules that involve suffixes ending in *-lyap*.

Consequently, in the case of *pradhāya*, the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā*—as prescribed by the rule *dadhāter hiḥ*—does not occur; likewise, in the case of *pradāya*, the substitution of *t* [for the final vowel] as prescribed by the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* does not occur.
And the proof for this is the inclusion of the term *lyap* in the rule *jagdhiḥ lyapi kiti*, at the very beginning [of the section].

For otherwise, in the case of *prajagdhya*, since the substitution of *jagdhi* would be established by the rule "before a suffix beginning with *t* that has the *k*-marker" (*kiti*) due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) even while the suffix is still in the state of *ktvā*, he would not have included the word *lyapi*.
Thus it has been said:
"Once *jagdhi* is established, because it is *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *lyap* is prescribed by the rule *ti-kit-i*.
This indicates that *antaraṅga* operations are superseded by *lyap*.
Now, just as the substitute *jagdhi* is *antaraṅga*, so too is the substitute *lyap* *nitya*.
Because it would follow that [the substitution] applies both to what has been performed and what has not been performed.
Thus, since the two suffixes *ni* and *antaraṅga* are subsequent, the suffix *lyap* ought to occur;
therefore, the mention of *lyap* is for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution of *jagdhi* takes place when *lyap* follows—how then can this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?
It is said that the substitution *jagdhi-* is also obligatory,
because even when the substitution *lyap* has been applied, that [obligatoriness] applies by virtue of the *asiddha-paribhāṣā*.

Now, in the case of *prajagdhyā*, how can the letter *l* in *lyap* receive the designation *it*, given that since the substitution *lyap* is not prescribed within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for suffixes (*pratyaya*), it lacks the status of being a suffix?
With the word *pratyayasya* (of the suffix) understood from the previous context, the letter *i* at the beginning of a suffix receives the designation *it*.
Otherwise, if the *ś* of the root *śīṅ* were to receive the *it* designation, it would serve as a qualifier in the rule *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.3.11).
For if [the rule] were stated simply as *īṅ*, it would include the root *īṅ* (meaning "to go") as well.

Because this [suffix] possesses the status of a suffix by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva* substitute, it receives the designation *it*. If this is so, then the objection raised by Rakṣita regarding the rule *dvigurekavacanam*— namely, that if the technical term "singular" (*ekavacana*) were understood here, then since this [suffix] is not prescribed within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of suffixes, it would lack the status of a suffix, and consequently the *nakāra* of the singular case-ending *pañcamī-ekavacana* (the ablative suffix *-tas*) would not receive the designation *it*—

For instance, in the case of the word *pañcapalī* when the alternative of non-elision (*anantyapakṣa*) is adopted, because it has multiple referents, once the suffixes *bhyas* and so forth are applied, and subsequently the singular suffixes of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and others are applied in their place, the status of being a "substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*) still exists there as before; thus, the designation *it* would result.

To this it is replied: just as *lyap* is prescribed in the place of the suffix *tkā*, the suffixes *ṅasi* and so forth are not prescribed in the same manner once *bhyas* and the others have been applied.

Rather, since the plural number would have applied when there are many [objects], the singular number and the suffixes beginning with *ṅasi* are prescribed. In the case of the suffixes kta, lyuṭ, tumun, and those having the sense of khala, the rule regarding "non-identity of form" (vāsarūpavidhi) does not apply.

Therefore, the *kta* suffix and the *lyuṭ* suffix in the neuter sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) always supersede the *ghañ* suffix in the same sense; thus, one does not say *hāsam* for "laughing" or "laughter," but rather *hasanam* or *hasitam*.

Likewise, when words expressing desire are used as adjuncts (*upapada*) with verbs having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*), these two—the *tumun* suffix and the *liṅ* and *loṭ* moods—always supersede [the *ghañ*].
Regarding the expression "he wishes to eat" (*icchati bhoktum*): likewise, by the rule *āto yuc*, the suffix *khal* in the rule *iṣad-duḥ-su-ṣu* always sublates [the former];
thus, "the Soma becomes easily drunk" (*īṣatpānaḥ somaḥ*).

However, where suffixes such as *kta* and others are themselves the exceptions (*apavāda*)—that is to say, where they are the general rules (*utsarga*) [in relation to other suffixes]—then the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpavidhi*) certainly applies to any other suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) that is an exception occurring prior to the section on feminine derivations (*stryadhikāra*).

For example, regarding the rule for the suffix *ac*, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for words such as *bhaya*; thus, even though *lyuṭ* falls within the domain of *ac*, it also occurs by the rule of non-identity of form, resulting in both *bhayam* and *bhayanam*, as well as *varṣam* and *varṣaṇam*.
And the authority for this is the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya: "The word *vṛṣabha* [is derived] from the root *vṛṣ* because of the sense of 'pouring' (*varṣaṇāt*).

however, the suffix *lyuṭ* indeed occurs by virtue of the rule of non-identity of form (*vā'sarūpavidhi*)."

In the rule *ktalyuṭtumunkhalartheṣu*, the term *kta* refers to the neuter *kta* suffix,
because of its association with *lyuṭ*; that is, because the *kta* suffix is understood here as being co-referential (*sahacarita*) with *lyuṭ*.

Furthermore, because the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* prescribes the present tense (*laṭ*) in the domain of the suffix *kta*— meaning "one who studies that" or "one who knows that"— otherwise, the present tense would be superseded by the rule *ñītaḥ ktaḥ*, and the form *medyati* would not occur.

It is not, however, purposeless, because its meaning is clear;
and this [purpose] is indeed necessary.

Otherwise, even if there were a general apprehension [of the suffix], the *kta* suffix prescribed after the root *svap-* could not be sublated, because of the functional capacity of the inclusion of the augment *ñi* in the rule for *ñi-svap-*. Thus, if the suffix *lyuṭ*—being prescribed in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*)—is understood to be included by virtue of the apprehension of the *kta* suffix prescribed in the sense of "state," then one would simply have prescribed *lyuṭ* without having prescribed *kta* at all.
For this very reason, [the form] *hāsam* will not occur.
However, the mention of the suffix *lyuṭ* must not be rejected, because the suffix *kta* does not occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) after transitive roots.
In that context, by the force of employing both forms, the *lyuṭ* prescribed as a general rule is understood.

Therefore, it is rightly stated that because there is no application of the *asarūpa* rule [which allows for alternative suffixes] when a suffix ending in *lyuṭ* is used as the instrument, the suffix *ac* does not occur.
And this must necessarily be so;
otherwise, the commentary (*vṛtti*) stating that "there are seventeen suffixes" in the rule beginning with *vuñ-chaṇ* would be incorrect.

Because by the rule *parimāṇākhyāyām*, the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed, thereby superseding the vowel-ending [suffixes]. Now, if this were so, then the statements made by Rakṣita regarding the rule *vā'sarūpo'striyām*— namely, that "the neuter *kta* suffix, when accompanied by *lyuṭ*, is always desired as a superseder"—

and likewise the statement made regarding the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*— namely, that "in the context of *ktalyuṭtumunkhalartheṣu*, the neuter *kta* suffix is understood as being accompanied by *lyuṭ*"— would be incorrect.
It is said:

here, the association with the suffix *lyuṭ* is not intended for the sake of expressing the neuter gender; rather, it is for the sake of a rule together with *lyuṭ*. That is to say: "The suffixes *kta* and *lyuṭ* are used in the sense of a neuter abstract action (*napuṃsake bhāve*)."
The intention of the author of the *Anunyāsa*, however, is as follows:

in the rule *ktalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is understood to be prescribed only for the abstract action (*bhāva*), because of its association with *tumun*. The mention of both [suffixes] is for the sake of clarity.
And this must also be stated by you:
for even in the view that there is a grasping of the universal (*sāmānya*), the mention of the suffix *kta* is indeed purposeless.
Just as it was stated that, because of the suffix *lyuṭ* [denoting] instrument or locus, the suffix *ac* does not occur due to the absence of the rule for non-identical forms (*asarūpa-vidhi*).

Likewise, even with the suffix *lyuṭ* [denoting an abstract state], since there is no absence of the rule for non-identical forms (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*), the suffix *ñ* [and thus *ghañ*] does not occur; consequently, the form *hāsam* will not arise.
Nor should it be argued that because of the inclusion of the term "grasping" (*grahaṇa*), the absence of the rule for non-identical forms applies only to the *lyuṭ* denoting instrument or locus.
For if that were understood, there would be no purpose [for the specific mention].

Is it not the case that this is the purpose: so that when [the suffix] *kta* follows transitive roots, it does not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), but rather [the form] "kāram" is produced? For if there were a general inclusion of *lyuṭ*, then "kāram" would not occur, because *lyuṭ* would supplant *ghañ*.
It is said in reply:
For that which is undesirable is not produced by a grammatical indicator (*jñāpaka*), since a teacher’s indicator serves only to indicate what is intended.
Therefore, because both [suffixes] are mentioned here, the *kta* suffix prescribed as a general rule is not understood [to apply].
Thus, in this way, there is no *ac* suffix [applied] to the instrument (*karaṇa*) either by means of the *lyuṭ* suffix or by the rule for non-identical suffixes (*asarūpa*).
Furthermore, under this interpretation, the commentary stating "there are seventeen suffixes" would not be inconsistent;
for in the view that grammatical formation (*pada-saṃskāra*) occurs first, the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is derived [first], and the designation of its quantity is understood only subsequently.
Alternatively, the expression "seventeen suffixes" will be formed by means of the *gha* suffix.

Alternatively, in the derivation of the word *pratyaya* according to the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.18], when the alternative of bodily obstruction (*kāyabādhā*) is adopted, the operation of the suffix *ac* is superseded by the rule for the suffix *lyuṭ*.

Furthermore, under the alternative of mutual rule-obstruction (*śāstrabādha*), the rule for *lyuṭ* is itself superseded by the rule for the suffix *gha*. However, when the suffix is actually applied, the suffix *ac* occurs because it is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned).
Since the suffix *lyu* does not apply when *ac* is not in operation— because the rule for *lyuṭ* has already been superseded by the rule for *gha*—
there is no circularity (*cakraka*).

Regarding the authority for this, the author of the Nyāsa stated that the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the rule *vā'sarūpo'striyām* indicates an understanding of the term as a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Jayāditya stated that the mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes [in the rule] *pra-eṣātisarga* [Pāṇini 3.3.163] was intended for this purpose.
Others say it is because of the mention of *vibhāṣā* in the rule *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu* [Pāṇini 3.4.24]. || 28 ||
In the absence of the present, there is recourse to what has occurred in the past. || 29 ||
In the absence of a present [form], recourse is made to what has occurred previously.
For example, in the case of *vṛkṣaiḥ*, even after the substitution of *e* for *ai* by the rule *jhalyet*, the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* by the rule *ato bhisa ais* would still apply.
This has been stated as follows:
"Even when this [shortening] has been performed, because of the consideration of what previously existed (*bhūtapūrvya*), the *ā* is nevertheless constant; such being the case.

Likewise, from the root *ā-chi* (meaning "to stretch"), when the *liṭ* suffix is applied, after reduplication and the shortening of the reduplicated syllable have been performed, this vowel *ā* is two-moraic by virtue of its previous state. Therefore, because of the inclusion of the *tapara* marker in the rule *ādeḥ*, the long vowel does not occur.
And thus, in the case of *āñcha*—as in *āñcha*, *āñchatuḥ*, *āñchuḥ*—the augment *nuṭ* does not occur by virtue of the rule *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*.

Nor should it be argued that, in the same way, after the suffix *san* has been applied to the root *pibati*, and after reduplication and the shortening of the abhyāsa have taken place, this vowel *ā* would still be considered "two-mora" (*dvimātra*) by reference to its prior state; and therefore, because of the specific mention of *tapara* (a long vowel), the substitution of *it* [for *ā*] in *pipāsatī* would not be applicable.

In the case of *pāpaṭhiṣati*—derived from the root *paṭh* with the suffix *yaṅluṅ* followed by the desiderative suffix *san*—the purpose of the *tapara* (the long vowel marker) is fulfilled by excluding the present two-mora [vowel]. Furthermore, because the rule excludes the absence of a present [vowel], in the word *gaur*, where there was previously an *eṅ* ending, the elision of the vocative (*saṃbuddhilopa*) does not occur according to the rule "after an *eṅ* short vowel, the vocative is elided. However, in *he paṭo*, since a present [vowel] exists, the elision does take place.

And here, the mention of *at* (the vowel *a*) in the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For that [mention] will prescribe the suffix *ṇyat* by the rule *ṭahaloḥ ṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124), which applies after roots ending in consonants. Since the suffix *yat* would thus be established by elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*) as applying only after bases ending in vowels, the mention of *at* is made for the purpose of ensuring that it occurs even after what was previously a base ending in a vowel—such as in *dhitsyam* and *ditsyam*—where the elision of *am* has already taken place under the condition of being an *ardhadhātuka* suffix, provided that the locative case there is one of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).
And this is its purpose only if, in this context, there is the understanding of "what was previously so" (*bhūtapūrvagati*).
Dissimilarity [of roots] is not caused by their suffixes. 40.
The irregularity (*asarūpatva*) caused by the suffixal element (*anubandha*) is not resorted to.
Therefore, in the case of *goda*, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur.
And the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the optional prescription of the suffix *śa* in place of *ṇa* by the rule *dadātidadhātyor vibhāṣā*.

If there were asārupya (lack of similarity) caused by anubandhas (indicatory letters), then forms such as *dāyaḥ* and *dadaḥ* would be established by the rule *vāsarūpa* itself through the suffixes *ṇa* and *śa*.
Now, if asārupya were indeed caused by anubandhas as well, then the inclusion of the term *arūpa* in the rule *vāsarūpo'striyām* would be purposeless.
Therefore, by implication, one must resort to that asārupya which resides within the actual form (*pravṛttigata*).

Furthermore, there is no dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) in the application of the suffix *kāṇ* [to the same base]; therefore, the rule for dissimilar suffixes (*asarūpavidhi*) will not apply. And this has also been stated.

Alternatively, the mention of *asarūpa* (dissimilar suffix) would be for the purpose that, when there is similarity in the subsequent element (*anubandha*), the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*asarūpavidhi*) should not be understood to apply. [Examples:

*igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.135] results in *ka*; the addition of *ka* by the rule *mūlavibhujādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*; *pacādyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.134] results in *ac*; and *harateranudyamane'c* [Pāṇini 3.2.9] results in *ac*.
For if that were the case, then because there would be no compound with a permanent upapada, one could also have *mūlānāṃ vibhujāṃśasya haraḥ*.
But this is incorrect,
because the rule *mūlavibhujādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.5] would then be rendered purposeless.
And because of the statement: "By way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*), that which has an upapada takes precedence over that which lacks an upapada.

Let it be that the suffix without an upapada occurs due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal); however, the suffix with an upapada will occur by means of the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*). If this were so, then in the case of *śāstrakṛt* and *śāstrakāra*—which are formed from the roots *kṛ* and *kṛ* with the suffix *kvip*—there would be no co-occurrence [of both forms], because the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes does not apply there.
There is no application of the suffix *kvip*, because it is not heard [in usage].
Thus ends the first chapter on suffixes (*pratyayapāda*) in the *Paribhāṣāvṛtti* composed by the illustrious Sīradeva.
