Between that which is stated by its technical definition and that which is stated as a conventional term, only the latter is to be understood, not the former.

The term *lakṣaṇa* refers to that which is derived from a definition (*lākṣaṇika*) by way of metaphorical application. That which is "stated literally" (*pratipadokta*) is specifically established. Between these two, only that which is stated literally is to be understood, and not the derivative form produced through etymological analysis (*khaṇḍato vyutpādita*).
For example:

from the root *iṅ* with the suffix *ṇic*, after the substitution of *ā* for *krī*, *jī*, and *iṅ* before *ṇi* has been applied, and the augment *puk* has been added so that the form *āpi* is established, the substitution of *āy* does not occur when *lyap* follows by virtue of the rule "vibhāṣāpaḥ.
Thus, one says *adhyāpya gataḥ*.
However, for the root *āp* as specifically prescribed [in the rule], it occurs as *prāpya* and *prāpayya*. Likewise, from the root *vas*, with the suffix *kvip*, there is the form *uṣ*.

In the sense of "one who moves having burned" (*uṣā carati*), when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word ending in the third case, the suffix *ka*—prescribed by the rule *is-us-uk-tāt kaḥ*—does not apply because the word *uṣ* is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a secondary grammatical operation).
Regarding "auṣika": it occurs after a word ending in the suffix *apratyaya* as explicitly prescribed [by the rule]. For example: "dhānuṣka" (a bowman).

If this were the case, then in the rule *hvāvāmaśca*, the inclusion of *meṅ* would not occur by virtue of the mention of *mā*. This is not so; for by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *gām-ādi*, [the rule] applies even to that which is derivative (*lākṣaṇika*).
Nor should it be said that, in this way, there would also be the inclusion of *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*māna*).
This is because it is not intended that the *lug-vikaraṇa-paribhāṣā* should be set aside by the *gāmādā-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā*.
As for the fact that the author of the *Nyāsa* stated in the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* that the *lug-vikaraṇa-paribhāṣā* is also set aside,
that is merely the opinion of certain individuals.

Regarding what was stated by Maitreya in the commentary on *hvāvāmaśca*— namely, that for those who hold the view that there is no distinction in the application of rules such as *gāmādāgrahaṇeṣu*, this [sūtra] is intended to set aside the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* or to set aside the *niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*—
it should be understood that the root *mā* (in *mā māna*) is included because it possesses a *luk*-elided suffix.
In that regard, the claim that it is intended to set aside the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā* is incorrect.
For in this way, because they possess an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*), there would be no application of the rule to *māṅ* and *meṅ* alone;

rather, it would apply only to *mā* as the root *māna* when it is without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*). And in the deliberation between a form without an indicatory letter and one with a dropped suffix (*luka-vikaraṇa*), the paribhāṣā concerning forms without indicatory letters prevails due to its being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation.
However, under an alternative interpretation, the statement that the mention of *aster bhū* with the *śtip* affix is for the sake of variety (*vaicitryārtha*) would be inconsistent.
For if there were no mention with *śtip*, the rule regarding the elision of suffixes (*lug-vikaraṇa-paribhāṣā*) would lead to the undesirable consequence of including only the root *asu kṣepaṇe*.

Now, one might argue that since the rule concerning roots without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*) applies specifically to suffixes (*pratyaya*), it has no operation here when a verbal root (*dhātu*) is being mentioned.

Just as it was explained by the author of the Nyāsa regarding the rule *na kavateyaṅi* that "the root *kau* is not included [in the prohibition] because of the paribhāṣā concerning the elision of the *vikaraṇa*," so too,
although it has been stated that this [rule] is for the purpose of overriding the paribhāṣā concerning roots without an *anubandha*, [it is nonetheless necessary].

That is incorrect, because if the paribhāṣā "that which lacks a subsequent element" were to subvert [the present rule], then due to its being based on a technical definition (*lākṣaṇikatva*), there would be no inclusion of the root *miṅ*;
rather, there would be the inclusion of *māṅ* (in the sense of "to measure") alone.
It is replied:
This was not stated by Rakṣita for the sake of establishing a formal rule (*vyavasthā*).

Rather, it is intended to demonstrate that, in every respect, the paribhāṣā concerning the elision of suffixes (*lugvikaraṇa*) is not sublated by the paribhāṣā concerning the inclusion of *gām-ādi* [roots].
For instance:
This is the view of some: that for certain [rules] the definition-paribhāṣā is sublated, while for others both paribhāṣās are sublated, but not even the paribhāṣā regarding lopa-vikaraṇas.
However, this is incorrect;
for in the rule *ghumāsthāgā...* the author of the Nyāsa has stated that there is also a sublation of the paribhāṣā regarding lopa-vikaraṇas.

"In that case, [the phrase] 'or for the purpose of overriding the paribhāṣā concerning that which lacks a connection'—this word *vā* does not indicate an alternative position; rather, it signifies a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
This is the meaning:"
The paribhāṣā concerning the mention of *gāmādā* sublates both the paribhāṣā concerning the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the paribhāṣā concerning that which lacks an *anubandha*.
Alternatively, the word "or" (*vā*) is indeed seen even in the sense of conjunction;
as for example, in the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *saṃgraha*, the author of the Nyāsa stated: "either correctly (*samyak*) or completely (*samantāt*)."
This is its meaning:
"correctly" (*samyak*) and "completely" (*samantāt*).
For it is not universally accepted that a word analyzed into its parts is necessarily etymological (*lākṣaṇika*).

Therefore, in the rule *vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau* regarding the prescription for pronominal status (*sarvanāman*), the term "bahuvrīhi" refers specifically to the bahuvrīhi compound defined by the rule *diṅnāmāny antarāle*, as in the example *dakṣiṇapūrvasyai dehi* ("Give to the one situated between the south and the east"),
and not to the bahuvrīhi defined by the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*. Thus,
when someone is confused about which direction is east and which is north, [one says] *pūrvottarāyai* ("to the one who is both east and north").
And likewise, this [rule] was stated even when the vowel *ṛ* was included in the rule *ṝta iddhātoḥ*.
Furthermore, there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this in the rule *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau*, namely that the suffix *khiṣṇuc* begins with the vowel *i*.
As it has been said:
Because *bhuvaḥ* is acute-accented, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is established as beginning with the vowel *i*;
however, for the sake of establishing the accent of the negative particle *nañ*, it is desired that [the root] begin with the vowel *i*.
And this paribhāṣā is not universally valid.

And that [rule] is understood to be *anitya* (non-eternal) because of the qualification "until *yāvat* and *purā*" [Pāṇini 3.3.4]. Therefore, in the rule *dādhāghvadāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20), by the mention of *ghu*, there is also the inclusion of the root *dheṭ*. This very fact—that although one could have said *apit*, the term *adāp* was used—is the reason for the absence of the technical paribhāṣā [stating that a rule applies only to what is explicitly mentioned]; thus, the point is established from that alone.
But this must be stated:
in the case of the form *adhyāpayati*, [the substitution of] *puK* occurs for the phoneme *a* which is characterized as *lākṣaṇika*. 41.
That which has undergone a modification in one part is not different [from the original].

Therefore, in the case of *abhavat* here, once the elision of the vowel *i* (in *iti*) has been performed, both the designation of *sārvadhātuka* and the designation of *pada* are dependent upon the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
Likewise, in the case of *kariṣīṣṭa*, by the mention of *soyuṭ* in the rule *syasicsīyuṭ*, there is the inclusion of the mere *sī* [augment].

However, in the case of *gṛhṇāti*, even by means of the status of being "as if non-existent" (*an-ādiṣṭa-adhikāra-an-ādiṣṭa-sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, the change to *ṇ* in *hinumīnā* is established.
This is established by logic (*nyāya*).
For instance, even when its ears are cut off, a dog remains a dog, and not a horse nor a donkey.
They also cite an indicative proof (*jñāpaka*).
In the *āḍhya*-type sūtras, there is a prohibition [of the substitution] by the rule *āt tv-ā-vi*.
In some cases, even a modification assumes the nature of its original cause.

By the rule *tena nisamupavibhyaḥ hvaḥ*, the *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed for the root *hve*; this occurs even when the prefix is part of the verbal base (*prakṛti*), as in *nihvayate* and *saṃhvayate*. Furthermore, the evidence (*jñāpaka*) here is the formulation of the prohibition against the substitution of *ā* for the root *vyeñ* by the rule *na vyo liṭi*, which refers to the modified form (*vikṛta*) *vyeñ* as having the marker *it*.
Regarding this, they say:

in the rules *na vyo liṭi* and *nisamupavibhyo hvaḥ*, only the base (*prakṛti*) ending in the long vowel *ā* is intended; the modification [into *vye*] occurs by virtue of the *āt* designation [assigned to the base] within the grammatical rule itself.
Therefore, in the rule *dādhāghvadāp*, the mention of *dā* and *dhā* includes *deṅ* and *dheṭ* even when they function as verbal roots (*prakṛti*);
thus we have *praṇidayate* and *praṇidhayati*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is also the cognition of its quality (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
A quality (*guṇa*) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
That which possesses such a quality—as in "one who has brindled cows" (*citragu*) and so forth—is called *tadguṇa*.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, according to the grammatical treatise, there is a comprehensive cognition (*saṃvijñāna*) precisely of that which is accompanied by the qualifier.
For example, by the rule "sarvādīni sarvanāmāni" (P. 1.1.27), the designation of *sarvanāman* is established for every [word] beginning with *sarva*, such as in the form *sarvasmāi*.

However, in the rule "tasau matvarthe" (P. 1.4.19), because the suffix *taddhita* *matup* is included within the scope of the term *an* (as indicated by the inclusion of *udaśvit*), the operation of the designation is accomplished through that very *matup* suffix.
In that case, this [rule] is not required.
Just as in the expression "the curd must be protected from crows," by way of indication (upalakṣaṇa), it is protected even from a crow;
so too, because of the word "api" in the Sūtra, it should be understood that in some instances there is also a non-co-implication of the quality (atadguṇasaṃvijñāna).
This has been stated by Pāṇini as established through the presence or absence of those qualities, just as in common usage:
"In common usage, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is seen both when the [object] possesses that quality and when it does not;
for example, 'bring the long-eared one' (*lambakaram ānaya*)."
"Bring Citragu.
Furthermore, there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) here: in the *āḍhya-ādi* rule, after stating "in the sense of *cvī*," the prohibition "except when *acvī*" is stated.
There is also a logical argument (*yukti*) in this regard.
For instance:
in the expression "those of which *sarva* is the first," the words *viśva* and so forth do not constitute the external referent (*anyapadārtha*),
because the word *sarva* cannot be a constituent part (*avayava*) of them.
Because it does not initiate that [action],
and because there is no *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of proximity, as such a usage is not expressed by the language.

For by the term *lambakarṇa* ("long-eared"), one does not denote someone whose ears are long and situated near [the head]; rather, it denotes that very person whose [ears] are the constituent parts. Therefore, the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is indeed the aggregate itself. Nor is there an inconsistency regarding the plural number in the rule *sarvādīni*, since the aggregate is a single entity.

Because it is accepted that the referent of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) is a collection (*samudāya*) in which the distinction between its constituent parts is prominent, the use of the plural number is entirely appropriate.
Thus, since the word *sarva* ("all") is included within the collection, it also receives this designation [of "all"]. || 44 ||
Or rather, the rule regarding non-identity of form does not apply to suffixes used in the sense of habitual action (tācchīlika).
For example, from the root *alaṃkṛ*, by means of the suffix *iṣṇuc*, the form *alaṅkariṣṇu* alone arises;
the form *alaṅkāraka* does not arise by virtue of the rule for dissimilar suffixes (*asarūpa-vidhi*).
And here there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed in the rule beginning with *nindahiṃsā-* for the purpose of superseding the suffix *tṛc*.
For if, by the rule of *asarūpa* (irregular formation), suffixes such as *ṇvul* were to occur in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*),
then once *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *ṇvultṛcau*, forms such as *nindakaḥ* and *hiṃsakaḥ* would be established;
what then would be the purpose of prescribing *vuñ*?
This indicates that, regarding words denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*), suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not occur by virtue of the rule concerning dissimilar forms (*vasarūpa-vidhi*).
Thus, it has been established that for words denoting habitual action, there is no rule of dissimilar form with respect to non-habitual (*atācchīlika*) suffixes.
Now, however, it is being established that for words denoting habitual action, there is no rule of dissimilar form even with respect to other words denoting habitual action.

In the rule *jucaṅkramya-dandramya-sū-gṛdhi-jvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ*, the mention of the root *pad* is redundant for the sake of the suffix *yuc*, because the form *padana* is already established by the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*. If that is so, then in the case of *laṣa-pata-padaḥ*, the suffix *ukañ* would supersede *yuc* from the root *padyati*. This is not so.
Or, by the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the suffix *yuc* may also occur.
That very prescription of *yuc* indicates that there is no *vāsarūpa* rule for suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*) with other suffixes expressing habitual action.
Consequently, the suffix *tṛn* does not occur after the root *kṛ* preceded by *alam*; thus, one says *alaṃkartṛ*.
And this [rule] is general. The fact that the suffix *yuc* is prohibited for the words *sūda*, *dīpa*, and *dīkṣa* indicates [this].
For if there were no rule of "non-identity of form" (*vā'sarūpa*) regarding suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), [the prohibition would be unnecessary].

In that case, [one might argue] that because the suffix *ra*—specifically prescribed by the rule "namikampi-smy-ajasakamahiṃsadi-pa-raḥ"—will sublate the suffix *yuc*, what is the need for a prohibition?
By doing so, he indicates that in some instances there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*). Thus, in the forms *kamrā* and *kamanā*, the co-occurrence of *ra* and *yuc* is established.

In the forms *gantā* and *akhilaḥ*, as well as *gāmukaḥ*, the co-occurrence of *tṛc* and *ukañ* is established. In the forms *vikatthī* and *vikatthanaḥ*, the co-occurrence of *ghinuṇ* and *yuc* is established. || 45 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, on the agentive voice (*karmāṇi*), in the commentary on the Paribhāṣās.
Exceptions stated earlier sublate only the rules immediately following them, not those that come later. || 46 ||
Exceptions that precede [a general rule] sublate only those general rules (*utsarga*) that are immediately following and situated nearby, not those that follow later.
Here, the word "later" (*uttara*) refers to a meaning that is separated [by intervening rules].
For example:

The exception *hvāvaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.32) sublates only the suffix *ka* when it follows a root that lacks a prefix (*anupasarga*) and is in immediate proximity; it does not sublate the suffix *ṇini* used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*) even when there is an intervening element, as in *svargahvāyī*.

This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) applies when considering a specific object of sublation, and not with reference to the entire aggregate—as stated by the author of the *Nyāsa* regarding the rule *iko jhal* (1.2.9).

Therefore, just as the substitution of *iyaṅ* is sublated by the elision of *ṇi* according to the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (6.4.52) in the case of *bhakṣitam*, so too in the case of *kāritam*, the substitution of *yaṇ* according to the rule *eranekāco’saṃyogapūrvasya* (6.4.82) is likewise sublated.
And here, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) in the rule *sarvebhyaḥ* within the section on measurement (*parimāṇākhyāyām*).
For that [inclusion] is intended to subvert the suffix *ap*, as in the cases of *dvau kārau* and *trayaḥ kārāḥ*.
Otherwise, according to the principle of "an exception [applies] before [the general rule]," it would have been a subverter of *ac* alone, which is proximate [to it].
This very *paribhāṣā*, whose nature is that "either a rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes," is what was stated in the *Nyāsa* on the sūtra *votāpyoḥ*:

"If there were a mention of *aṅ* here, then [the form] would result as *vautāpyoḥ*; for once the *guṇa* substitution has been made with the following vowel, there ought to be a *vṛddhi* substitution with the preceding one."
"There is no fault because it is based on a sūtra.

This is appropriate; for, by the rule *om-āṅoś-ca*, the substitution of a single long vowel (*dīrghatvam*) for the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇe*) following *akaḥ* is set aside by the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatvena*).
But this does not apply even to the rule *vṛddhireci*.

For otherwise, since the forms *votāpyoḥ* would already be established by the rule *omāṅośca*—which, as an exception (*apavāda*) to both the *vṛddhi* and the long vowel [substitutions], results in a single substitute (*pararūpa*)—it would be incorrect to say that "this [form] is established from the very mention [in the sūtra]. And this [objection] is not valid.

[Objection: This is not so, because the prescription of *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel) in the rule *om-āṅoś-ca* would otherwise be purposeless when [the suffix] *sarvanāmnaḥ* is applied to *dīrgha-bādhana*.
[Response: That is not correct;
for in cases such as *achā-chādanam*, the purpose is the removal of the nasalized *ā* (*ān*) by means of *pararūpa*.

Otherwise, in this alternative view, due to the rule for lengthening with a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*), the long *ā* would also be nasalized. Thus, regarding what was stated by Maitreya in the rule *omāṅośca*:

"Where there is no single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with *āṅ*, there is a distinction [from the previous case] by way of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) and the lengthening with a homogeneous vowel; therefore, a single-substitute is illustrated as *āūḍhā*, *oḍhā*, and *adyoḍhā*."
That is to be considered.

This justification for the immediately preceding rule of substitution is incorrect, because in that context the authors of the Vṛtti and others have explained the *pararūpa* (substitution by the subsequent form) as an exception (*apavāda*) to all [other rules]. For this very reason, it is stated in the Vṛtti: "Thus, *ādyoḍhā* is cited as an example.
Thus ends the section on the *bahula* suffixes in the Paribhāṣāvṛtti. 3.
The status of not ending in a vowel (anejantatva) is not caused by an affix (anubandha).
Therefore, in the rule *dādhā ghu adāp*, the mention of *dā-dhā* includes *deṅ* and *dheṭ* as well.

Otherwise, even though their indicatory letters (*anubandha*) have been elided, because they would lack the state of ending in *e* (*ejanta*) in their original instruction (*upadeśa*), there would be no substitution of *āt* for them—just as there is none in the case of *cetā* and *stotā*.
This [conclusion] is incorrect.

Because the inclusion of the root *grah* in the rule *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.62)—despite the fact that the term *aj* was already mentioned therein—indicates that an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is not to be taken into account when a grammatical operation depends on the original form (*upadeśa*).

For example, in the case of the root *piṣ* (DhP 7.10), in the form *praṇipeṣṭā*, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not occur due to the prohibition in the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā kakhādāvaṣanta upadeśe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.18). Similarly, here too, even though the *anubandha* has been elided, the substitution of *ā* must certainly take place by virtue of the root ending in *e*.
This, however, is the illustration:
by the rule *adābiti* (Pāṇini 1.1.20), which prohibits the designation *ghu* for the root *dāp* in the sense of "cutting," the prohibition of the *ghu* designation for *daip* is also established,
as in the example *avadātaṃ mukham*.
In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that in the *Dvita* class (the second class of roots), one should read *dāp* as "purification" (*śodhana*).

Now, if this is the purpose [of the rule], then let it be formulated as *dā-dhā-ghv-apit*. For in this way, since *daip* also has the marker *p*, the prohibition of the designation *ghu* is established.
And there is brevity;
furthermore, one need not even resort to a paribhāṣā based on an indicatory letter (anubandha).
It is said:

If [the rule] were formulated as *dā-dhā-dhv-apa-iti*, there would be no authority for the principle that the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa-paribhāṣā*) does not apply here. However, if it is formulated as *ad-au*, then just as the root *daip*— even though it is defined by a technical rule— is included in the prohibition,
so too its inclusion in the positive injunction (*vidhi*) by the mention of *dā-dhā* is justified.

And likewise, regarding the rule *māṅo vyatīhāre* (Pāṇini 1.3.29), it was stated by Rakṣita that this is the purpose of the indicator (*jñāpaka*): although [the inclusion of *dā* and *dhā*] is established by the rule *dādhā ghu āp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20), nevertheless, it has been demonstrated in that very same work that the [specific] mention was not made in that manner. However, when the mention is made as *apau* in the dual number, [it means] those two for which the letter *p* does not exist; thus, in the prohibition, because of the capacity of the mention of *dā* and *daip*, even in the positive injunction, [the mention of] *dā* and *dhā* [is understood] within the mention of *dā-dhā*.
A deviation from the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) can certainly be explained;
however, it was not done so here because even if the augment *puK* were applied [to the root *dā*], there would arise the suspicion of the prohibition by the rule *apāv*.
If, on the other hand, the form *apitau* were used, although this objection would be avoided, it was not done that way for the sake of stylistic variety (*vaicitrya*).
And here, the indicative proof (*jñāpaka*) is the mention of the form *māṅ* with the vowel *ā* substituted for *i* in the rule *māṅo vyatīhāre*.
For if it were not *ejanta* (ending in a semivowel), that substitution would not occur.
Nor is this a mention of the root *māṅ* meaning "to measure," because it is impossible for that root to function in the sense of reciprocal action (*vyatīhāra*). || 47 ||
And that which has been drawn forward does not apply to what follows.
That which is drawn forward by the particle *ca* (and) is not connected with what follows.

Therefore, in the rule *bhuvo bhāve* ("after the root *bhū*, [the suffix] *yat* [is used] in the sense of a state"), there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the *yat* that was drawn forward by the *ca* in the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca*; however, there is a recurrence of the *kyap*.

The function of this [sūtra] occurs in cases where, although recurrence is already established by means of the circumflex accent (*svarita*), a drawing forward is nevertheless performed by means of the particle *ca*.

However, where the particle *ca* is used for the purpose of carrying forward (*anuvartana*) [the rule] after one has reached cessation upon seeing a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), this [rule] does not apply there.
Therefore, in the case of *antarāntareṇayukte*, the second [particle, *ca*,] is carried forward.
Maitreya, on the other hand, considers this [rule] to be general.
As it has been said:
"In the rule *iko jhal*, because [the previous rule] is drawn along (*anukṛṣṭatvāt*), this too is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

And the indicator (*jñāpaka*) here is the mention of the suffix *ṇamul* in the rule *avyaye 'yathābhipretākhyāne kṛñaḥ tkvāṇamūlau* within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of *ṇamul*; for if that which is drawn along were still to apply, then it would have been stated as "*tkvā ca*" (and also *tkvā*).
And this [rule] is optional;

and that optionality, although already implied by the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca*, is understood to be set aside by the re-employment of the term *ekājuttarapade* in order to exclude that optionality. 48.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on Relation.
Thus ends the third chapter. || 3 ||
Exceptions in the middle sublate preceding rules, but not subsequent ones. || 49 ||
For example:
by the rule "the suffix *ka* is used in the senses of cause, habitual action, and conformity," it supersedes the previous suffix *aṇ*.
Thus: *vidyā yaśaskarī* ("knowledge that brings fame").
The suffix *ṇini* in *tācchīlika* (denoting habitual action) does not supersede [the application of] *śrāddhakārī*.
Likewise, by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*, the substitution *iyaṅ* supersedes the preceding [vowel];
it does not supersede the subsequent *vṛddhi* or *guṇa*, as in *āyaka*, *āyamana*.

In the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam*, because the term *saṃprasāraṇa* is understood from the preceding context, the explicit mention of *saṃprasāraṇa* there serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition also applies to the subsequent rule *śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite*. Thus, we have forms such as *yūnaḥ paśya* (see the youth) and *yūnā yūnā* (with the youth, with the youth).

Precisely for this reason, by virtue of the inclusion of the term *saṃprasāraṇa*, when a prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* is to be applied, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)—even as governed by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*—does not operate; nor is the intervention caused by that substitute disregarded.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of *vivyathe*, the inclusion of the term *saṃprasāraṇa* must be for the purpose of setting aside that *saṃprasāraṇa* which would otherwise apply without intervention by the rule *vyatho liṭi*?
This is not so.
If this were the only purpose, then one would have formulated the rule simply as *vyatha* without mentioning *saṃprasāraṇa*;
for by the rule "there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* when there is a *saṃprasāraṇa*" in the case of *vyatha*, the form *vivyathe* would already be established.
Alternatively, one might formulate the rule as *vyatho yaḥ liṭi* instead of *vyatho liṭi*.
A supporting indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the application of the *svarita* accent in the rule *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ*, as explained in the *Vṛtti* and *Nyāsa*.
For that [accent] follows by virtue of its *svarita* nature from the preceding rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām*.

Therefore, in this case, by the rule *tenāna upadhālopino’nyatarasyām*, the suffix *ṅīp*—which would otherwise apply—is superseded due to its subsequent position, and instead *ṅīṣ* alone occurs by the rule *bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīṣ*.
Thus we have *ghaṭodhnī*.
Otherwise, because *ṅīṣ* is an intermediate exception (*madhyepavāda*), it would supersede only the two preceding rules, namely *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*].
There is a difference between the suffixes *ṅīṣ* and *ṅīp* regarding accent (*svara*). Accent, too, is a differentiator;
as they say:
A word is divided in three ways: by form, by meaning, and by accent.
And so Maitreya has explained in the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*):
"If this [sūtra] were to occur prior to the heading on feminine endings (*stryadhikāra*), then there would be another fault."
"Īhā" means effort (*ceṣṭā*).

When the elision (*lopa*) of "yasya" and "ca" has been performed, the single-substitute vowel (*ekādeśa*) would not be acute (*udātta*) according to the rule *udāttenodāttaḥ*. Regarding this, they raise an objection.

In the case of *īhā* and *ceṣṭā*, although the quality of being accented (*udāttatva*) does not apply by the rule "the single substitute [for an udātta and a non-udātta] is udātta" once the elision of the vowel *a* has been performed, nevertheless, the quality of being accented does indeed exist by the rule "and [the syllable] following a non-udātta where an udātta has been elided. Furthermore, there is no distinction between these two [types of] udātta vowels.
It is said that [the rule] exists.

For instance, when the quality of being acute (udātta) is applied by the rule "when one part [of a compound] is acute, [the other] is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*), which belongs to the section concerning what is not established (*asiddhādhikāra*), then—because of the principle "that which is not established in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*)—the preceding [operation] is considered non-existent; consequently, for that which follows an acute or circumflex vowel, the [subsequent] lower-pitched vowel (*sannatara*) [is applied].
Thus, by this [rule], the *ekāra* and *aikāra* vowels do not become *sannatara*; "more depressed" (*sannatara*) means "more gravely accented" (*anudāttatara*).

However, when [the grave accent] is applied by the rule "and [the substitution of the grave accent] for a grave vowel where there is elision of an acute," then because that [grave accent] is already established, if there were a *sannatara* following an acute or a circumflex (*udāttasvaritapara*), it would indeed be *sannatara*.

It should not be argued that even though the single-substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffix *akāra* must still be relied upon so that the suffix remains "preceded by a low-pitched vowel" (*sannatareṇa*).
This is because the suffix has been replaced by the single substitute;
how, then, could it possess an initial acute accent?

However, it is the accent of the *ekādeśa* [substitute] that is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), not the *ekādeśa* itself. But even so, since the accent of the *ekādeśa* must be declared established by the rule "that which is internal (*antaraṅga*) is established," the accent of the *ekādeśa* being established, there ought indeed to be the suffix *sannatara*. It is replied: [The answer follows:]... [text omitted] ...it is replied: [the *ekādeśa* substitute is established for the purposes of the application of the accent, but its specific phonetic form remains unestablished until the subsequent rules apply].
For in that [treatise], there is an enumeration:
"The purpose of the single-substitute *ay*, *āv*, and *āva*; the accent of the present participle (*śatṛ*); the low-pitched (*anudātta*) *e*; and all low-pitched vowels.
But even so, because it is followed by a circumflex (*svarita*), there must necessarily be a nasalized vowel (*sannata*).

Because the single-substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the circumflex (*svarita*) arises in the single-substitute position of an acute (*udātta*) and a grave (*anudātta*) vowel due to phonetic proximity (*āntaratamya*).
This is not so;
for that most proximate [circumflex] vowel is sublated by its status as acute.
If it is argued: "Since that [rule] is not established (*asiddha*), how can there be sublation by it?"—we say: No.
For a general rule (*utsarga*) operates only after setting aside the domain of its exception (*apavāda*); thus, it does not operate within the domain of the *svarita* or the *udātta*.
But surely, since it is not established, how can this be called its domain?
It is said: by means of its being unestablished (*asiddhatva*), the operation of the acute accent (*udāttatva*) at that time is precluded;
however, its lack of scope (*aviṣayatva*) is not established.
Furthermore, an exception (*apavāda*) operating within its specific domain necessarily subverts a general rule (*utsarga*),
just as the substitution of *dad* for *dā* takes effect.
Likewise, in this case as well, the circumflex accent (*svarita*) must be understood as subverting the acute accent (*udātta*).
Even so, the *sannatara* (the more intensive desiderative) would still be unavoidable here.
For when the suffix *akāra* is applied to the roots *īh* and *ceṣṭ* by the rule *gurośca halaḥ*, the *san* must occur even before the suffix *ṭap* arises, because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal).
Therefore, this [reading] must be understood as having been protected by Rakṣita.
The detailed points to be understood exist in the preserved texts themselves.
For instance,
in the *ṅyāpprātipadika* sūtra, it is stated that even among words ending in *āp*, the forms ending in *ḍāp* and *cāp* [are excluded] for the reasons previously mentioned.

Likewise, in that very same context, regarding the rule *cenaḥ striyām*, [the example] *bahudaṇḍinīkā* is given as an instance where the optional application of the suffix *kap* is prescribed after a word ending in *in*.

Similarly, in the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*, [the forms] *kartrī* and *hartrī* are examples where there is no *guṇa* substitution because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *gher ṅiti*; since that [suffix *ṅīp*] is prescribed for a *sup* (nominal suffix) that begins with a *ṅit* sound. Furthermore, in the rule *na krīḍādibahucaḥ*, a prohibition is stated for the feminine word *kroḍā*, whereas it is observed that it must necessarily occur from the masculine word [ending in *bahu-c*]. || 49 ||
A rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding.
Whether it be a positive injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), it applies only to that which immediately precedes.

For example, by the rule *chandasi* ("in the Vedic language"), the status of being *apit* (not having *i* as its *it*-marker) is optionally applied to what immediately follows *si* in the rule *serhyapicca*, but not to the substitution of *hi*, which is separated from it.
Thus: *yuyuhi* or *yuyohi*.

Likewise, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* in the rule "neṭi" applies only to the immediately preceding rule, "vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ," as in *adevīt*. It does not apply to the prohibition of *vṛddhi* in the rules "na sici vṛddhiḥ" or "mṛjer vṛddhiḥ," as in *alāvīt* and *amārjīt*.
In some cases, however, by the force of a formal declaration (*pratijñāna*) that a vowel is *svarita*, both injunctions and prohibitions apply even to what is separated [by other elements].
For example, in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, there is an injunction for *ṅīp* even though it is separated by *ḍāp*.
Similarly, in the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is enjoined even though it is separated [by other suffixes].
Likewise, in the rule *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ*, there is a prohibition of both *ṭāp* and *ṅīp*.
This meaning is stated as being obtained through the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
They also cite an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) [for this].
The rule *saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* prescribes the suffix *ṅīp*.
For that *ṅīp* is prescribed again because it is intervened by the *ṅīṣ* of the rule *taddhita-bahuvrīher-ūdhaso ṅīṣ*;
and since a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding, the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the rule *na ktici dīrghaśca* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this principle].

Even so, by this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), in the case of *yantiḥ* and *santir*, there would be a prohibition only of the immediately preceding rule, "of that which has an anudātta vowel as its upadeśa," and not of the separated rule, "before *k* and *jhal* suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*. It is for this purpose [that the rule] is formulated. || 50 ||
The Pāṇinīyas are those who have not composed a *vyūha*. || 51 ||
They cause even a treatise that has already been composed to be set aside. || 52 ||
*Vyūha* is a specific deliberation or determination;
it refers to determinations formed through specific qualifications.
The meaning is that the followers of Pāṇini deviate even from a rule that has already been established.

In the case of *paśya papuṣaḥ*, although the suffix *śas* is prescribed after the word *papivas*, nevertheless, according to the rule *akṛtavyūhāḥ*, when the form *papāvas-as* is established, the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) takes precedence over the augment *iṭ* because the operation dependent upon vocalization is stronger. Consequently, since the condition of being followed by a consonant beginning with *v* (*valāditva*) no longer exists, the augment *iṭ* does not occur.

Regarding this, they say: let there be *iṭ*. Since the form *papuṣaḥ* is established by the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) according to the rule *usyapadāntāt*, [the objection is refuted].
And this is incorrect, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "not after *u*" (*na-ut-padāntāt*) in that rule. [Objection:

Even so, once the substitution of *yaṇ* for *iṭ* has been made, the result is established by the elision of the *v* sound (*vali lopa*), since the *saṃprasāraṇa* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*.

Because the elision of *v* is not based on a *saṃhitā*-text, and because the rule "there is no [operation] when there is non-adjacency of vowels" (*acor anantaraye 'vidhānāt*) does not apply here due to the lack of vowel-adjacency, this case is not covered by that prohibition.

Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *yaṇ* would not even apply by virtue of the maxim regarding external elements (*bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*), for there is the specific statement: "there is no [application of the prohibition] when there is non-adjacency of vowels" (*nājānantarye*).
To this it is replied:

when the elision of *val* (the semivowel) is to be applied as an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, the substitution of *yaṇ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) because it is external (*bahiraṅga*); thus, since the *yaṇ* itself does not exist, how can there be an elision of the *val*?
The status of the *yaṇ* substitution as external is due to its dependence upon *saṃhitā* (continuous phonetic connection).

However, in the case of *varttate* and *vardhete*, because the substitution (*ekādeśa*) is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *ato ṅitaḥ*; consequently, the elision of *v* (*vali lopaḥ*) would be difficult to achieve.
Others, however, maintain that this purpose is already established by the maxim regarding the disappearance of the cause (*nimittāpāya-paribhāṣā*).
And it should not be argued that the existence of the cause remains due to the maxim of non-existence (*asiddha-paribhāṣā*).

In the maxim *asiddhavad atrābhāt*, which falls under the jurisdiction of the section on *bhā* (the substitution of *bh* for *ā*), the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) belonging to the jurisdiction of *bhā* is treated as if non-existent (*asiddha*). Consequently, because the constituent parts of the grammatical element (*aṅga*) are deficient, this maxim has no scope for operation.
Now, one might object: since the two elements rely on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*), how can the maxim *asiddhavad atrābhāt* apply?
It is said:

in a *paribhāṣā*, whatever cause is external (*bahiraṅga*), such as *saṃprasāraṇa* and so forth, its own cause—such as *sva* and so forth—is also the cause for this rule, "the *saṃprasāraṇa* of *vasu*.
Even that which is a cause through a mediated sequence is relied upon as the cause of the *paribhāṣā*.
This very purpose is why the established authority (*siddhādhikāra*) is desired for this subject matter (*bhādhikārīyakārya*).
Thus, there is indeed a commonality of cause (*samānanimittatva*).
And this is necessarily so.
In examples such as *papuṣaḥ paśya*, the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64) must be explained as providing for the elision [of the long ā];
for the rule *usyapadāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.96) does not apply here,
because the *saṃprasāraṇa* would have already occurred when that [elision] was to be applied.
This is incorrect;

for when the rule *usi apadāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.95) is to be applied in the absence of an intervening *acor* (vowels), the prohibition by the paribhāṣā *nājānantarye* (the rule that a grammatical operation does not apply when there is immediate succession of vowels) would prevent its application.

If this is so, then in the rule *usi apadāntāt*, the term *usi* refers only to that which is explicitly mentioned (*pratipadokta*), and thus in the case of *papuṣaḥ*, where *usi* is derived through a grammatical derivation (*lākṣaṇika*), the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) does not occur.

For this very reason, the author of the Nyāsa stated regarding the rule *asiddhavad atrābhāt*: "For in that [rule], there is the inclusion of that which is prescribed by its specific wording (*pratipadokta*).

Now, one might object: in the rule *usyapadāntāt*, it was stated that there is an inclusion of the general term because the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is defined by a technical rule" (*lākṣaṇika*) is set aside. To this it is replied:
He thinks thus:
"The subversion of technical definitions and conventional designations should not be undertaken,
because there is no purpose for it."

Let it be that this is a definition and a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). Nor is it the case that, in the Vedic example *papuṣaḥ paśya*, under the view that the designation *sārvadhātuka* applies, the hearing of the vowel *ā*—due to the absence of both *āto lopa iṭi ca* and *usyapadāntāt*—constitutes a flaw;
for the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* occurs because of its Vedic character.
Precisely because this *asiddhaparibhāṣā* does not exist, it was stated by Rakṣita regarding the rule *apṛkta ekāl pratyayaḥ*:
"When it is said *vā apṛktasya*, there is no fault even in cases such as *darviḥ* where [the suffix] is *apṛkta*; therefore, it need not be stated."
And likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) even in the case of *rājakṛtvānam ācaṣṭe* and *rājakṛtvayati*.

Similarly, regarding the rule *janasanakhanakramagamoviṭ*, it was stated by Rakṣita that the vowel *i* [in *viṭ*] is for the purpose of qualifying [the suffix] when it is not followed by a consonant cluster (*apṛkta*).

If that [ik-ādeśa] were not present, then in the derivation of *paralokadṛśvayatīti*—where the causative suffix *ṇic* has been applied and the *ṭi*-portion elided—the letter *v* would have to be elided.
Therefore, the vowel *i* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*).

This is established because the rule "the external is as if non-existent compared to the internal" renders the *ṭi*-elision non-applicable here due to its being considered "as if unestablished" (*asiddha*) by the rule *asiddhavad atrābhāt*. Thus, [the presence of *i*] is justified.

If this is so, then what was stated by Rakṣita regarding the rule *yuvo ranākau*— namely, that the mention of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) *y* and *v* sounds is useless when referring to the *y* and *v* sounds that serve as causes for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "stem" (*aṅga*)—
is incorrect. For, according to the sequence previously mentioned, there would result the undesirable application of those substitutes in forms such as *rājakṛtvayi* and *paralokadṛśvayi*.
It is said:
prior to the section on *bh* (the *bhādhikāra*), they state the section on *asiddha*.
According to that opinion, the rules for *uṭ* and elision (*lopa*) lack the status of being "belonging to the science" (*śāstrīyatva*) because they occur before the *bhādhikāra*.

Therefore, when the paribhāṣā "asiddham" (the subsequent is as if non-existent) is to be applied, the rule "asiddhavat atrābhāt" (it is as if non-existent within the same scope of application) does not operate; thus there is no fault.

And the indicator (*jñāpaka*) here is the inclusion of the word "samarthānām" (of those that are semantically connected) in the rule "samarthānām prathamād vā" (optionally after the first [member] of those that are semantically connected).
For instance:
If this [condition] were not present,
then the mention of "samartha" (capable/related) would be useless for the purpose that a taddhita suffix should apply only when its meaning has been fully established.
Regarding the rule *gorataddhitaluki*, some say that the mention of *ataddhita* (not a taddhita) is unnecessary.
Indeed, this [rule] is formulated so that [the suffix] might not apply when there is elision (*luk*) of the *sup* case-ending; for example, in the form *rajagavīyati*.

In this case, since the suffix *ṭac* has already been established prior [to the application of *kyac*], when *kyac* subsequently occurs and the *sup* is elided, even though *ṭac* would have applied, it is withdrawn, and thus the desired form arises. || 52 ||
Thus ends the section on feminine bases ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, and *p* in the *Paribhāṣāvṛtti* composed by Sīradeva.
When a term without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is mentioned, it does not include a term with an indicatory letter.
When a term with a single indicatory letter (*anubandhaka*) is employed [in a rule], one that has two indicatory letters is not included.
Therefore, in the prohibition of the sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by the rule *tena saha supā*, only the suffix *tavya* (without the anubandha) is understood, not *tavyat*.
Likewise, in the rule *diva ut*, the substitution of *u* does not occur for the verbal root *div*; thus, the form is *akṣadyūḥ*.
In the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the suffix *yat* with a single indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka*) is intended to be included, not *ṇyat* with two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*).
The evidence for this here is the rule *vāmadevād ḍyaḍḍyau*;

the fact that *ḍyaṭ* and *ḍya* have the indicatory letter *ḍ* (which causes *ṭi*-lopa) would otherwise be unnecessary, since the form *vāmadevyasya* is already established by the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *yasyeti ca*.
This indicates that their existence is established by that [very fact].
As it has been said:
"Since it is already established by the elision of *iti*, for what purpose are *yay* and *tau* prescribed as having the *ḍi*-marker?"
"Let there not be the apprehension that the accent of the negative particle [in *na vāma-devyaḥ*] applies to the meaning of that [suffix], as in the case of the *vāmadevya* hymn.

Some authorities state that the paribhāṣā regarding suffixes without an *anubandha* (unmarked suffixes) concerns the scope of suffixes; however, this was stated by the author of the *Anunyāsa* in the rule *jṛ-vraścyoḥ kvi*.

Thus, in the rule *na ca kavater yaṅi*, what the author of the Nyāsa stated— that although the root *kauti* of the *adādi* class is not included by virtue of the *lugvikaraṇa-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding roots with elided suffixes), the mention of *kavatiḥ* by means of the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the inclusion of the root *kuvarti* of the *tudādi* class— is justified. Otherwise, how could the *lugvikaraṇa-paribhāṣā* be invoked in a domain where the *niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding roots without indicatory marks), which is more internal (*antaraṅga*), applies?

The internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*) of the rule concerning suffixes without indicatory marks (*niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*) arises because the designation *it* is applied at the very time of instruction; whereas the external nature (*bahiraṅgatva*) of the rule concerning the elision of verbal suffixes (*lumvikaraṇa-paribhāṣā*) results from the fact that the elision of the suffix is prescribed at a later time,
and also due to the specific knowledge of the particular recitation of the list (*gaṇapāṭha*).
Others, however, state that the paribhāṣā applies generally to those [roots] lacking an *anubandha*.

For this very reason, the author of the Nyāsa stated that the mention of *aster bhūḥ* by means of the *śtip* affix is for the sake of variety (*vaicitryārtha*), and not for the purpose of excluding the root *asu kṣepaṇe*;
for the exclusion of that [latter root] is already established by the paribhāṣā regarding those lacking an *anubandha*.
Furthermore, this paribhāṣā concerning that which has a single following element does not apply in the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*,
because of the force of the inclusion of the marker *ṅ* in *vasu*.
Consequently, when *vasu* is mentioned, there is the inclusion of both *kvasu* and *vasu*.

But surely, if the term *vasu* were not mentioned [in the rule], and it were simply stated that "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *vas*," then vocalization would also apply to the root *vas* meaning "to cover" in the example *varmavasah paśya* ("look at the armor-clad one").
This is not so,
because the root *vas* meaning "to cover" possesses an *anubandha*.
Furthermore, one should not suspect that the form *vas* without an *anubandha* (i.e., the root *vas* ‘to dwell’) is being referred to here;
for in this context, the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution is established only by virtue of the *kvip* suffix.

Now, one might ask: why does the *anubandha* of the suffix not apply in the case of *vidvasitvā*, which is derived from the *kvip*-ending form *vidvān* (from *vidvas*) acting as if it were *vas*—as in “he acts like one who knows” (*vidvān ivācarati*)—where the rule *udito vā* would require the optional addition of the augment *iṭ*?
This is indeed a connection with a collective [of rules].
It is said:

because there is no expression [of such a meaning], the *kvip* suffix does not occur here; therefore, the status of being marked by *u* (*ugit*) is not for that purpose. Thus says Rakṣita regarding the rule *videḥ śatur vasuḥ*.
In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that *vasu* also possesses two indicatory letters (*anubandha*).
Thus, regarding the rule *videḥ śaturvasuḥ*, the Bhāṣya says:
"The mention of *vasu* contains two *s*-sounds; therein, one is for the sake of its actual phonetic form (*śrutyartha*), while the other is for the sake of its having two indicatory letters."
Others, however, say:
"By virtue of the status of having a substitute (sthānivadbhāva), the suffix *vasu* also does not have a single *anubandha*.
This is not correct.

For by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the operations pertaining to the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters), but not of the *anubandhas* themselves.

This might be argued: "In the case of the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, [the substitution] does not apply to that which has two *anubandhas* when there is a mention of that which has one *anubandha*"; however, since there is nothing here with a single *anubandha*, [Rakṣita] states this in that context.

If this is so, then as for what was explained by Rakṣita regarding the rule *auṅa āpaḥ*: "The *anubandha* does not become [present] through *sthānivadbhāva*; rather, it is the operation [that is extended], because the *sthānivadbhāva* rule is for the sake of the operation of the original (*sthānin*), and *anubandhas*..."
"It is for the sake of the *kārya* (the grammatical operation), not for the sake of the *kāryas* (the operations themselves).

This is incorrect; because even in that case, according to the previously stated sequence, due to the prohibition concerning that which has two *anubandhas*, there would be no inclusion of the *auṅ* [dative plural] which has *auṭ* as its substitute.
According to this very logic, it is appropriate to conclude that in the *gaṅkuṭādi* sūtra, there should be the inclusion of only the root *gai* (meaning "to sing").

For likewise, the substitute *gā* which takes the place of *iṇ*, being accompanied by an *anubandha* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, would also not be included. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the letter *ṅ* need not be attached to the substitute *gāṅ*.
Because, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle, the substitute *gā*—which is the substitute for *iṅ* in the case of the root *iṅ*—is not included [in the rule], since the letter *ṅ* is absent;

for if the *ṅ* were not present, there would be no authority for the application of the *niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding suffixes without an *anubandha*) here. Now, one might object: "If this *paribhāṣā* were valid, then in forms such as *naḍakīya*, derived from the rules *utkarādibhyaś chaḥ* and *naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca*, the substitution of *ī* by the rule *āyan-n-ādi-sūtra* would apply precisely because [the suffix] is without an *anubandha*."
But it is not [the case that] in the *chaṇ* suffix and others [the designation applies] because they possess an *anubandha*, as in the expression "Taittirīya.
It is replied: in the rule beginning with *āyannādi*, there is no mention of a *pratyaya* (suffix), but rather a mention of a *varṇa* (phoneme).

Now, for the sake of deriving forms such as *naḍakīya*, why is the suffix *cha* applied to the *naḍa*-group by the rule *naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca*, and then the augment *kuk* added? Why not simply say *naḍādibhyaḥ kuṭ ca*? For in that case, there would be brevity due to the ablative (*pañcamī*) reference "from the *naḍa*-group," and the *gaṇa*-sūtra *takṣṇo nalopaśca* would not need to be composed.
Because the elision is already established by the very designation [of the word] as a *pada*. And thus, regarding this, Rakṣita says:
"If *kuṭ* were applied at the beginning of the suffix, then the rule stating 'the elision of *n* in *takṣṇī*' would be purposeless."
"But then, the substitution of *īya* for [the suffix] *pratyaya* and so forth would not take place.
To this it is replied:
"But surely, if *kuṭ* is applied at the beginning, then by the rule *svādiṣu*, the technical designation of 'word' (*pada*) would apply, and thus the *avagraha* (separation) would result."

As it has been stated regarding the form *ekādākinī* (in the sense of "alone" or "without companion"): "When *ākinic* is to be applied here, the prescription of *ākinic* is for the purpose of removing the *avagraha*.
It is replied:
Maitreya considers that the designation *bha* applies because of its inclusion in the list beginning with *ayasmaya*.
But is this not *chandas*? It is said:
by the force of the recitation there, the designation *bha* will apply even in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*).

For this very reason, in the rule *ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ*, the prescription of the substitute *in*—rather than *na*—is explained in the *Nyāsa* for the sake of establishing forms such as *atijarasin*. Now, one might object: "Even so, the substitute *iy* would not occur; for at the time of the instruction of the suffix, there ought to be substitution by *ekādeśa*. This is not so.
Since those who possess the traditional scriptures (āgama) are born as those who follow the scriptures (āgamin), there would be the presence of the letter *ka* [at the beginning].
Now, if it were not to be by way of substitution (*ādeśa*), then one should simply apply the suffix *cha* without adding the augment *ku*, according to the rule "from *naḍa* and others, *cha*."
Therefore, even when *ku* is applied, there ought to be the substitution of *ī*.
It is said in reply:
"For in that case, there would be an excessive burden of interpretation. (54)
When that which has a specific marker (anubandha) is mentioned, that which does not have that marker is not included.
That which has that very [perception] as its continuous accompaniment is "possessing that accompaniment"; when that is apprehended, there is no apprehension of another thing devoid of it.
And because the doubling is prescribed when there is the marker *ca* in the term *caṅ*, it does not occur when that marker is absent,
as in *adarśat*.
This meaning is obtained through the force of the utterance of the suffix.

They say that another meaning of this [rule] is: "The mention of that which has such a suffixal connection (anubandha) applies only where that [suffix] is present; where it is absent, its mention does not occur.
And thus, in the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*, Rākṣita explains by means of this [principle] that the mention of the nominative singular case-ending (*prathamaikavacana*) is intended.
Thus ends the section on *raktapāda* in the *Paribhāṣāvṛtti* composed by Sīradeva.
In the rules concerning vowels, a consonant is as if non-existent.
In the formulation of rules regarding accents such as the udātta, a consonant shall be treated as if it were non-existent.
Consequently, because the letter *t* of the suffix *tavya* and others is non-existent, the vowel *a* at the beginning of the suffix becomes udātta;
for example, in *kartavyam*.
In the case of *rājadṛṣat*, although the compound ends in a consonant (*hal*), it possesses the udātta accent on its final syllable by virtue of the rule *samāsasya ca*.

In the case of *udaśvitvān*, however, because there is an intervention by the letter *t* [between the vowel and the suffix], the *matup* suffix does not follow immediately after a short vowel; thus, it would not receive the udātta accent by the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup*.
Yet, this accent would nonetheless apply to it by means of this very paribhāṣā.
In this regard, the author of the *Vṛtti* has provided a solution by not relying on the application [of the rule] to the *lakṣya* (the actual form).
However, even in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samāsasya*, it is stated that "when *hal* or a vowel is to be applied" (*halsvaraprāptau*) in order to avoid this same fault. To this, it is replied:

Since vowels are prescribed [by rules] regarding accentuation, there is no possibility at all for consonants to receive an accent; so why is it said, "when a consonant is subject to receive an accent"?
To this, it is replied:
In rules such as *uccair udāttaḥ*, the genitive reference to *ac* (vowel) has been removed;
furthermore, whatever objection might arise in this regard has already been refuted in that very context.

Moreover, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) here is the rule *bilvādibhyo 'ṇ*, which serves to set aside the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed] after words beginning with an unaccented vowel (*anudāttādi*). For if a consonant were present [at the beginning], then words such as *bilva* would not be classified as "beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudāttādi*).

Since the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*) is a property of the verbal root (*aj-dharma*), there is no possibility [of the suffix *mayaṭ*] arising at all. Furthermore, it should not be said that [the mention of *mayaṭ*] is for the purpose of superseding *mayaṭ*;
for if this were for the purpose of superseding *mayaṭ*, the explicit mention of *aṇ* in the rule *bilvādibhyo ’ṇ* would be rendered meaningless.
For this is its purpose:
the word *pāṭaliputra* is recited here so that the suffix *aṇ* may occur [after it].
If permission were granted for whatever is obtained [by other rules], then the suffix *añ* would not apply by virtue of the rule *anudāttādeśca*;
however, it has been stated that *añ* is not applicable here because [the base] begins with a consonant (*hal*).
Furthermore, the fact that the suffixes *imanij* and others are marked with the *cit* indicator is established as evidence for this [interpretation].
Otherwise, since this suffix *iman* would end in a consonant (*hal*), the vowel [suffix] *a* would not apply to that which ends in it; thus, its designation as *cit* would be purposeless.
Furthermore, another example of this [rule] is found in *paurvārddhikaṃ* and *dākṣiṇārddhikaṃ*, where [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *ñ-n-ity-ād-in-nir-ayaṃ*.
Its meaning is as follows:

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after the word *ardha* when it follows a directional term (*dik*), and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *yañ* also occurs. If this is so, let the mention of the word "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) not be made here; it should simply be stated as "the suffix *ṭhañ* after [a word denoting] a direction" (*diśaṣṭhañ*).
And this is the meaning:

[the suffix] *ṭhañ* occurs after the word *diś* when followed by the word *uttarārdha*. This is not so; for if it were stated simply as *diśaṣṭhañ*, there would be a literal apprehension (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) of the form *diś*. However, since the term *pūrvapada* is employed, there is an apprehension of the meaning "direction" (*dig*).
In that case, let only the term *pūrva* (preceded by) be employed;
from this alone, the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) will follow.

For instance, regarding the rule *parāvarādhamottamapūrvācca*, although one could have simply said *parāvarādhamottamebhyaḥ*, the inclusion of *pūrva* is stated in the *Vṛtti* for the purpose of preventing the suffix *ṭhañ* in the case of *parārddhya*.
This is not so.

Since the inclusion of the word *pūrva* [in the rule] establishes that the meaning is what is intended when the term *pada* is mentioned, the suffix *ṭhañ* would also apply after the compound *bahupūrvārddhya*,
because the word *ardha* preceded by a directional term (*dik*) is present here as well.
Indeed, by the inclusion of the word "pūrva," it would not be possible to achieve both the inclusion of the sense [of direction] and the exclusion of the suffix from words such as *bahupūrva*.
However, when the word *pada* (member of a compound) is included, the suffix occurs only after words such as *pūrva*,
because in those cases alone the word *pūrva* exists as the prior member (*pūrvapada*) of a compound.
However, it does not occur after the word *ardha* when preceded by a polysyllabic element (*bahuc*),
because in that case [the word *ardha*] is not a prior member (*apūrvapada*).
Therefore, both the mention of "prior" (*pūrva*) and the mention of "word" (*pada*) must be made.

This being the case, that which was stated by Maitreya regarding the rule *dikpūrvapadāṭṭhañ*— namely, that just as the purpose of the inclusion of the term *pūrva* was explained in the preceding sūtra, so too here, even though the term *pada* is not mentioned, the inclusion of the word-form itself is precluded by the inclusion of *pūrva* alone— that is not correct. 56.
The section on "Your Honor" is concluded. || 3 ||
Adverbs have the status of objects and take the neuter gender. || 57 ||
For example:
"He recites softly";
"He cooks well."
Now, why is it that both neuter gender (*napuṃsakatva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) are resorted to?
Let there be neuter gender alone; from that itself, expressions such as *mṛdu pacati* ("he cooks softly") are established.
True.

If *mṛd* and the other words were indeed objects (*karman*), then because they would appear in the nominative case (*prathamāntatva*), rules such as *temayādi* (the substitution of *te*, *me*, etc., for *tvam* and *aham*) would apply optionally in sentences like *grāme mṛdu te pacati* according to the rule *sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā*. However, if *mṛd* and the others are in the accusative case (*dvitīyāntatva*), the application of *temayādi* is obligatory.
Now, why should there not necessarily be two forms— *grāme mṛdu te pacati* and *grāme mṛdu tava pacati*?

They must indeed occur when there is no subsequent reference (*ananvādeśa*), because of the rule stating that all [pronouns] beginning with *annāu* are optional (*vibhāṣā*) when there is no subsequent reference.

In the case of an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference), however, the form *mṛdu te pacati* always occurs as such; for if words like *mṛdu* were to end in the nominative case, then even in an *anvādeśa*, there would be an optionality according to the rule *sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā*. For example: *atho grāme kambalaste svam*.

Furthermore, [the example] "In the village, the blanket is yours" (*grāme kambalas tava svaḥ*) shows that both the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and the neuter gender (*napuṃsakatva*) must be applied. They say that this point is not established by the *Nyāsa*.
For instance, in the expression "he cooks soft," the act of cooking possesses the status of an object (*karman*) because it is pervaded by such actions as desiring and resolving. To explain:
someone desiring a result perceives the result, thinking, "this is the result of this [action]"; having perceived it, he desires it; and thereafter, he resolves to perform it.

Since an action that is currently being performed (*gamyamānā*) serves as the cause for the factors of action (*kāraka*s), the object of the action of cooking (*pākakriyā*) becomes the object of the action of requesting (*prārthanādikriyā*) which is being performed;
therefore, its qualifier is indeed an object (*karman*).
Furthermore, because an action is of a non-substantial nature (*asattvabhūta*), it is appropriate to designate its qualifier using the neuter gender, which is the general grammatical gender.

But surely, it has been stated that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to that which is the cause of an action (*kriyānimitta*), and a cause is by nature already established (*siddhasvabhāva*).
An action, however, is by nature yet to be accomplished (*sādhyasvabhāva*); so how could it possess the status of an object?

In that case, the rule prescribing the suffix *ṭha* (i.e., *-ika*) after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*)—such as in the expression *tatpraty-anupūrvam-īpalomakūlam*, where the words are adverbial qualifiers of the action (*kriyāviśe�ṣaṇa*)—makes this known.
Even an action whose nature is that which is to be accomplished (sādhya) is resorted to as a means (sādhana) with respect to actions such as requesting or resolving.
Thus ends the fourth quarter on the suffix *ṭhak* in the commentary on the Paribhāṣās.
Thus ends the fourth chapter. || 4 ||
There is no extension of a rule (tadantavidhi) when a nominal stem (prātipadika) ending in a suffix that causes the elision of the case-ending is involved. 58.
The treatment as if possessing a designation [of the whole] applies, except when [the word] is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*).

The rule of extension to what ends with a given element (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself possesses both the suffix that causes the apprehension of the meaning and the suffix that causes its utterance.
Therefore, in the case of the rule "from *naḍa* and others, the suffix *phak*," it applies only to the simple stem;
thus, we have *nāḍāyana*.
Not after that [suffix].
As in *sautranāḍi*.
And the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) does not apply with respect to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
By the rule "the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, etc., and *sūtra*," the form *sāṃgrahasūtrikaḥ* ("one who studies the *Sāṃgrahasūtra*") arises here alone.

Due to the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the suffix does not occur after the word *sūtra* alone; thus, one who studies the *Sūtra* is called *sautra*.
These two paribhāṣās were pointed out by the author of the Bhāṣya in the sūtra *yenavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.72),
immediately after the rule *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.86) with the rule *sapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 5.2.87).
Thus it has been said:
For what purpose is the rule "sapūrvāt" (from that which has a preceding element) prescribed?

Since the word *pūrva* qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), by the rule of "extension to what ends with [the specified element]," the suffix will apply even from a stem preceded by something; and since it will also apply from a simple stem by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation," this [rule] serves no purpose. Nevertheless, it was formulated for the sake of providing an important technical indication (*jñāpana*).

And this indicates that these two *paribhāṣās*, beginning with "that which possesses a marker" (*grahaṇavat*), exist. For this very reason, having explained that the pair of *paribhāṣās* beginning with "that which possesses a marker" pertains to the domain of the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*) because they were indicated therein, [the commentators] explain that in the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya*, the inclusion of words ending in *go* is effected through the application of the principle of taking what ends in that [i.e., *tadantavidhi*].
Furthermore, others state that this is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) applicable generally both when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is prescribed and when it is not.

Accordingly, the prohibition in the rule *śeṣo ghyasakhi* applies only to the word *ghi* itself and not to that which ends in it; thus, in the example *atisakher āgacchati*, the prohibition does not apply.
Moreover, the refutation (*pratyākhyāna*) of these two views has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*.

As it has been said: first of all, regarding the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*), there is freedom as one pleases; for a *tadanta-vidhi* (an operation applying to that which ends with a specified element) occurs through the qualifier, not through the qualified.

In that regard, within the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*) such as "the second case ending [is compounded] with *śrita*, etc. (*dvitīyā-śrita*), the previously established rule *sup-supā* ("a nominal ending in a case-suffix is compounded with another nominal ending in a case-suffix") is not qualified by *śrita* and the others.

Rather, by that very [term *prātipadika*], words such as *śrita* are qualified by the inflected forms (*subanta*) beginning with *śrita*; therefore, because there is no application of the rule regarding suffixes ending in a specific element (*tadantavidhi*), there is no compound in the case of *kaṣṭaṃ paramaśritaḥ*.

In the rule for the prescription of suffixes, *naḍādibhyaḥ phak*, the term *yat prātipadikāt* which is supplied from the context qualifies *naḍādi* itself—meaning "from the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) beginning with *naḍa*"—and thus [the suffix] does not apply here [in the following example].
The offspring of Sūtranaḍa is "Sautranāḍi.
However, where that which is under discussion (prakṛta) is qualified by the item being apprehended, there the rule of "ending-in" (tadantavidhi) certainly applies;
for example, when the item under discussion, namely the *upapada*, is qualified by the mention of *bhaya* or by words such as *āḍhya*.

Therefore, by the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that), we have forms such as *abhayaṃkaraḥ* ("one who causes fearlessness") and *anāḍhyaṃ bhaviṣṇuḥ* ("one who is about to become wealthy").

Furthermore, because the term "itself" (*sva*) is understood to carry over [from a previous rule] and due to the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were its own designation), the suffixes also apply to the simple base, resulting in forms such as *bhayaṅkaraḥ* ("fear-inducing") and *āḍhyaṅkaraṇaḥ* ("making wealthy").

In the rule *kr̥t-vastu-sthādi-sattrāntāt ṭhak*, although the status of ending in those [elements] is already established through *tadantavidhi*, the explicit mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the purpose of preventing the suffix from applying to the simple bases alone.
Otherwise, by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *svam*, [the shortening] would apply even from a simple [stem].

For this very reason, the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāvaḥ*) does not operate. However, in a case such as *gokulam*, by the recurrence of the mention of *svam* and due to the treatment as if possessing a designation, the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) would result; in that situation, the treatment as if possessing a designation is [prevented] by the force of the inclusion of the "ending in that" (*tadantagrahaṇa*).
The author of the Bhāgavṛtti has resolved this by stating that [the word *go*] does not exist [as a separate entity] in the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya*;
furthermore, the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *sva-* is not accepted by all authorities. (59)

In rules prescribing compounds and suffixes, the extension of a rule to that which ends with a specified element (tadantavidhi) is prohibited, except in the case of the mention of ugit- stems or vowel sounds.

Therefore, although words such as *śrita* function as qualifiers of nominal endings (*subanta*), because there is no extension of the rule to include what ends with them (*tadantavidhi*), the compound *paramaśritaḥ* does not occur [by P. 2.1.40]. Likewise, in the formation of suffixes, [the rule] *sautranāḍiḥ* (P. 4.1.97) would not apply;

however, by the statement "except in the case of the mention of *ugit* and vowels," through the extension of the rule to what ends with that [suffix], we obtain forms such as *atibhavatī* and *dākṣi*.
Otherwise, [the suffix] would arise from a word that does not denote Viṣṇu.

For this reason, some recite this Vārttika in the form of a *paribhāṣā* within the rule concerning injunctions (*yenavidhi*): "But it is established because the relationship between qualifier and qualified is unrestricted. (60)
Thus ends the second chapter on grains in the commentary on the Paribhāṣās.
Svārthika suffixes may deviate from the gender and number of their base.
In the case of *kuṭira*, there is a transgression of gender;
in *apkalpam*, there is a transgression of both gender and number;
and in *pacatorūpam* and *pacantirūpam*, there is a transgression of number.

Because of the word *api*, they do not overstep [the rule] either; for example, *aśvaka* (a contemptible horse). And the evidence for this is the mention of the word *striyām* ("in the feminine") in the rule *ṇacaḥ striyāmañ*.
For if one does not disregard the grammatical gender, the form *striyam* cannot be used;

because the suffix *ṇac* is prescribed specifically for the feminine in the rule "in the sense of mutual action (*karmavyatihāra*), [the suffix] *ṇac* [is added] in the feminine," the suffix *añ* is also established as feminine.
This is another example of this [rule].
In the words *dvipadikā* and *dviśatikā*, there is a transgression of both masculine and neuter gender.

For here, [the sense is] "he gives two feet" or "he gives two hundred," and by the rule *pāda-śata-saṃkhyāder vīpsāyāṃ vun lopaś ca*, the suffix *vun* is applied and the final vowel *ā* is elided. Regarding this, they raise an objection:
Now, for what purpose is this suffix *vun* prescribed? Let only *kan* be prescribed; for by that as well, the form *dviśatikā* is established.
And in this way, since the rule "the suffix *kan* is applied after *sthūla* and others in the sense of manner" would apply, there would be no need to mention *kan* [separately].
For this very point will follow [later].
It is said: if *kan* were prescribed, then when the final syllable is elided, the form *dviśatikā* would not result.

Likewise, because the designation *bha* would not exist [in that case], the designation *bha* being the basis for the substitution of *pad* for *pāda*—as in the term *dvipadikā*—the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* would not occur.
Alternatively, even if the substitution of *pad* were to occur, the form *dvipadikā* would still not be possible;
since the substitute *pad* would end in a consonant (*hal*), the form would have to be *dvipatka*.
And thus, as for what was stated there by Rakṣita—
that even with the suffix *kan*, the form *dviśatikā* is established [by the rule] *sthūlādibhyaḥ prakāre kan*, so that *ekā* need not be applied— it is incorrect,
because in the case of *dvipadikā*, both the technical designation *bha* and the resulting form would fail to be established due to the absence of the substitution of *pad* for *pada*.
When the suffix *kan* is applied and the final syllable is elided, even the form *dviśatikā* would not be established.
Therefore, how can it be said that "even when *kan* is prescribed, *dviśatikā* is established"?

Furthermore, if the mention of elision (*lopagrahaṇa*) were not required, then the statement that "the form would not be established because there would be no substitution of the word-form caused by the designation *bha*" would be inconsistent.

For instance, just as the notion of "bhas" does not exist, so too the word *pād* ending in /d/ does not exist; how then can it be said that its form is not established? Insofar as, once the final letter is elided and the substitution of the whole word (*padādeśa*) is accepted, when the final vowel /a/ undergoes the *it*-designation (*ittva*), the form *dvipadikā* is indeed established. Furthermore, the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) in the subsequent section must certainly be rejected.
Now, the rejection of that [position] is improper.
It is said: that which was stated, "and form is not established," should be understood to apply to both cases.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
neither "dviśatikā" nor "dvipadikā" is established. Others, however, say that Maitreya’s intention here is difficult to comprehend.
This applies not only here, but elsewhere as well.
For instance, in the *Vibhaktipāda*, regarding the rule for the suffix *adhunā*, Rakṣita stated:
"If this were the suffix *adhunā*, then [the author] would have prescribed the suffix *adhunā* in the preceding rule itself."

This should not be stated for the purpose of an irregular formation (*anipātana*); for once the substitution of *iś* for *idam* has been made, and the elision of the *ya*-portion (*yasyeti lopa*) has occurred, the form *adhuna* is already established. Therefore, because he provides a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*), it is inferred that this is not the suffix *adhunā*.
In that case, it is indeed "now" (adhunā).

Moreover, the specific distinction regarding its usage was intended by the author of the Vṛtti. In the Bhāṣya, however, this is treated as the suffix *adhunā* itself, because it was mentioned in the initial sūtra by way of the counter-example "strī adhunā" ("a woman now").

However, such a split of the rule (yogavibhāga) would be purposeless; for if one intended to express that "at this time, in this matter," then by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the augment *num* would not occur. || 61 ||
The Śatapāda is completed. || 4 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter. || 5 ||
Vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) and an operation dependent upon vocalization are stronger [than other operations]. || 62 ||
In the case of *juhāvayiṣati*, the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, which sets aside the suffix *yuk* prescribed by the rule *śācchāsāhvāvyā*.

In *juhūṣati*, the semivowel substitution occurs prior to reduplication by the rule *abhyastasya*; and in *juhuvatuḥ*, the semivowel substitution and the resulting single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) occur precisely by setting aside the elision of the vowel *ā*.
