Therefore, by the rule *aci śnudhātu...* and so forth, the substitution *uvaṅ* is established.

Otherwise, if the *ā* were elided by *āto lopa iṭi ca*, then because that [elision] would be considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddhavat*) according to *asiddhavad atrābhāt*, the *uvaṅ* substitution would not occur.
How then, when the word *brahman* is the upapada, does the form *brahmajya* arise from the root *jināti* after the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*?
In this case as well, in forms such as *juhuvatuḥ* and *juhuvuḥ*, there ought to be the substitution of *iyaṅ* just as there is the substitution of *uvaṅ*;
nor should the substitution of *yaṇ*— by the rule *eranekāco 'saṃyogapūrvasya*— be invoked here,
because the base (*aṅga*) does not consist of more than one vowel.
And thus, the undesirable form *brahmaji* would result. It is replied:
since it must be stated that "after [stems] ending in a *saṃprasāraṇa*, the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed," the suffix *ḍa* must be applied.
As it was stated in the rule *yathāhvaḥ prahvaḥ*;
or rather, this [rule] applies only in certain instances and not everywhere.
For this very reason, the author of the Nyāsa stated regarding the rule *sahivahor odavarṇasya*:
This [rule] applies in some instances, but not everywhere.

Therefore, in the case of *brahmajyaḥ*, *āhvaḥ*, and *prahvaḥ*—formed with the suffix *kap*—the elision of the vowel *i* occurs, overriding both the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) and the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute replacement). Because that elision is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent operations), the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* do not take place. Thus, when the rule *iko yaṇ aci* is applied, forms such as *brahmajyaḥ* are established.
And there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for its existence in the *Bhāṣya*: regarding the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, the mention of *ubhayeṣām* (of both) was stated.

For that [mention] was made so that, in forms such as *vavraśca*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) should take place, overriding the *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (retention of the first consonant). By this, since the *saṃprasāraṇa* operates by overriding other grammatical operations, it makes known the existence of this [paribhāṣā].
Furthermore, its rejection is stated in his commentary (*bhāṣya*).
In forms such as *juhuvatuḥ*, the formation of the *saṃprasāraṇa* and that which depends upon the *saṃprasāraṇa* is established by means of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

However, because an interpretation (*vyākhyāna*) is simpler than resorting to a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), this [rule] was indicated by the author of the *Nyāsa* through the inclusion of the term "vowel" (*avarṇa*) in the rule *sahivahorodavarṇasya*; the purpose of that [inclusion] is as follows: *ūḍha-*...

In the case of *ūḍhavān*, [one might argue that] after the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*), the substitution of *au* for the vowel *u* should not take place. However, this is not a valid objection.

Since the substitutions of *dha*, *ḍha*, and the elision of *ḍha* are subsequent to both the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the substitution of the preceding form, once the substitution of *au* for the vowel *a* has been effected, we shall subsequently apply the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the substitution of the preceding form; thus, nothing undesirable results.
Thus, the inclusion of the term *avarṇa* (a vowel) here serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this principle].
Now, regarding the form *juhūṣati*, how is it that the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitution occurs by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*?

For, according to the view that reduplication applies to the *sthānin* (the original element), once the reduplication of *hūs* has been performed, the substitute *juhūs* is a different word; consequently, there is no longer a distinction between base and suffix.
And reduplication does not apply only to that which stands at the beginning of a word (mūrdhanya),

because [the preceding rule] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham*. However, the statement "that which is non-existent with respect to what precedes does not undergo reduplication" is merely a general tendency (*prāyika*).
Because of the statement "both [occur] when there is repetition," it is said:
through the determination of reality, on account of the relationship between cause and effect, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs based on the preceding cognition (*pratyaya*).

Likewise, it is protected by the *ekāc-sūtra*. In this regard, the following is the common solution: by the force of the teaching that the roots beginning with *sic* are *ṣopadeśa*, by the mention of *stauti* in the rule *stauti-ṇyoreva*, and by the prohibition in the rule *sico yaṅi*, it is made known that even when there is doubling in place [of the original] through the determination of identity based on the non-difference of the audible form (*śruti*), grammatical operations are still performed.
"Otherwise, what occasion would there be for the substitution of *ṣ*?
To this it is replied: "But how was it stated that [the rule] *sico yaṅi* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?"
Since the substitution of *ṣ* would otherwise apply by the rule *upasargāt sunīti* etc., that [mention of *pari*] must serve to prohibit it.
As for the form *paritosicyate*,
this has been stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *sico yaṅi*.

The application [of *ṣatva*] that would arise from the rule "after a preposition, before *sunoti*" is sublated by the prohibition of *ṣatva* based on the status of being the beginning of a word (*padādi*), because it is immediate; it is not sublated by the rule "after *sica*, before *yaṅ*". Therefore, it is stated that this prohibition applies everywhere.
When the prohibition "after *sa*, and at the beginning of a word" (*sātpadādyoḥ*) would otherwise apply, *ṣatva* is prescribed by the rule concerning prepositions (*upasargāt*).
By the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*, there is a prohibition specifically of the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*.
Furthermore, by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply,
because the *s* [in question] is not an *ādeśa* (substitute).
This is not so;
such a meaning for it exists only when [the rule] is established.
Now, however, the substitution of *ṣ* will be prescribed by the sūtra even for that which has not yet been reached, such as the prefix (*upasarga*) and so forth.
Therefore, for the purpose of prohibiting that [substitution], the rule *sico yaṅi* should indeed exist. Nor should it be argued that *sātpadādyoḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*;
because of its association with that [former rule], *sico yaṅi* is likewise an exception to the substitution of *ṣ* characterized by the rule [for suffixes].
Since concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is stated only when both [possibilities] exist,
and since this exception (*apavāda*) characterized by the substitution of *ṣatva* is not possible here, such concomitance is untenable.
It is replied:

In the view that there is doubling [of the suffix] in its place (*sthāne-dvirvacana-pakṣe*), even in the case of *parisesicyate*, since the portion of the *sic* suffix containing the *yakāra* is doubled, the substitute *sesic* lacks the designation *sic*. Consequently, how could the substitution of the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) by the rule *upasargād...* (Pāṇini 8.3.65) apply via the mediation of *sic*, such that the prohibition *sicaśca yaṅi* (Pāṇini 8.3.112) would be necessary? Alternatively, one might argue that in this case, the rule should simply be formulated as *sicaśca yaṅi*.

And this is the meaning: since the rule "there is ṣatva [substitution] for *siC* after a prefix" (P. 8.3.65) would already establish that *parisesicyate* is correct—provided one excludes the *yaṅ* affix—the fact that the rule "for *siC* when *yaṅ* follows" (P. 8.3.66) was formulated is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of] P. 8.3.59 (*ādeśapratyayayoḥ*). Regarding this point, while the discussion concerning P. 6.1.95 (*omāṅośca*) was being protected, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) was stated under the *bahula* section in relation to the maxim of the "prior exception" (*purastādapavāda-paribhāṣā*). || 62 ||
When [a suffix] is applied to both sides of a base, it is not as if it were the end of the preceding element or the beginning of the following one. 63.

From the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (P. 6.1.84), by the continued application of the term *pūrva*, the rule *antādivacca* (P. 6.1.85) effects that a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) behaves like the final letter of the preceding element with respect to the operation of the preceding element, and like the initial letter of the following element with respect to the operation of the following element.

In this regard, so that a grammatical rule may be applied as far as possible: by virtue of the preceding element being treated as its final letter, in the case of *amū* (from *adas*), the rule *adaso'serdādu do maḥ* (P. 8.2.80) applies; likewise, by virtue of the following element being treated as its initial letter, in the case of *agnī vṛkṣau*, the status of being a *pragṛhya* vowel applies.

The meaning of the sentence is this: where a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) depends upon both the preceding and the following elements, in that case, due to this dependence on both sides, there is neither the status of being "final" (*antavat*) nor the status of being "initial" (*ādivat*).

Consequently, in the word *vṛkṣam*, because the single substitute is not included by the inclusion of the preceding element, the base (*aṅga*) does not end in the vowel *ā*; and because it is not included by the inclusion of the following element, the *m* does not have the status of being part of a case-ending (*suptva*), and thus the lengthening [of the vowel] does not occur.
Similarly, in *prohyate*, the rule *upasargād ṛti dhātau* (Pāṇini 6.1.91)—which prescribes the substitution of short *u* for *o* after a prefix—does not apply.

In this regard, it should not be said that since the substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included by the mention of the "preceding" element (*pūrvagrahaṇa*), one should apply the long vowel by relying on the status of *makāra* as being a *suptva* (an affix) through the principle of "that which is modified in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛta*).
For if the *ekadeśaparibhāṣā* were to apply here, the *ubhayatāśrayaparibhāṣā* would be rendered without scope.
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) was recited by the author of the Bhāṣya in the context of the rule *antādivacca*.
Therein, the worldly principle (*laukiko nyāyaḥ*) was stated:
just as when there is a single servant belonging to two [masters] of equal power, he proceeds to act for the sake of both through their business in order to avoid conflict. || 63 ||
In a rule based on phonemes (varṇa), the status of being "end" or "beginning" does not apply [to the constituent parts]. 64.

Therefore, in the case of *khaṭvābhiḥ* and *mālābhiḥ*, because the preceding [vowel] lacks the status of being "final" (*antyavat*), the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* (as prescribed by *ato bhisa ais*) does not occur. However, the inclusion of the marker *r̥* (in *ataḥ*) serves its purpose in cases such as *somapābhiḥ*.

Likewise, in *juhāva* from the root *hve*, because the *pūrvarūpa* resulting from *saṃprasāraṇa* lacks the status of being "original" (*anādivat*), the substitution of *au* for *ā* (as prescribed by *āta au ṇalaḥ*) does not occur.
Likewise, in the case of *asyai aśvaḥ* and *asyā aśvaḥ*, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution by virtue of the rule *āṭaśca*.
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is cited in the *Bhāṣya* under the sūtra *antādivacca*.
Kaiyaṭa has stated that the evidence for it is the mention of the "non-application" (*asiddhatva*) of the augment *tuK* in the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*. To explain:

If this [paribhāṣā] did not exist, then in the case of *adhītya*, since the long vowel resulting from the *savarṇadīrgha* rule would be included by the mention of "the subsequent" (*para*), the *tuk* augment—which depends on a short vowel—would already be established; thus, the statement that *tuk* is "as if unestablished" (*asiddha*) would be purposeless. [Objection: But if this [paribhāṣā] exists, then in the case of *kṣīrapeṇa*, the substitution of *ṇa* (by the rule *ekājuttarapade ṇaḥ*) would not apply to the preceding element because it is not followed by a single-vowel word (*anantavat*). Since the condition for the rule depends on a single vowel (*ekāc*), and [in this case] the condition depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*), a prohibition is indeed appropriate there.
In the case of *śriyām*, the substitution *iyaṅ* would not occur because it lacks the status of being either a "prior" (*ādivat*) or a "subsequent" (*paravat*) element relative to another.

It is not desired that the treatment as "end-like" (*antavadbhāva*) or "beginning-like" (*ādivadbhāva*) apply when a single-substitute operation (*ekādeśa*) proceeds by depending upon two letters, one preceding and one following;
for since the function of such an extended application (*atideśa*) operates only in those specific cases, a prohibition is appropriate only there.
But here, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, the rules for *ṇatva* and *iyaṅ*—which depend respectively on that single vowel and the subsequent vowel *ā*—are not precluded.
As they have said:

"Since the words 'beginning' (*ādi*) and 'end' (*anta*) here denote constituent parts, the operation of this extended application (*atideśa*) pertains to the production of those parts, but not to the production of the whole."

Thus, in cases such as *khaṭvābhiḥ* and so forth, although the final element is treated as if it were the preceding one (*pūrva-pratyantavad-bhāva*), what is obtained is its status as a constituent part (*tadekadeśatā*) and not its identity with it (*tadrūpatā*). Therefore, how could there be the contingency of [the application of] *ai*? This very point was stated by the author of the Nyāsa: "This is an extension (*atideśa*) that does not imply identity (*atādrūpya*). (64)
The first chapter on single-syllable words is completed. || 1 ||
When a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned [in a rule], that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included.

And this is an exception to the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*). Wherever there is a mention [of an element] either by its technical name (*saṃjñā*) or by its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), there even that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is included, and not only that which begins with the element from which the suffix is derived.

For example, the compound *kṣepa* is formed with a word ending in the suffix *-kta*, together with a prefix (*sagati*) and an agentive factor (*sakāraka*). [An example is] *udake viśīrṇam avataptekulasthitam*.
According to the rule *aṇ-inuṇaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in *inuṇ* that possesses a prefix.
Regarding the term "sāṃrāviṇa": it refers to a state of universal clamor or a great tumultuous sound.
And the evidence for this is the inclusion of the term "immediate" (*anantara*) in the rule *gatir anantaraḥ*.
By that, when a word ending in *-kta* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the accent of the *gati* belonging to the immediately preceding member is prescribed;
as in *udbhataṃ* and *avadhūtaṃ*, but not for a separated [member], such as in *abhyuddhūtaṃ*.

In this regard, if this *paribhāṣā* did not exist, then by the very *paribhāṣā* concerning the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), there would be no possibility at all for [the application of the rule] to the word *uddhūta*, which is a composite ending in a suffix; so what would be the use of the mention of "immediate" (*anantara*) for the purpose of excluding that? That it was included serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this *paribhāṣā* exists. However, this is merely an indicative mark (*liṅgamātra*).
This [rule] is established precisely by the admission of the commentator Kātyāyana;
otherwise, what would be the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the inclusion of the term "preceded by a *kāraka*"?

By this *paribhāṣā*, even in the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca*, when there is the mention of *kṛt*-affixes, the inclusion of those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* would also follow. As for the solution provided in that regard, [it concerns] *gatikārakopapadānām*...

It has been stated in the *paribhāṣā* rule "the expression of a compound is used [when the meaning is already expressed by its components]" (*kṛdbhiḥ samāsavacanam*) that this rule does not apply depending on the specific nature of the linguistic example (*lakṣya*).

Consequently, in the case of *prajñāsukaraḥ kaṭaḥ*, the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *khityanavyayasya* and the insertion of *mum* prescribed by *arurdviṣadajantasya* do not occur, just as in the case of *kūlamudrajaḥ*. 65.
The rule concerning the addition of suffixes at the end of compounds is not mandatory.
Therefore, in the phrase *bhuvāraṇyāśaṃsādhṛtadhanuṣāhūya tṛṇavat*, the suffix *anaṅ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 5.4.74] does not occur after the word *dhanus*.
Likewise, in the phrase *bahvāmpi taḍāgāni*, the suffix *a* [prescribed by Pāṇini 5.4.74] does not occur.
And there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [the non-necessity of the suffix]: the inclusion of the word *adhvan* in the rule *sphigapūtavīṇāñjodhakukṣisīranāmanām ca*.
For, since the word *apāt* is carried over from the rule *taddhitaśca*, that inclusion of *adhvan* is made so that the final syllable of *adhvan* following *apa-* may be udātta.

If the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) were obligatory, then once the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *upasargād adhvanaḥ*, the desired udātta accent on the final syllable would already be established simply because the suffix is marked with the *cit* designation; thus, he would not have included the word *adhvan* in that rule.
Furthermore, this very fact makes known that this *paribhāṣā* exists.

Likewise, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrddhasu bahuvrīhau*, the mention of the word *mūrddhan* without a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) serves as an indicator (*liṅga*). For if the compound-endings were obligatory, then just as the forms *pād* and *dat*—which are specified with their compound-endings applied according to the rules "there is elision of *pāda* after words other than *hastin*, etc. and "the substitute *datṛ* for *danta* when expressing age"—are mentioned, so too would the word *mūrddha* have been mentioned [with its ending applied].

If the form *mūrdhnaḥ* were specified with the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applied—as in the rule *dvitribhyāṃ ṣa mūrdhnaḥ*—then the citation would have been *mūrddheṣu*. Since, however, it is cited without the application of the compound-ending suffix, this indicates that the rule for applying such suffixes is not mandatory (*anityatva*).
Consequently, even in cases such as *dvimūrdhā* and *trimūrdhā*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is maintained.
Since this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is made known in the *Bhāṣya*,
therefore that which was stated— namely,

that because the author of the *Bhāgavṛtti* [states] in the *Pratyayavidhi* section that the rule for compound endings (*samāsānta*) is not universal (*anitya*), this technical rule does not exist in the *Bhāṣya* due to a lack of evidence— is incorrect.
Surely, for the sake of brevity, the designation of the compound-ending suffix was not made; otherwise, there would be prolixity in saying "mūrddheṣu.
If that were the case, one should have said "mūrddhapāddatsu.
And thus it is indicated that the sequence of compound-endings has not been transgressed. || 66 ||
The section on Bahuvrīhi compounds is completed. || 2 ||
The rule characterized by the coming together [of causes] is the causeless condition for its obstruction.
A rule characterized by immediate sequence does not become the cause for its own sublation;
the meaning is that an action which is enjoined immediately after another does not contradict that immediate sequence.
For example, in the case of *grāmaṇī-brāhmaṇa-kulam*, once the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied, the augment *tug* does not occur.
This is not a valid purpose [for the rule],
because it is already established by the principle that "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)."

Regarding the statement "in the *vṛtti* and in the *paddhati*," the purpose [of the rule] is that once the substitution of *ad* has been applied by the rule *acca gheḥ*, the suffix *ṭāp* should not occur.
But this too is not [the case], because the substitute *ad* is marked with a *t* (tapara). Vāmana stated that the purpose of that [marking] is so that *ṭāp* shall not occur.
This, then, is the purpose:

when *num* is applied due to the occurrence of a case ending (*vibhakti-saṃnipāta*) in forms such as *śatāni* and *sahasrāṇi*, that *num* is not a cause for the elision of the case ending; consequently, the designation *ṣaṭ*—by the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*—does not apply.
If it were to apply, then by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk*, there would be elision of the case ending.
Likewise, in the case of *kumbhakārebhyaḥ*, once the substitution of *ai* for *e* has been applied, the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* does not apply.

And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya in the context of the sūtra *kṛnmejanta*. The evidence for it is the statement prohibiting lengthening in the case of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*.

For if this rule were not in force, since the suffixes *ṅīp* (which causes the insertion of *ṛ*) would not be a cause with respect to the feminine forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*—which have *ṛ* as their final phoneme when derived from *tri* and *catur* on account of the case endings—the prohibition of lengthening would be logically justified even when such lengthening would otherwise apply.

Otherwise, however, because the *ṅīp* suffix would intervene, the rule for lengthening the vowel before *nām* (Pāṇini 6.4.3) would not apply, and thus the statement of the prohibition would be purposeless;
furthermore, there would be no distinction between the long and short forms of the *ṅīp* suffix itself.

In the rule *anityā ceyaṃ kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*, when the suffix *ya* is applied by the rule *ṅeryaḥ* due to the cause of the final vowel *a*, and the lengthening is performed by the rule *yādau supi ca*, they say that by this [lengthening],
the elision of *y* by the rule *yasyeti ca* is established in the case of *dākṣi*. Likewise, in the case of *yā sā*, the suffix *ṭāp* is established.

But how can "kaṣṭāya" serve as an indicator [of the existence of the *sup* case ending], given that by the power of the pratyāhāra "yañ" in the rule "ato dīrgho yañi," the lengthening is already established in "kaṣṭāya" by the rule "supi ca"? It is replied:

Regarding the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* ("there is shortening for *pv* and so on"), according to the view that *pv* and so on do not end in a *gaṇa*, once the substitution of *jā* for *jñā* and *jan* has been applied in the word *jānāti* by the rule *jñājanorjā*, the state of shortness would apply. To prevent this, the prescription of a long-vowel substitute was stated; otherwise, if in the case of *jānāti* there were to be shortening by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*, then [the author] would have simply used the short form *jā* from the rule *jñājanorjā*.
[Objection: Is it not the case that in the word *jayataḥ*, the prescription of a long-vowel substitute for the initial [of the suffix] must be for the sake of the Vedic revelation of the long vowel?
[Reply: This is not so;
for even when the substitution of *ja* has been made, one cannot claim that the lengthening occurs by the rule "lengthening before a *yañ*-suffix" (*ato dīrgho yañi*).

If, however, the view is that *pv* and the others do not belong to the *āgaṇa* group, then in the case of *jānāti*, the rule *pvādīnām* does not apply. Alternatively, the absence of the short vowel is stated by means of the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*; or, once the shortening has been applied, the lengthening occurs again by the rule *ato dīrgho yaṅi*.

In that case, because of the capacity for the inclusion [of the long vowel] by means of the *yakāra* in the *pratyāhāra*, it is indeed possible to state its length; therefore, this is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for [the rule's] non-eternality.
However, if it were non-eternal, this very point would be the indicator:
namely, the mention of *tuka* in the rule *nalopaḥ supsvarasaṃjñātugvidhiṣu kṛti*.

If this [vowel lengthening] were eternal, then in the case of *vṛtrahabhyām*, that [lengthening] would not occur by this very rule; thus, the mention of *tuṅ* (the augment *t*) would be purposeless. 67.

The inclusion of the terms *an*, *in*, *as*, *man*, and *gra* applies the rule of "that which ends with" (*tadanta-vidhi*) both when followed by a meaningful element and when followed by a meaningless one.
Therefore, by the rule "there is elision of 'an'," just as it occurs for meaningful [stems] such as *rājñaḥ* and *rājñā*,
so too does it occur for meaningless [stems] such as *dadhnaḥ* and *dadhnā*;
likewise, it applies by the rule "*inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau*".
Just as [the suffix *ini*] occurs in the case of "brāhmaṇakulāni bahudaṇḍīni" (Brahmin families possessing many staffs),
so too would it occur in the case of "bahuvāgmīni" (possessing many eloquent ones).
Likewise, [the rule] "atvasantasya cādhātoḥ" [would apply].
Just as [the suffix] *supayāḥ* occurs,
so too does *nistatā* occur from *nirgatā*. Just as there is a prohibition of the *ṅīp* suffix in the case of *manaḥ*, as in *sudāmā*, so too is it [prohibited] in the case of *suprathimā*.
And this statement of Kātyāyana is recited as a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). Its basis is the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *arthavat-paribhāṣā*.
They say that this non-eternality is established because of the separate mention of the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* in the *ap-tṛc-tṛn-...*-sūtra.

The separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* is for the purpose of excluding the substitution of *arvan* for the word *tṛ* [in the case of *tṛc*] by the rule "for *arvan*, *tras* [is substituted], provided it is not preceded by a negative particle.

If the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* were eternal, then the exclusion of the word *tṛ* from the substitution of *arvan* would already be established by the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* alone; thus, the separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* would be purposeless.
And the fact that this was done serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the non-eternality of that paribhāṣā.

Now, is it not the case that the distinction between *tṛn* and *tṛc* was not adopted merely for the sake of excluding the inclusion of the word *tṛśabda* from the rule *arvādeśatṛśabdagrahaṇa*, since its inclusion [in the rule] is indeed intended? And yet, if this were so, would there not be long-vowel substitution in the case of *arvantau* and *arvantaḥ*?
Since the augment *num* is applied because of its permanence (*nityatva*), the lengthening (*dīrghatva*)—which is prescribed for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)—will not occur.
It is replied:
due to the recurrence of the term "preceding" (*pūrva*) from the rule *vā ṣapūrvasya nigame*, it is considered that the lengthening will indeed occur prior to the *num*.
And this must necessarily be stated;
otherwise, even in the case of *bahvāmpi taḍāgāni*, the long vowel would not occur once the *num* augment has been applied.

Another, however, says that the separate mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc*, even though they are included under the general term, is for the purpose of indicating that sometimes a specific [sub-variety] is understood.
Therefore, in the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* (P. 6.3.37), although a general statement is made, only the *ka* belonging to a *taddhita* suffix is understood, not the letter *ka* in its entirety.
Consequently, it is unnecessary to state the rule: "In the prohibition regarding words ending in *ka*, the inclusion of *taddhita* suffixes must be made."
In this view, the fact that the *paribhāṣā* is not universally obligatory (anitya) is evidenced by the inclusion of the term "loṭ" in the rule *āni loṭ*.
For instance, in the case of *pravayāni māṃsāni*, the absence of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is established simply because the suffix is devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*). || 68 ||
An internal operation (aṅga) is stronger than that which depends on the phonetic form (vārṇa).
The operation pertaining to the constituent element (*aṅga*) prevails over the operation pertaining to the phoneme (*varṇa*) because it is more powerful.
Therefore, in the case of *bhavati*, the *guṇa* substitution alone occurs, overriding the *yaṇ* replacement.
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is qualified by the condition "having a common locus" (*samānāśraya*); therefore, it does not apply when there is a difference of locus.

Consequently, in the case of the root *siv*, when the Uṇādi suffix has been applied and the form *siu-na* has resulted, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs instead of the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), because the former is *antaraṅga*. Thus, we have *syona*.

And on this point, the inclusion of the *ch* with the *t*-augment (*satukka*) in the rule *cchoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). If [the substitution] were to apply even when based on different factors (*vyāśraye*), then in forms such as *viśnaḥ*, the *ś* would replace the *ch* of the base (*āṅga*) due to the cause of the nasal (*anunāsika*), thereby overriding the *t*-augment caused by the letter *ch*. Once that [substitution] had been made, the *t*-augment would no longer exist because its cause would be absent; so what would be the purpose of including the *ch* with the *t*-augment?
Nor should one suspect the application of the *tuṅ* augment by means of the *asiddha* paribhāṣā,
because *tuṅ* has already been superseded [by another rule].
However, the author of the Nyāsa stated this [paribhāṣā] even in the case of different substrata (*vyāśraya*) in the context of the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*.

Regarding the statement that "when [the rule] *cyavante* and *plavante* occur, the internal (*āṅga*) operation is stronger than a phonetic (*vārṇa*) one," and thus the *guṇa* substitution occurs prior to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) replacement;

in this regard, the fact that the suffix *naṅ* is marked with the *ṅ*-indicator in the rule *yaj-yāc-yata-viccha-praccha-rakṣo naṅ*— which is applied for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*— serves as the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) that this [principle of internal superiority] applies even in certain cases where the two operations depend on different bases (*vyāśraya*).
Otherwise, since there would be no possibility of a *guṇa* substitution when the augment *tuk* follows *vi-ci*, the designation of *ṅit* for the negative particle *naṅ* would be purposeless.
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) has been made known by the inclusion of the term *asavarṇa* in the rule *abhyāsasyāvarṇe*;
for that [term] is employed for this purpose:
so that in forms such as *īṣatuḥ*, *īṣuḥ*, *ūṣatuḥ*, and *ūṣuḥ*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* do not occur before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa-ac*).

And if the superiority of an *aṅga* operation over a [rule concerning] phonemes (*vārṇa*) did not exist, then—since the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) would be internal (*antaraṅga*) and thus applied first—the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would not even arise; therefore, the purpose of the rule "asavarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.102) is to indicate that this *paribhāṣā* exists. To this, it is replied:

If *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* do not occur before a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*), then they would likewise not apply in the case of *eyeṣoḥ* and *uvoṣa*, because here too, by the rule "when a subsequent [element] is present, for a preceding operation" (*acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*), there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*; and since a subsequent homogeneous vowel exists, [the substitution should not take place].
Thus, in the absence of such a rule, the mention of "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*) would indeed be purposeless.
It is said:
here the status of being "as if the original" (sthānivadbhāva) does not apply, because the reduplication (abhyāsa) precedes the vowel from which the substitute was prescribed.
For it is thus:

Since the *guṇa* substitution occurs first, the reduplication takes place by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) according to the rule *dvirvacane'ci*.
Once the reduplication has been performed, because the restriction in the rule for *sthānivadbhāva* specifies "only in the case of reduplication," the *guṇa* remains as the single preceding form;
it is not performed again after the reduplication.
Therefore, when *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are to be applied by the rule *tenācaḥ parasmin*, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the place of the original) does not occur.
For if that were the case, then the substitution of *iyaṅ* would have to be prescribed for the reduplicated syllable of *arti* itself; thus, one would have simply said *arti-abhyāsasya tyap*.

This very mention of *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous vowel) is the foundation for the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) which states: "That which precedes a vowel for which no specific operation has been prescribed is treated as if it were the original [vowel] with respect to the operation. 69.
For that which precedes an unspecified vowel, it is treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva) with respect to a grammatical operation.

The status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the place of the original) according to the rule *yo hyacaḥ parasmin* applies to that which precedes an unindicated vowel (*anādiṣṭāt acaḥ*) with respect to an operation (*kārye*).

Therefore, in the word *paṭayati*, the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel of the syllable *pa-*—which precedes the vowel of the syllable *ṭā-* that is not itself subject to the rule—is treated as a *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*.
However, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to an operation concerning what precedes an indicated vowel (*ādiṣṭāt acaḥ*), as in the examples *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvaḥ*.
Therefore, the rule *aco ñṇiti* does not apply here;

for in this case, there is no possibility of the two vowels *ai* and *au* occurring before the suffixes *ñ* and *ṇ*, since *ai* and *au* are prescribed as replacements for the preceding vowels *e* and *o* by the rules *vṛddhireci* and *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*.

However, the author of the *Nyāsa* has resolved this difficulty by applying the principle: "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is considered as not having taken effect (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)."
According to his view, it should be cited as "he caused [it] to be made."

It is understood from the purposeful technical designation (*nipātana*) of *iṭ* that, in certain instances, what precedes an enjoined vowel (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvasya*) attains the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivattvam*).

For if there were no *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the operation [of a rule] concerning what precedes an enjoined vowel, then the statement made by the author of the *Vṛtti* regarding the purposeful designation of *iṭ* would be incorrect. To explain: in the case of *upeyivān*, once reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has occurred and the lengthening (*dīrgha*) has been applied by the rule *iṇo yaṇ kitīti*, the subsequent formation of a single syllable (*ekāctva*) through homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*) ensures that the addition of *iṭ* is established by the rule *vasvekājādghasām*. Thus, the purposeful designation of *iṭ* is justified.

Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of the rule *dīrgha īnaḥ kiti* prescribing a long vowel, there ought not to be substitution by homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*), because that rule finds its application in cases such as *īyatuḥ* and *īyuḥ* where the *yaṇ* replacement occurs. Furthermore, there is no possibility of obtaining a long vowel through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*.

Because reduplication occurs before the marked vowel (ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt), it is precisely for this reason that the prohibition— "it is not as if it were the original" (na sthānivat)— is applicable with respect to the rule concerning homogeneous vowels (savarṇavidhi). Thus, in forms such as *śiṇḍhi* and *piṇḍhi*, [the substitution of ṣ and ṭh for s and t is not treated as the original].

Likewise, that which he will state regarding the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca*— where, in the prescription of lengthening, one applies the substitution of *yaṇ* by virtue of the status of being a *sthānin* in the case of *riryatuḥ* and *riyūḥ*, and then, after reduplication has occurred,
the lengthening does not take place due to the status of being a *sthānin* by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*— that is rendered consistent.
And this meaning—namely, the sense of the rule *parasmin pūrvavidhau*—is recited as a *paribhāṣā* (metarule).

It has been stated therein that "priority" (*pūrvatva*) is understood either with reference to the vowel (*aj*), with reference to the substitute (*ādeśa*), or with reference to the cause (*nimitta*).
Among these, when priority is understood with reference to the vowel, then this is the meaning [of the rule].

An *ajādeśa* (a substitute for a vowel) which is caused by a subsequent element (*paranimittaka*) is treated as the original (*sthānivat*) in a rule concerning a preceding element. Why is there *sthānivadbhāva* in a rule concerning a preceding element? [Because it applies] to a vowel (*ac*). Thus, its dependence on a preceding vowel is its very root. And they cite an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
In the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*, there is the mention of *asavarṇa*;
or else, there is the statement *at smṛdṛtvarapra-thamradastṝspaśām*.
For by that [statement], *at* is prescribed in order to set aside the application of *sanvadbhāva*.
Furthermore, if there were to be the status of being *sthānivat* even with respect to what precedes an enjoined vowel, then one would not even perform the substitution of *āt*.
When a verbal root (prakṛti) is mentioned, that which ends in the yaṅluṅ suffix is also included.
By the rule *tena vido laṭo vā*, the optional substitution of *ṇal* and other affixes applies even to the *yaṅ*-luṅ form:
*veveda*, *vevidatuḥ*.
veviduḥ | vevetti | vevittaḥ |
"It knows" means: it experiences.
The fact that this [rule] is established by logic (*nyāyasiddhatva*) has been demonstrated by the author of the *Nyāsa* in the rule concerning the root *śīṅ* and others.

To explain: under the view that there is reduplication in place of the original element (*sthāne-dvirvacana*), the designation "base" (*prakṛti*) applies due to the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

And since that very same [root] is repeated twice in the case of a double application (*dvir-prayoga*), it is logical that when the base form (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, the *yaṅ-luk* (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) should also be included.
They also cite an indicator (*jñāpaka*):
the mention of the term "penultimate" (*upadhā*) in the rule *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*.

Although it would have been sufficient to say *ūdorgohaḥ* for the sake of brevity, the inclusion of the term *upadhā* is made so that the substitution does not apply to the vowel *au* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in forms such as *jogṛhati*, which lack the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*).
This result would only follow if, when a verbal root (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, the form ending in *yaṅluk* is also included.
But surely, the mention of *upadhā* in the rule *gamahanajanakhanaghasām* is for the sake of what follows;
otherwise, there would be elision of the final letter (*alontyasya lopah*). It is said in reply:

In the view of those who maintain that [the suffixes] are indicators (*jñāpaka*), it must be established there that [the rule] *ataḥ* applies; however, this [rule] does not apply when there is a mention by means of the *śtip* [suffix]. And so says the traditional authority (*smṛti*).

“[The following] five [conditions do not apply] in the case of *yaṅluk*: that which is specified by a *śit* affix, that which is specified by a *śap* affix, that which is specified by an *anubandha*, that which is specified by a *gaṇa*, and that which involves the mention of a single vowel (*ekāj*). The specification by a *śit* affix is seen in the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca*.
The specification by a *śap* affix is seen in the rule *bharajñapisanām*, where the word *bhara* occurs.
By means of the *anubandha*, [the rule] "ruṭ after the root *śī*" applies;
by means of the *gaṇa*, [the rule] "after *vata*, *tati*, *tanoti*, etc.
applies; and by means of the mention of "monosyllabic" (*ekāj*), [the rule] "from a monosyllabic root that is unaccented in its original form (*upadeśe*)."
There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*. In this verse, the word "something" (*kiṃ cit*) is to be understood as the remainder.
This is for the purpose of including that case where the verbal root (*dhātu*) is qualified by the mention of "a single vowel" (*akac-grahaṇa*).

However, where there is a reference to a constituent part of a verbal root—as in the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*, where the mention of *ekāc* (a monosyllabic root) is not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa formation—they say that by this means, the reduplication in the *yaṅ*-lopa form results in *bobhavati*. Now, one might ask: how is the suffix *śap* produced in *bhavati*, given that the *sārvadhātuka* affix *śtip* denotes the absence of an agent (*akartṛvācin*)?
It is said:
"Because it has the marker *ś* (in *śtip*), the suffix *śap* occurs even when [the verb] does not express the agent.
This is not so.
Because the designation *śit* serves its purpose in prohibiting the substitution of *ā* by the rule "ādeca upadeśe 'śiti" (Pāṇini 6.1.45);
and because in the case of *roditi*, it serves the purpose of introducing the augment *iṭ* by the rule "rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.2.76).
Furthermore, if the designation *śit* were absent, [the suffix] would be treated as an *ārddhadhātuka*, and consequently, the augment *iṭ* would apply by the rule "śtipīṭ" (Pāṇini 7.3.75).
Now, by the rule *titutratathasisusarakaseṣu*, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*.
Even so, because it is an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, the elision of *ṇi* would still occur by the rule *smeraniṭi*.
If that is the case, then the *śap* [suffix] occurs precisely because of the specific mention of the roots *indh* and *bhū* in the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca*.

How then is it that the author of the *Nyāsa*, while explaining that "the suffixes *ik* and *tip* should be stated [to apply] when there is a mention of a verbal root (*dhātunirdeśe*)," says that [the suffix *śap* applies] by virtue of the inclusion of the letter *ś*?
It is replied:

the word *śitkaraṇa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has the inclusion of *ś* as its cause" (*śitaḥ karaṇaṃ yasya*), and by this term *śitkaraṇa*, the very mention of the root *bhū* is being expressed.
This is the meaning:
by the force of the formulation "it exists" (*bhavati*), [the word] "sound" (*śabdi*) is implied.
However, another says:

The two *ś* sounds in *śtip* are *anubandhas*; because the governing context of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) does not apply in the rule *laśakvataddhite*, they do not receive the technical designation *it*.
This point was stated by the author of the *Anunyāsa* regarding the *paribhāṣā* concerning what is taught in a single *yoga*.
Thus, by the force of the second *śit* marker, [the suffix] is *śap*. (71)
That which is external is unestablished (asiddha) with respect to that which is internal.
When an internal operation is to be performed, that which is external is considered as if it were not established.

Therefore, in examples such as *pacāveda*, because the external *guṇa* substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the replacement by *ai* occurs according to the rule *eta aini*. In *grāmaṇi-brāhmaṇakulam*, the insertion of *tuK* does not occur by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*.
In *nārkuṭaḥ* and *nārpatyam*, the rule *khar-avasānayoh* does not apply.
In the word *rājanye*, the elision of the final consonant due to being a *saṃyoga* (conjunction of consonants) does not occur.
And the evidence for this is the prescription of *ūṭh* in the rule *vā ūṭh*.
For there it is stated:
"Let the previously mentioned *samprasāraṇa* itself be prescribed for the letter *v*; from that, let there be the formation of the single substitute [of the preceding and following sounds]."

Then, by the rule for the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the *u* of the suffix *ṇvi* is replaced by its *guṇa*, *o*; subsequently, by the rule "vṛddhir eci," this results in *vṛddhi*, thereby establishing the form *praṣṭhauha*.
Furthermore, when a word ending in something other than *a* is the upapada, the suffix *ṇvi* is not observed after the root *vah* in Vedic usage.
Why, then, was the insertion of *ūṭh* prescribed? That [prescription] serves to indicate that this *paribhāṣā* exists.

The *samprasāraṇa* is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it is prescribed when a suffix that serves as the cause for the designation *bha* is present; therefore, when the internal (*antaraṅga*), more internal (*abhyantaraṅga*) *guṇa* dependent on the suffix ought to be applied, the external *samprasāraṇa* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).
Since the vowel *u* would thus not exist, how could there be a *guṇa*?

This technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) is non-eternal (*anitya*). Furthermore, that non-eternality is indicated by the fact that, in the rule prescribing the *tuṅ* augment—namely, *nalopaḥ supsvara*—the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as if it were not established (*asiddha*). To explain:

If this [rule] were eternal (*nitya*), then in the case of *vṛtrahabhyām*, when the internal (*antaraṅga*) *tuk* is to be applied, the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the external (*bahiraṅga*) elision of the *n* would already be established; thus, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for its non-eternality.
Now, one might object: since the rule is already established, the statement that it is "not established" must be for the sake of a restriction (*niyamārtha*).
In the context of the definition of *kṛt* suffixes, [the rule] "asiddha" applies only with respect to *tuk*, not with respect to the definition of *cha*.
Therefore, in the case of *vṛtrahacchatram*, when *tuk* is to be applied, the principle that "the external (*bahiraṅga*) is asiddha with respect to the internal (*antaraṅga*)" does not operate.
Furthermore, it is not the case that when both a general injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible, the injunction alone is superior.
This is because both the restrictive rule (*niyama*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*) are equal in their requirement for two meanings.
It is said in reply:
in the case of *vṛtrahacchatram*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is not external (*bahiraṅga*), but rather the *tuṅ* augment itself is external, since the *tuṅ* depends upon two words.

In the case of *vṛtrahabhyām*, however, since the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) depends upon the case-ending (*vibhakti*), it is considered extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Furthermore, regarding its non-eternality (*anityatva*), in the form *amū*, when the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitution of *u* and *m* (in *amūbhyām*) is to be applied, the extrinsic single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not become "as if non-existent" (*asiddha*). Likewise, in *papuṣaḥ paśya*, because the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is as if non-existent, the suffix *iṭ*—which would otherwise be triggered by the presence of a consonant (*val*) according to the rule *vasvekājāddhasām*—does not occur.
And regarding this, the absence of its occurrence has been stated [in the verse] "those who have not performed the *vyūha* [are those for whom there is no other means]" (72).
There is no establishment of externality in the absence of immediate succession. || 73 ||
This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to what precedes it.
The *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply in the absence of an immediate sequence with a vowel (*acor-ānantarya*). Therefore, in forms such as *bahavaḥ*, the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* takes effect.
Likewise, in *akṣadyūḥ*, [the substitution] is governed by *iko yaṇ aci*;
in *yūnaḥ* and *maghonaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitutions are governed by *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*.
If this is so, then in *pacāvedaṃ*, these [substitutions] would also apply by virtue of *eṅi pararūpam*.

Even here, in the absence of *ac*-proximity (*acorānantarya*), since the external *aguṇa* substitution has already taken effect, it would be appropriate to prohibit [the application of] the maxim "an internal operation prevails over an external one" (*siddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*).
This is not so;
for this prohibition applies only where both an internal and an external operation would otherwise apply simultaneously in the absence of *ac*-proximity, as in the example *bahavo 'kṣadyūḥ*.
For in this case, when the external operation has taken effect, both *guṇa* and *ūṭh* still exist, while the internal operations of *av* and *āy* replacement are yet to be applied.

In the example *pacāvedam*, once the external single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made, the immediate succession of vowels (*ac-ānantarya*) is lost; thus, the two conditions for the rule "in the immediate succession of vowels" (*acorānantarye*) no longer exist.
How then can there be a prohibition of this [rule]?

If this is so, then even in the case of *adhītya* and *pretya*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, there is no immediate succession (*ānantarya*) between two vowels; how, then, is the justification for [the rule] *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* established as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?

For indeed, according to the view that "first the verbal root is joined with the prefix," at a time subsequent to the long vowel, when the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *tuṭ* is to be performed, there is no immediate succession between two vowels. If that is the case, then according to the view that "first the verbal root is joined with its grammatical factor" (*sādhana*), it is stated in the case of *adhītya* and *pretya* that "there is no immediate succession of vowels" (*nājānantarya*).

For in this view, since the *lyap* is applied before [the application of] *ekādeśa*, this [rule] indeed exists even when there is no immediate sequence of vowels (*acorānantarya*), whether the operation is internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*).
Nor, in this view, does the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* become redundant because the *tuk* is applied on account of its being internal;
for as much as the *tuk* is internal, so too is the lengthening (*dīrgha*) obligatory (*nitya*).
Therefore, between these two [rules], which are both permanent and internal, lengthening would occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule.

Alternatively, even in the case of the principle that "the root is first joined with a prefix," when the grammatical derivation is analyzed according to the maxim *akṛtavyūhāḥ* ("those who do not disregard what has already been formed"), there exists the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of vowels.
Furthermore, regarding the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*, the author of the Nyāsa has explained it as "of the root, only that which is caused by it."

When an operation governed by the *saṃhitā*-section is to be performed, the rule *nājānantarye* (P. 1.1.59) subverts the principle that "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*).
Since the rule *eta ai* (P. 3.4.93) prescribes an operation established in a different context, why would a prohibition be stated regarding its application?
This very point was stated by Maitreya in the commentary on the rule *chvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (P. 6.4.19).

In the case of *acorānantarya*, that which results in two [operations], one internal (*antaraṅga*) and one external (*bahiraṅga*), is what is prohibited there; however, in this case, since the external [condition] has already been established and the absence of *acorānantarya* has ceased, the internal [operation] applies—so how could there be a prohibition of it? This is the meaning of the passage beginning with those words. The sense of this is as follows:
The word "exists" (*asti*) is to be supplied [as the verb]. This is the meaning:

when there is a sequence of non-thieves (*acora-anantarya*), and in a situation where both exist—namely, where an external operation (*bahiraṅga*) has already occurred and an internal one (*antaraṅga*) is about to occur, or where an internal operation has already occurred and an external one is about to occur—the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* is prohibited.
Thus [it is said].

The proof for this is the statement that "the substitution of *tuK* is not established" (*ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*), which declares the substitution of *tuK* to be non-established (*asiddha*) in relation to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

If the status of being non-established applied to an external operation (*bahiraṅga*) even when there is immediate succession between vowels and consonants (*aj-ac-ānantarya*), then in cases such as *adhītya*, where the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *tuK* is to be performed, the external operation of homogeneous vowel lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*)—which depends on two words—would already be non-established by the very rule "an external operation is non-established with respect to an internal one.
Consequently, the specific statement regarding its non-establishment would be redundant.
And by this [rule], the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā is not set aside; thus the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā has been stated. || 73 ||
A grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name (saṃjñā) is not invariably obligatory.

In the case of *tena dhāma svāyambhuvam yayuḥ*, because the condition for *guṇa* is absent, the substitution *uvaṅ* is established. Likewise, in *jyogiṣam*, the *vṛddhi* of the *aṇ* class does not occur.
And in *pañcabāṇaḥ kṣiṇoti*, there is no *guṇa*.
In the word *udaśvitvān*, there is no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *śvi* when the suffix *kvip* is applied.
And there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this: in the rule *orguṇaḥ*, where one ought to have said *orot*, the mention of *guṇa* is the indicator;
likewise, in the rule *uto vṛddhir luki hali*, where one ought to have said *aut*, the mention of *vṛddhi* is the indicator.
By this, the *vṛddhi* does not occur in the form *stuyāt*.

And thus, regarding the rule *kṅiti ca*, that which was stated in the *Vṛtti*— namely, that the designation of *yāsuṭ* as having the marker *ṅ* (ṅit) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the property of being *ṅit* does not belong to substitutes based on the original *lakāra*— is now justified. Otherwise, the designation of *yāsuṭ* as *ṅit* would be for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *vṛddhi* not caused by *niṅ* (as in *stuyāt*), so how could it serve as an indicator?
But even so, its status as a *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) is improper, because in examples such as *vinuyuḥ*, it serves the purpose of the prohibition [of guna] by the rule *jusi ca*.
This is incorrect;
for even if the suffix were marked with the *ṅit* indicator, the guna substitution prescribed by *jusi ca* would necessarily still apply here.
[Objection: This [rule] is formulated only for the domain of *kṅit* suffixes. [Response: No;
by the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, that which is *ṅit*-ness according to the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* is what is sublated by this [present rule], but not even that which depends on *yāsuṭ*.
It is said:
if this were the only purpose,
then one could simply carry forward the term *aci* from the rule *kasyāci* and prescribe the *guṇa* substitution before *jus* when it begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*).
The *ṅittva* of *yāsuṭ* is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Regarding the rule *apiḥ padārthasaṃbhāvanā...* (P. 1.4.96), Rakṣita has explained that in the example *stuyāt*, the augment *pi* does not become *ṅit*. Consequently, by the rule *kṅiti ca* (P. 1.1.5), there is no substitution of *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, in *stuyāt*, there is no lengthening by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (P. 7.4.25).

Because the *yak* affix belongs to the *sārvadhātuka* category. But is it not the case that this is stated as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory proof) for the sake of establishing forms such as *acinavam*? For, by the rule "the *pic* [affix] is not *ṅit*," the absence of *ṅittva* ensures that *guṇa* substitution is indeed established.
It is said: this is the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra, not that of the author of the Sūtras.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Nyāsa on the rule *serhyapicca*:
If [the rule] were formulated as *ser hiṅit*, then by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would possess the property of being *pit*.

Otherwise, since even in that case [the rule] states "that which is marked with ṅ does not have the property of being *pit*," what occasion would there be for the property of being *pit* to apply? [Objection:

But if the author of the Sūtras did not intend this principle that "that which is marked with ṅ does not have the property of being *pit*," then you might argue that in the form *brūtāt*, the augment *iṭ* would occur according to the rule *bruva īṭ* due to the status of being a substitute for the *pit* [element].

It is said: even when there is a possibility [of both applying], sublation occurs; thus, by the *ṅit*-ness of *tāt*, the *pit*-ness of *tip* must be sublated. Likewise, in the case of *bhindyāt* as well, because the *ṅit*-ness of the optative (*liṅ*) is sublated by the *pit*-ness of *tip*. || 74 ||
When two things are taught as being invariably connected, upon the removal of one, there is the removal of both.
For example:

in *dhīvarī* and similar forms, the substitution of *r* for the suffix *van* is taught by the rule *vano ra ca* as being conditioned by the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. However, in forms such as *pañcadhīva*, where it is derived from the sense "bought with five female fishermen" (*pañcabhir dhīvarībhiḥ krītā*), the suffix *ṭhak* belonging to the *ārhīya* group is elided by the rule *adhyarddhadvigor lug asaṃjñāyām*; once this elision (*luk*) has occurred, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is also withdrawn by the rule *luktaddhitaluki*, and consequently, the *r* substitution is likewise withdrawn.
Regarding the rule "after *chid* and others, [the suffix] *ay* is always [used]," the author of the Bhāṣya stated that this is established by reasoning (*nyāyasiddhatva*).
As he said:
"This is a worldly principle: among things enjoined together, upon the removal of one, there is the removal of both."
For example, when it is said, "This must be done by Devadatta and Yajñadatta," in the absence of Devadatta, Yajñadatta does not do it either.
The author of the Bhāṣya has also explained this as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *bilvakādibhyaś chasya luk* (Pāṇini 4.3.135).
For there it is stated that the mention of *vilvakādibhyaḥ* is actually a reference to *kuk*.

Furthermore, this *kuk* [augment] belongs to *naḍa* and so forth, as it is prescribed in conjunction with the suffix *cha*. Since *cha* alone can follow words such as *bilva*, when it is stated that there is elision (*luk*) for the group beginning with *bilvaka*, the elision will occur only for *cha*—which is the suffix conditioned by the technical designation *bha*—even when the suffix is present.
Why, then, was the mention of *cha* made? It was done so that the elision should apply to *cha* alone;
otherwise, by the rule of simultaneous prescription (*sanniyoga-paribhāṣā*), there would also be the removal of *kuk*. This is the purpose.
And thus there is evidence for the existence of this technical designation (*paribhāṣā*).
To this it is said:
"But if it is stated that 'there is elision (*luk*) after *bilvaka* and so forth,' would there not be elision of the suffix in general, regardless of its specific type?"
And likewise, in a case such as *bilvakād*, there would also be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*).
It is replied: because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "taddhita" from the rule *halas taddhitasya*, this will not occur.
But even so, in the case of *bailvakaḥ*—meaning "a part or a product of the *bilvaka*"—the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule *kopadhācca*.

If that is the case, then because the word *taddhite* is understood from the rule *apatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti*, there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix that bears the designation *bha* when another *taddhita* follows. Even so, [elision] would still occur in cases such as *bailvakaḥ* (meaning "belonging to the *bilvaka*") and *vailvakīyam* (meaning "this belongs to the *vailvaka*").
This is not so; the elision (*luk*) is prescribed for that suffix which is ordained after words such as *bilvaka*.
However, in this case, the suffix *cha* is not ordained after *bilvaka*, but rather after *bailvaka*.
And this [suffix] is *anitya* (irregular).

That irregularity is indicated by the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in the rule *taddhiteṣvacām ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117), which states "before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel, the first vowel is increased.
For in that context, after asking "What is meant by 'before a non-*aḍha* suffix'?", the counter-examples *śyaineyaḥ* and *rauhiṇeyaḥ* are provided.
Furthermore, if this [suffix] were eternal (*nitya*),
then when the *yasya* portion is elided by the rule *iti ca*, the *nakāra* would also necessarily be removed by the *sanniyoga-paribhāṣā*.
Consequently, since there would be no distinction in the case of *puṃvadbhāva*, the prohibition *na aḍhaḥ* would be rendered meaningless.

[Objection: But how can it be purposeless? For when there is elision (*lopa*), by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* [Pāṇini 1.1.57], the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies; and by the rule regarding the definition of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) or the maxim regarding what is not established (*asiddhaparibhāṣā*), the connection with the feminine suffix *ṅīp* indeed exists. This being the case, since the maxim concerning simultaneous application (*sanniyoga-paribhāṣā*) does not apply, the substitution of *na* for *m* is not precluded. [Reply: It is said in response:
An operation is performed by means of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) and so forth;
however, there is no presence of the elided phoneme, nor does this imply the non-application of the rule regarding simultaneous occurrence (*sanniyoga-paribhāṣā*),
because that rule applies to every instance of disappearance (*apāya*).
The evidence for this is likewise of that same nature.

Otherwise, even when the *luk* elision of *cha* has been applied, the removal of *kuk* would not occur, because it would still exist by virtue of the rule regarding the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) and so forth. || 75 ||
Even when the suffix *ṇa* is used in the sense of "having that as one's characteristic" (*tācchīlika*), the grammatical operations produced by the suffix *aṇ* take place.

The suffix *aṇ* signifies "done"; thus, even when the suffix *aṇ* occurs, it means "this is her habit" (*śīla*). Consequently, even from a word ending in the suffix *aṇ*—such as *caura* (thief) or *tāpasa* (ascetic)—the feminine suffix *ṅī* is applied due to its inclusion in the *chatrādi* group:
*caurī*, *tāpasī*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "tācchīlike" (when denoting one who has that habit)?
It should be stated that the suffix *ṇa* is applied after the roots *śīl*, *kām*, *bhikṣ*, and *ācar*.
Examples: *māṃsaśīlā* (one whose habit is meat) and *māṃsabhikṣā* (one who begs for meat).

From the words *prajñā*, *śraddhā*, *arcā*, and *vṛtti*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form feminine nouns such as] *prājñā* and *brāhmaṇī*. In these cases, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur due to the application of *aṇ*.
This [rule] is illustrated by the example *kārmastācchīlye*.

In that context, while the term *tacchīlam* (having that as one's habit) is being carried over from the previous rule, the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the *chatrādi* group; thus, *kārma* is derived as an irregular form (*nipātana*) from the word *karman*.
To this, it is said:

Since the form *kārma* is established by the elision of the *ṭi* suffix according to the rule *taddhiteṣvacām ādeḥ*, it is improper to posit a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) for the purpose of that elision; nor is there any preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *an*,
because that rule is prescribed specifically for the suffix *aṇ*.
If that is the case, then this indicates that such a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) exists. To this it is replied:

if the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is indeed applied even when the suffix *aṇ* has the sense of "having the habit" (*tācchīlika*), for what purpose is the suffix *aṇ* itself not simply prescribed in the sense of "having the habit"?
And thus, it would not be necessary to provide an indicator (jñāpaka).
It is said: "It was not composed for the sake of variety. (76)
An operation being stated with respect to a verbal root applies only to that [root] when it is followed by an affix.
Whatever grammatical operation is prescribed for a verbal root (*dhātu*) occurs only when that root is followed by an affix (*pratyaya*).

Consequently, in the case of *rajjusṛgbhyām*, although the forms ending in *kvip* possess the status of verbal roots, the substitution of *am* (as prescribed by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti*) does not take place because the following *sup* suffix is an affix belonging to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Similarly, by the rule *aci vibhāṣā*, the substitution does not occur in *girau* or *giraḥ*.

Similarly, in the case of *udakamagbhyām* and *prāṇanagbhyām*, the augment *num* [is applied] by the rule *masjinaśorjhali*. If that is so, just as there is no *num* in *prāṇanagbhyām*, so too the substitution of *ku* (the change to *k*) based on the root *naś*, as prescribed by the rule *naśervā*, would not optionally occur either.

It is said: since the substitution of *k* for *g* (*kutva*) is prescribed for a word (*pada*), this *kutva* does not depend on the root or the suffix; however, the augment *num* depends precisely on the root and the suffix.
Relying on this very paribhāṣā, the letter *k* of the suffix *kāmyac* in the form *upayaṭkāmyati* receives the designation *anit*.
In forms such as *śriyau*, *śriyaḥ*, *bhruvau*, and *bhruvaḥ*, the substitutes *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occur even when they follow nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*).
This is because of the formulation of the rules *oḥ supi* (Pāṇini 6.4.83) and *varṣābhvaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.84),
as well as due to the specific grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*) found in *parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.18) and *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.30).
The authors of the Vārttikas, however, recite a different paribhāṣā:
"When a verbal root is mentioned by its own form, the operation is to be understood as applying only to that which possesses a suffix.

For according to this reading, in the case of *dṛgbhyām* and *dṛgbhiḥ*, the augment *am* would occur even after the nominal suffix (*sup*), because in the rule *anudāttasya cardupadhasyānyatarasyām*, there is no mention of the root's own form (*asvarūpa-dhātu-grahaṇāt*).
This has also been explained by Rakṣita under the rules *vibhāṣā* and *majervṛddhiḥ*.
The evidence (*liṅga*) for this paribhāṣā is found in the rule *dāṇḍināyanādi*, regarding the word *bhrauṇahatya*, where the substitution of *t* is specifically prescribed (*nipātana*).

For if this paribhāṣā did not exist, then the substitution of *t* would already be established by the rule *hanasta’ciṇaloḥ* when the suffix *ṣyañ* follows; thus, the specific prescription (*nipātana*) would be purposeless.
To this it is replied:
this would be an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *k* for *g*.
It is said in reply:
The substitution of *k* (kutva) will occur by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating "not after *kvā*, etc.
Furthermore, it must also be stated for the sake of the elision of the *ṭi* suffix;
for, since the rule *hanasta’ciṇaloḥ* would apply—because it is subsequent—it would subvert the elision of the *ṭi*.
Nor is it for the sake of preventing the increase of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*), because the increase of the penultimate vowel is superseded by the initial increase (*ādivṛddhi*),
as in the case of *tvāṣṭraḥ* and *jāgataḥ*.
Nor is it for the purpose of subverting the vowels beginning with *n* (the *ṇatva* rule),
because that [subversion] is desired.
Thus ends the fourth quarter (pāda) of the sixth book (adhyāya) in the Paribhāṣāvṛtti composed by Sīradeva.
Thus ends the sixth chapter. 6.
That which falls within [the scope of] that is included by the mention of it. || 78 ||
The meaning is that whatever falls within the scope of something else is included by the mention of that [latter].

Therefore, in the case of *sarvakaḥ*, even though it contains the augment *aK* (*sākacka*), it retains its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and thus the substitution of *śī* for *jas* occurs according to the rule *jasaḥ śī*.
Likewise, in the case of *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*, once the augment *aiC* has been applied, the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) applies by way of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*).
This is a worldly convention;
for example, as in the case of "Bhaṭṭagrāma. Therein, even those who are not bhaṭṭas receive the designation "bhaṭṭa," and likewise, even those who are not mallas receive the designation "malla."
And here, the proof is the word *akoḥ* in the rule *nedamadasorakoḥ*.

If this [restriction] were not present, then the prohibition stated for *idam* and *adas* would not apply in cases such as *imakaiḥ* and *amukaiḥ* simply because they are different words once *akac* has been added;
so what would be the purpose of the prohibition *akoḥ*?
Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya stated in the Vārttika-sūtra:
"If this is so, how then did that same Blessed One [Patañjali], in the rule *nedamadasorakoḥ*, reject the prohibition by establishing the restriction *idamadasoḥ kāt*? It is replied:
This is the intended meaning:
let this not be an indicator (jñāpaka) for the absence of *ak* [in the sense of "not being *a*"].
In the rule *etattadoḥ sulopo 'kor anañsamāse hali*, the word *akoḥ* will serve that purpose.
Regarding the rule *yuvoranākau*,

in the context of the example *paśyayatīti* (he causes to see) under the discussion of *paśyām ācaṣṭe*, whatever criticism and so forth was raised has already been stated under the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* regarding the principle that "those whose internal structure is not yet formed do not undergo [subsequent] grammatical operations" (*akṛtavyūhāḥ*). || 78 ||
Even exceptions (nipātana) are non-obstructive. || 79 ||

Because the rule for the *nipātana* (irregular formation) in the sense of "purāṇaprokteṣu" is an absolute exception, the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* along with the augment *tuṭ* also occur by the rule *sāyaṃciraṃprāhṇepragevyayebhyaṣṭyuṭyulau tuṭ ca*.
Thus, the usage of Bhāravi, "dadhataḥ purātanamunermunitām," and the usage of Māgha, "purātanīrnadīḥ," are both justified.
And the proof for this is the rule *trestrayaḥ*, which serves to establish the form *trayāṇām*.
For if *nipātana*s (irregular formations) were only those that subvert [the application of general rules], then the form *nijāntrayāṇām* would be established [by that very subversion].
However, since *nipātana*s can also be non-subverting, the rule *trestrayaḥ* becomes meaningful for the purpose of precluding the usage *trīṇām*.
Others, however, say:

"This is neither a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) nor the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. It has been explained in the sūtra beginning with *sarvādīni* that nipātanas are indeed [rules] that cause sublation."

Therefore, in that very same sūtra, the forms *bhāgavṛttiḥ* (meaning "the state of being an ancient sage") and *purātanīm nadīm* ("an ancient river") are erroneous readings; yet poets employ them out of mere conformity with tradition, for they do not possess the discerning eye of grammatical rules. || 79 ||
In the section on members [of a compound], that [term] and its subsequent member [are designated as the prior member]. || 80 ||

Therefore, in forms such as *asthidhi* and so on, and even in *priyāsthnā* and *priyadadhnā*, the suffix *anaṅ* occurs; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule stating that [the substitution applies] when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a marker (*grahaṇavat*).
And there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this: the mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) in the rule *yujerasamāse*.

For that [mention] is made so that the augment *num* does not occur in the case of *aśvayug*; if, under the heading of "stem" (*aṅga-adhikāra*), an operation did not apply even to what follows such a stem, then what occasion would there be for *num* to arise after the root *yuj-* in *aśvayuji*, such that the mention of "non-compound" would be required for the sake of its prohibition? Thus [it is established]. 80.
The completion of the sentence applies to each [word] individually. || 81 ||

In this treatise, sentences are completed with respect to each individual element; for example, the designation *vṛddhi* applies to each of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* individually, and the designation *guṇa* applies to each of the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* individually.
This principle is indeed worldly; it has been explained by the author of the Bhāṣya in the context of the expression "both have been studied.
As it has been said:
when it is said, "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra should be fed," it is not stated again for each one individually.
And yet, they are each fed individually;
in this matter, the very power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) is the authority.
There is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) here: in the rule *ṇaluttamaḥ*, the mention of "the last" (*uttama*) is a qualifier of *ṇal*.

For if there were not a connection with each individual word, then the mention of "uttama" (the last) would be connected with the triad beginning with *iḍ*, *vas*, and *mas*, and thus it would not serve as a qualifier for the suffix *ṇal* alone. || 81 ||
In some cases, the completion of the sentence occurs within a collective whole.
Just as in the rule "consonants that are not separated by vowels are *saṃyoga*," there is the prescription of the technical term *saṃyoga*.
Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāsa* stated: "For this purpose, the technical term *saṃyoga* has been made a long one.
This very principle is shown in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *vṛddhir ādaij*.
"Let the hundred Gargas be fined"—by this collective expression, kings become possessors of gold from the claimant;
yet here they do not fine them individually.
In this case as well, the expressive power of the word itself is the authority.
Some here state the following reasoning:

"In this case, the act of giving a hundred [cows] is the primary action (*pradhānakarman*), whereas the Gargas are the secondary object (*guṇakarman*) because they are subordinate to it. Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a distinction in the primary action based on a distinction in the secondary object."
They also cite an indicator (*jñāpaka*):
in the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, the word *prathamayoḥ* is employed to refer to the first and second sets of six case-endings (*vacana-ṣaṭka*).
For if the word *prathamā* were the technical name for the entire group of three endings beginning with *su*—namely, *su-au-jas*—then [the rule would have been formulated differently].
Furthermore, because of proximity, when [the suffixes] *ām*, *auṭ*, and *śas* are employed as a group of three, the designation "of the first two" (*prathamayoḥ*) becomes more appropriate.

If, however, the word *prathamā* were applied to each [suffix] individually, then the singular case-ending *su* would be grasped by the word *prathamā* due to its proximity; for the sake of brevity, one would have said *svamoḥ* instead of *ām*.
Therefore, by the designation "of the first two," it indicates that the sentence is completed by the collective whole.
And there is recourse to either of the two positions as desired.

However, some say it is "according to the completion of the sentence," just as in the case of "one should not eat with the Gargas," where one does not eat with each individual nor with them all collectively.

Thus, when the rule prescribing *sva* and so forth attains syntactic unity with the grammatical treatise—such as "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) and "the accusative is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*)—those [terms] being denoted in those respective places are employed [as indicators]. || 82 ||
In this treatise, the qualities (guṇas) are non-differentiating. || 83 ||
Therefore, by the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*, the designation *vṛddhi* is established for the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, which possess both acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents.
In the world, qualities (*guṇa*) can function both as differentiators and non-differentiators;
for example, a single substance such as water is differentiated by its qualities, as in "this is cold" and "this is hot."

And non-differentiation is just as Devadatta does not abandon his own identity when described as "fair," "red," "black," or "old"; likewise, although both [the masculine and neuter forms] would have been applicable according to the treatise, this is a restrictive rule.

And this meaning is indicated by the mention of "udātta" in the rule *caturanaḍuhorāmudāttaḥ*; likewise, it is indicated by the mention of "udātta" in *asthidadhi...* and by the mention of "udātta" in *luṅlaṅ...*.

If the *guṇas* were [merely] differentiators, then only a vowel-form (*ākāra*) endowed with the quality of acute (*udātta*) would need to be pronounced; thus, the mention of "acute" (*udāttagrahaṇa*) would be purposeless.
Therefore, this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). 83.
Thus ends the section on the *yuvapāda*. 1.
Between the instructional and the preparatory, only the instructional is to be taken. || 84 ||

That which exists in instruction is *aupadeśika*; that which exists in practice is *prāyogika*. The suffix *-ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule for *adhyātma* and so forth. Between these two, only the *aupadeśika* is taken here.

For example, in the case of the suffix *tarap* in *taraptamapaugha*, the designation *gha* applies to the suffix *tarap* itself— as in *brāhmaṇitarā*. However, it does not apply to the usage where the suffix *tara* has been added [to a nominal stem], such as in *nadītaraḥ*.
But if it were *gharūpa*, the vowel would be short.
And the evidence for this is the mention of the root *śvi* in the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*.
