If the inclusion of the derivative form (*prāyogika*) were intended there, then since the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śyukaḥ kiti* would already be established— because after the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has occurred, the forms *śūnaḥ* and *śūnavān* end in a vowel— the mention of *śvi* would not have been made.
And this is incorrect;

because the term "upadeśe" (in the original instruction) is understood to carry over from the rule *ekāca upadeśe*, the prohibition by the rule *śyukaḥ kiti* applies to that which ends in /u/ in the original instruction (*upadeśa*).
However, in the case of *śūna*, there is no status of ending in /u/ in the original instruction, but rather only in actual usage (*prayoga*).

And likewise, regarding the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*, Rākṣita states that because the term *upadeśa* (in its original form) continues to apply, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *śyukaḥ kiti* would not otherwise apply; therefore, the mention of *śvi* is made. To this, it is replied:
The intention of the proponent of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) is this: in the rule *śyukaḥ kiti*, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "original teaching" (*upadeśa*) is not accepted.

For if that were so, an absence of the prohibition of *iṭ* would result in forms such as *tīrṇam*, because in the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*, the mention of the root *śvi* prohibits *iṭ* only for those [roots] ending in a long vowel (*ū*) that are taught as such in their original form (*aupadeśika*).
Is it not the case that the inclusion of the term *śvi* for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* is improper?

For in the form *uḍḍīna*, the absence of the augment *iṭ* is already established simply because the prefix *ud* is marked with the *di* indicatory letter. Furthermore, there is no purpose for this *paribhāṣā*.
In the rule *taraptamapau*, because of the association (*sāhacarya*) with *tamap* and by virtue of the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) regarding definitions, only the suffix *tarap* is understood.

Thus, since the letter *p* undergoes elision through its designation as *it* during the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), and since the letter *p* is absent at the time of applying the grammatical operation (*guṇa*), the aggregate *tarap* does not exist; how then could there be any suspicion that the word *nadītaraḥ* would receive the designation *gha*?
Furthermore, if this maxim were indeed applicable, then—
What is the purpose of including the term "upadeśa" (in the rule) *upadeśe 'janunāsikaḥ* and so forth?
It is said:
first of all, it does not serve as a primary restriction, because its purpose is merely to provide further elaboration (*prapañca*).
The second [position] is also not tenable;
for it is stated that "the criticism of a means as being no means is not a mark of respect for the form [of the teaching].
The third [position] is also not tenable.

Even in the case of the fourth [letter], it does not apply; for when the designation (*saṃjñā*) has been applied everywhere and the elision (*lopa*) performed, the designation is established by relying on the letter *p* through the principle of "having previously existed" (*bhūtapūrvagati*).
Furthermore, this is because the recourse to the *paribhāṣā* is intended for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*).
The rule for *iṭ* is stronger than all other rules.

Therefore, in the case of *śvayitvā*, the augment *iṭ* occurs precisely before the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*). Likewise, in the case of *na tkvā seṭ*, because the suffix is not marked with *k* (i.e., it is *akittvāt*), there is no semivowel substitution.

And here, the inclusion of the word "ca" (and) in the rule *sani grahaguhośca* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the purpose of drawing back [the previous rule]. Otherwise, in the case of *rirūṣati*, since the suffix *san* would be *kit* by the rule *iko jhal*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would be established by the rule *śyukaḥ kiti* alone; so what need would there be for the word "ca" to draw back the previous rule? However, the Teacher perceives that elsewhere the injunction for *iṭ* is stronger; thus, having first applied that [injunction for *iṭ*], because the condition of beginning with a *jhal* consonant no longer exists, the *kit*-status is absent. Therefore, he performs the drawing back of the previous rule by means of the word "ca. || 85 ||
When there is a choice between a verbal root with a *luk*-elision suffix and one without a *luk*-elision suffix, only the one without the *luk*-elision suffix is to be understood.

Therefore, in the term *gopoṣṭak*, there is the inclusion of only the root *pibati* which has the *alūm* (āl) vikaraṇa, and not of the root *pāti* which has the *lug* vikaraṇa. This [restriction] does not apply to the mention of *vid* in the rule *satsūddhiṣādi*.

Because the form *yujavid* is taken as ending in the vowel *a*, all verbal roots in the *gaṇa* that end in *a*—namely *vid* in the sense of "knowing," *vid* in the sense of "investigation," and *vid* in the sense of "existence"—are included.

And as for its existence, the mention of the *vikaraṇas* (conjugational suffixes) for the roots *sūti* and *sūyati* in the rule *svaratisūtisūyatidhūñūdito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.44) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). For it is stated therein:
"The general mention of *sūṅ* will result in the inclusion of both the root belonging to the first class (*adādi*) and that belonging to the fourth class (*divādi*)."
This is not [the case] for the root *sū* in the sense of "impelling.
Why then is there a mention of the *vikaraṇa*?

In that case, it indicates that there is this metarule (*paribhāṣā*): when *sūṅ* is mentioned, by the rule regarding the elision of *vikaraṇas*, only the [root] belonging to the *divādi* class would be included, and not that belonging to the *adādi* class.
The mention of both [the roots *sū* and *mū*] by means of the suffixal marker (*vikaraṇa*) serves as an indicator for this [rule].

Now, one might object that the mention of *sūti* by means of the suffix *śtip* is intended to indicate that, in some instances, the operations conditioned by a *pit* suffix do not apply when *śtip* is present.

Consequently, because *śtip* is not marked with *p*, the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution in the form *sūti*—by virtue of its being treated as having the marker *ṅit* according to the rule *kṅiti ca*—is established.

Likewise, in the rule *tathā manyakarmaṇyanādare vibhāṣā*, the mention of the root *manu* [in the Dhātupāṭha] should not be intended; this is established by the absence of the *gaṇa* (the list of roots). It is replied:
the specific mention of the suffixes in *sūti* and *sūyati* indicates the absence of the *pit* designation, and thereby makes known the existence of the *paribhāṣā*.

Otherwise, if the sole purpose of the mention of the suffixal marker (vikaraṇa) were merely to indicate the absence of the *pittva* property, then, having mentioned *sūtī*, one would simply have included *sūṅ* in the rule *svaratisūtisūṅdhūṅūdito vā*.
In that case as well, the inclusion of both *sūti* and *sūṅ* would serve the purpose of indicating the absence of *pittva*.
In this context, however, the rule does not imply the contrary— that among the *lug-vikaraṇa* and *alug-vikaraṇa* [roots], only the *lug-vikaraṇa* is to be understood;

for it is stated that "the formulation of a grammatical rule in a treatise is not intended for an undesirable result," and because in the rule *vetteḥ vibhāṣā*, the root *vid* is specified by means of the *śtip* affix.

For this is its purpose: that by the paribhāṣā "when there is an elision of a vikaraṇa, the root with that elided vikaraṇa is understood," there should not be the inclusion of *vida* (meaning "to investigate") from the *raudhādika* class.

If it were the case that when there is both a root with an elided vikaraṇa and one with a non-elided vikaraṇa, only the one with the elided vikaraṇa is included, then even if [the rule] were stated as *vidaḥ*, there would still be the inclusion of *vida* (meaning "to know") alone; what then is the use of *śtipā*?
It is not necessary to state that [the rule] is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅluk* formation;
for, by the mention of *śīṅo'yaṅluk* in the rule *śīṅo ruṭ*, the absence of the inclusion of *yaṅluk* is established through association (*sāhacarya*). || 86 ||
In this world, actions are performed for the sake of future activity. || 87 ||
The meaning is that actions are performed by relying on a future state of affairs (*bhaviṣyantī pravṛtti*).
For example, by the rule *śadeḥ śitaḥ*, the ātmanepada suffix is applied in the form *śīyate* based on the future status of being marked with *śit*.

Similarly, in the forms *ninyatuḥ* and *ninyuḥ*, because there will be multiple vowels (*anekāctva*) in the future, the substitution of *yaṇ* (by the rule *eranekāco’saṃyogapūrvasya*) occurs even before reduplication; otherwise, the substitution of *iyaṅ* would have taken place.
And the evidence for this here is the mention of *ekāc* (monophthongic) in the rule *vasvekājādghasām*.

For, since reduplication is mandatory in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, there would be no monophthongic root at all; thus, that mention was made for the sake of a root that will become monophthongic at a later time, after the application of the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) has taken place.
And its purposefulness would exist only if grammatical operations were to apply here by virtue of their future occurrence.
[Objection: But surely the mention of "ekāc" (having one vowel) would be for the sake of that verbal root which has one vowel prior to reduplication;
how then can it be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned meaning? [Reply:
It is said:
Before reduplication, all verbal roots (*dhātu*) are indeed monosyllabic (*ekāc*); therefore, the mention of *ekāc* [in the rule] would be redundant.
This is not so;
for it serves to exclude those roots such as *ciri* and *jiri* which are listed among the *svādi* group, as well as those polysyllabic (*anekāc*) roots that end in affixes.
This is incorrect;
for it should be stated that "it applies after roots with more than one vowel," since the suffix *ām* is prescribed invariably after such multi-vowel roots.
If you argue that it would then be for the purpose of excluding the root *jāgṛ*, [we reply: no.

[Objection: Because the rule *jāgarter guṇaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.85) prescribes the substitution of *guṇa* for the root *jāgarti* optionally before the suffixes *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ*, [the form *ajāgarīt* would be established even without the mention of the monosyllabic root].
[Reply: It is said in response:

If this [monosyllabic] mention were intended for that purpose alone, then one should have stated simply "not *jāgṛ*" (*na jāguḥ*), having removed the mention of the monosyllabic root (*ekāj-grahaṇam*). Thus, the inclusion of the term "monosyllabic" (*ekāj*) serves another purpose.
And this meaning does not apply to the root *jāgarti* as it does to *vasati*;
nor is there an exclusion for the root *tūrṇoti*.
This is not so;

the statement that "the status of *ṇu* is prescribed for *ūrṇu*" is itself an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because by the extension of the *ṇu*-status, the root *ūrṇoti* must necessarily undergo the grammatical operation (*ekācakārya*) pertaining to a monosyllabic base.
This is because that operation applies only when monosyllabism occurs after the reduplication has been performed.
And this is logical;
otherwise, the mention of the root *ghas* would be purposeless.
Since the elision [of the final consonant] by the rule *ghasibhasor hali ca* occurs earlier, the augment *iṭ* must apply here by the rule *ekācaḥ* itself, due to its higher priority.

For in that case, when [the suffix] *kvasu* is applied, the form *ajakṣivān* is established through the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule *gamahana-jan-khana-ghasām*, and then, by the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, [the reduplication occurs].
It is said in reply:
this is the intention of the proponent of the argument based on an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
First of all, because of the mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj*), the augment *iṭ* must apply to those [roots] that have already undergone reduplication.
If that *iṭ* is applied prior to the reduplication, then the principle of "priority" (*paratva*) is not violated. And thus it was stated by Rakṣita regarding the rule *vasvekājād dhātoḥ*.
Since the augment *iṭ* occurs by virtue of its higher status even before the doubling [of the root],
the mention of *ghas* is indeed rejected.

Alternatively, the rule "ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.28), which prescribes the feminine suffix *ṅīp* for roots that will undergo elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*), serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency: if the suffix *ṅīp* were present, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) would occur; yet if the elision of the penultimate vowel were present, the suffix *ṅīp* could not apply.
Furthermore, as for the form *vartsyat-pravṛttyā*, how is it possible?

For, by the rule "a syllable followed by a conjunct consonant is heavy" (*saṃyoge guru*), the designation "heavy" (*guru-saṃjñā*) would supersede [the condition for] the *guṇa* substitution of a light penultimate vowel (*laghu-upadha-guṇa*), and thus that *guṇa* would not apply.
It is said:

by accepting the qualification "prescribed," the fault is avoided, because the rule states that *guṇa* occurs before a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* affix that is prescribed after a root having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*).
Furthermore, there is no risk of *guṇa* occurring in the case of *kuṇḍitā*.

Because the addition of *num* occurs only when there is the actual mention of a verbal root (*dhātu*) by the inclusion of the term "root" (*dhātu*), [the rule does not apply here]. If it is argued that [the fault remains] because the rule would still apply to *ruṇaddhi* by treating "that which is prescribed" as the qualifier, then [we reply]: in that case, by the inclusion of the term "vowel" (*ac*) in the rule *nābhyastasyāci piti sārvadhātuke*, the *guṇa* substitution will indeed take place before a conjunct consonant.
Otherwise, in the rule *nenekti*, the mention of *ac* would have to be for the purpose of [indicating] the state of being a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*).
But it is not so;
for in the rule *anegeḥ*, the mention of *ac* serves the purpose of avoiding the prohibition of *guṇa*.
In that case, the designation *guru* does not apply to the two consonants [the root-final and the affix-initial] due to their proximity (*āntarya*),
because of the marking of *kn* as *kit* in the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ*,
and because that *kit* status is intended to prohibit the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) by the rule *halantācca*.
As it has been said:
"The fact that *kittva* is applied to *knusanoḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no *guṇa* substitution for a light vowel.
If this is so, then what was stated in the *Nyāsa* commentary regarding the word *dṛḍhaḥ* (from *sthūla-balayoh*) would be inconsistent.
For it has been asked therein: "For what purpose is the elision of the letter *ha* prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*),
given that once the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* is applied by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ*, the form *dṛḍha* is already established by the rule *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ*?"
The [substitution of] *satyam* is established;
however, in the case of *draḍhīyaḥ*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* is not established.

This is because, when the rule *ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ* is to be applied, the elision of *ḍha* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), and consequently, the designation "heavy" (*guru*) supersedes the designation "light" (*laghu*).
It is said:

he thinks thus—that the designation "heavy" (guru) does not apply when a vowel is to be treated as a single phonological unit (guṇa). Therefore, when the substitution of *r* is to be applied, the designation "heavy" would indeed apply.

And likewise, in the case of *kḷptaśikhaḥ*, because of the rule "guroranṛto 'nantyasyāpy ekaikasya prācām" (Pāṇini 8.2.86), a protracted vowel (*pluta*) indeed occurs due to the syllable being heavy (*guru*).
But this is incorrect;
therefore, regarding the rule "halāder laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.27), the counter-example provided is precisely "apākṣīt."
Because it lacks two factors.
For instance, just as [the sound] *si-ji-da* and so forth does not occur, so too the short vowel *a* does not occur.
Because lightness (*laghutva*) is sublated by the heaviness (*gurutva*) resulting from conjunction (*saṃyoga*),

one might then think that in the case of *draḍhīyān*, the designation of lightness should not apply everywhere since it is established only as a specific indicator (*jñāpaka*). Likewise, in *kḷptaśikha* as well, only the designation of heaviness (*gurusaṃjñā*) occurs.

Alternatively, when a *saṃyoga* occurs within a suffix (*pratyaya*) that begins with a consonant, if the technical designation *laghu* (light) would apply to that very same suffix, then by the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the *kit*-status of the suffixes *knū* and *san*, the designation *guru* (heavy) does not occur;
for the indicative power is uniform.
To illustrate: in forms such as *bhettṛ* ("one who breaks"), where the suffix *tṛc* follows, the substitution of *guṇa* would otherwise apply.
In the case of *apākṣīt*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* would also apply here; however, the mention of the *parasmaipada* ending is a qualification of the suffix *sic*.

In *draḍhayati* and *draḍīyān*, the replacement by the letter *r* occurs in the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the comparative suffix (*īyasun*), but not in the past passive participle (*kta*).
Likewise, in *kḷptaśikhaḥ*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is not based on the *kta* suffix, but rather on the conjunction of the base and the suffix.
Therefore, in this case, there is only the designation "heavy" (*guru*).
But another says:
because of the *kittva* (the property of having *k* as an it-marker) of *kn*, lightness is not sublated by heaviness.
Rather, however, a co-occurrence of both designations is effected.

Consequently, in cases such as *bhettā*, even though there is heaviness (*gurutva*), the *guṇa* substitution indeed takes place because it is based on lightness; likewise, in *kḷptaśikhaḥ*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is based on the designation of heaviness;
and in *apākṣīt*, the *vṛddhi* substitution would also be based on lightness.

Regarding the rule *ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ*, the author of the Nyāsa stated that the elision of the letter *ha* was prescribed to dispel the doubt that the substitution of *repha* for the *ṛ*-vowel applies only to that which is designated as "light" (*laghu*)—according to the maxim of the "rice in the jar" (*kumbhīdhānyanyāya*). This is the intended meaning: otherwise, because the elision of *ḍha* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), this *ṛ*-vowel would be designated as "heavy" (*guru*) rather than "light," and thus the substitution of *repha* would not take place. || 87 ||
The elision (luṅ), being a bahiraṅga operation, subverts even internal (antaraṅga) rules.
Even internal elements such as the augment *num* are superseded by the external *luk* (elision);
therefore, in *gomatpriyaḥ* ("one for whom a possessor of cows is dear") and *gomatyate* ("he behaves like a possessor of cows"),
once the *luk* of the case-ending (*sup*) has occurred, the *num* does not apply because the condition of being a *sarvanāmasthāna* no longer exists.
The characteristic of being a suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa) is not absent,
because of the prohibition [stated] as *na lumatāṅgasya*.
This paribhāṣā was made known by the author of the Bhāṣya in connection with the rule *pratyayottarapadayoś ca*.
For it has been stated therein:

in cases such as *tavāyam* (this is yours) and *tvadīyaḥ*, or *mamāyam* and *madīyaḥ*, when the suffix *cha* is applied; and in cases such as *tava putraḥ* (your son), *tvatputrī* (your daughter), *mama putrī* (my daughter), and *matputraḥ* (my son), where the following word is a nominal stem (*uttarapada*), the forms *tvam* and *aham* will occur by the very rule "the singular endings [take] *tvam* and *aham*" (*tvamāvekavacane*), since they are dependent on the case endings.
The elision (*luk*) that occurs subsequent to the formation of the compound is *bahiraṅga*; it will take place later.

Furthermore, the rule regarding the disappearance of a cause (*nimittāpāyaparibhāṣā*) would not cause even the *tvam* and *mām* forms to cease, because the cause still exists due to the fact that the *bahiraṅga* elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

Since the forms *tvam* and *aham* would have been established by the previous rule [Pāṇini 7.2.94], the fact that the present rule [Pāṇini 7.2.97] is stated—namely, "in place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *tvam* and *aham* are substituted when a case-ending or a secondary suffix follows"—indicates that there exists this *paribhāṣā*: "When a case-ending is elided, the operations conditioned by that case-ending do not take place.

Consequently, since *tvam* and *aham* would be superseded by that *paribhāṣā* once the case-ending is elided, and because the absence of a case-ending would mean that *tvam* and *aham* could not be obtained by the previous rule, the present statement becomes meaningful.

One might object: "In the case of *tvattaraḥ* and *mattaraḥ*, so that *tvam* and *mā* may occur when the suffix *tarap* is applied, there ought to be a mention of the 'affix' (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*) [in Pāṇini’s rule]. However, suffixes such as *tarap* and others, being *svārthika* (denoting the same meaning as the base), are prescribed from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, not from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because the governing rule regarding semantic compatibility (*samartha-adhikāra*) has ceased to apply.
This is explained in the commentary on the rule *samarthānām prathamād vā*: this governing rule extends up to the limit of *svārthika* suffixes."
The mention of the term *uttarapada* (subsequent member of a compound) must also be made.

This is so that in examples such as *tvatputraḥ* ("your son") and *tvaddhitam* ("beneficial to you"), the forms *tvam* and *mau* may occur, overriding the rules *tavamamau ṅasi* and *tubhyamahyau ṅayi*.

Otherwise, just as *tava* and *tubhyam* occur in *tava* and *tubhyam*, those same forms would occur here as well. However, once the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* is applied, the forms *tvam* and *mau* are specifically prescribed as exceptions to those two.
Thus, how is this an indicator?
It is said:
first of all, this is not a fault.

For it is established that even primary suffixes (*svārthika*)—even though the section on "capacity" (*samartha-adhikāra*) has ceased—occur after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*), because they are *antaraṅga* (internal);
this is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *kutsite* (Pāṇini 5.3.74):

"Having expressed its own meaning, a word denotes the substance independently; having then expressed the gender, number, and case-suffix of that which inheres in the substance, it subsequently applies to [meanings such as] affection, censure, and so forth."

Regarding the phrase "ending in a case-suffix" (*vibhaktyanta*): since meanings such as "dear" or "contemptible" qualify only that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is logical to state that suffixes such as *tarap* and others are added only after what ends in a case-suffix. Thus, it is correctly said that the mention of the "suffix" (*pratyaya*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

However, those who hold the view that—since in the rule for *tarap* and other suffixes, the base of *tarap* and so on is by its very nature a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*) or a long vowel (*āp*), and thus functions according to gender and number—they argue that these [suffixes] override the case-suffixes and are applied directly to the nominal stem itself because there is no other scope [for them].
According to his view, it has been stated in the *Vṛtti* that when suffixes such as *tarap* are prescribed, the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* does not carry over;
likewise, under the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*, examples such as *rājataroḥ* and *rājatamaḥ* have been cited.
They maintain that, in his view, the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
The very mention of the word *uttarapada* (in Pāṇini 7.2.98) is itself the indicator [of this]. The second [interpretation] is also free from fault;

for if, having set aside the substitution of *tav* and *mab*, the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* were to apply, then because exceptions (*apavāda*) share the same domain as the general rule (*utsarga*), those two substitutions would occur only for that which ends in *map*.

Regarding the phrase "not for all," it is by means of the particle *ca* that there is an attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the term "ending in *m*" (*maparyanta*). [If this were not the case,] there would have to be a sublation of the substitutes *tav-* and *tubhya-*.
In that case, the attraction of "ending in *m*" (*maparyanta*) which was effected by the particle *ca* would be rendered purposeless.
This is its purpose: if [the rule] were intended to apply as a substitute for the whole (sarvādeśa), it would indeed be a substitute for the whole;
therefore, in order to exclude that, the attraction (anukarṣaṇa) of the term "maparyantasya" by means of the particle "ca" is justified. || 88 ||
Thus ends the second chapter on the root *sici* in the Paribhāṣāvṛtti.
Even when [the literal sense] is possible, there is sublation. || 89 ||
The word "somewhere" (*kvacit*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By that [rule], there is the sublation (*bādhā*) of the past tense by the present tense;
likewise, in the case of *auṇiniṣati*, there is the sublation of the first doubling by the second doubling.
Likewise, in the case of *tāṣṭra* derived from *tvāṣṭṛ* by the suffix *jagat*, there is a sublation of both [Pāṇini 7.2.115] *aco ñṇiti* and [7.2.116] *ata upadhāyāḥ* through the initial *vṛddhi*.

This principle is indeed worldly, just as it is said: "Let curd be given to the Brahmins, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya. And there is an indicative proof for this in the recitation of the word *puṣkarasat* among the *anuśatikādi* group [of Pāṇini’s sūtras].

Otherwise, because the two rules would have different scopes (*bhinnaviṣayatva*), the initial *vṛddhi* [of the first vowel] would not be superseded by the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*), and thus the reading "Pauṣkarasādi" would be purposeless.

One might object: "In the sense of 'conquered by Puṣkarasat,' when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *tena dīvyati khanati*, as in *pauṣkarasādika*, the reading would indeed be for the sake of *vṛddhi* in the case of *ṭhak*; for there is no *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel before a *kit* suffix, since that is prescribed only before *ñ-ṇit* suffixes."
It is said:
the suffix *ṭhak* itself does not apply here because it is not so prescribed.
However, some say that the mention of the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) in the rule *supo ghuṅ-ghup-cchpratyayād yaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.103) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this.
That is not so;

for it has been explained in the *vṛtti* that the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is intended to provide for the application of suffixes such as *-kalpa* and others in the alternative view.
Otherwise, if the term "optionally" were absent, and the suffix *-bahuć* were applied invariably, suffixes such as *-kalpa* and others would not occur.
Nor should it be said that the suffixes *kalpa*, etc., will occur in the sense of "mostly" (*bahu*) when applied to the subsequent region;

for once *bahuC* has been applied, since the meaning of "partial non-completion" (*iṣadasamāpti*) has already been indicated by that very suffix, there is no further expression of what has already been expressed. How much less can there be an indication of what has already been indicated? Thus, the suffixes *kalpa*, etc., do not apply at all.
And this has been explained there by the author of the *Nyāsa*:

"For it is not necessarily the case that contradiction between the general and the particular arises solely from their location; rather, it also arises from their meaning. Since the meaning is common to many—such as the *kalpa* suffixes and so on—and because it has already been expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is no further expression of what has already been stated."

How much more so, then, is there illumination for that which has already been illuminated? This is the meaning [of the objection] expressed by the passage beginning with "tasyārtha" and so forth. || 89 ||
In this context, the application of the definition is like that of rain.
In this case, the characteristic proceeds like that of a rain-cloud;
as it has been said:
"Indeed, this treatise produces its effect like a cloud, not like fire which does not produce its effect without being ignited."
For fire does not burn what has already been burned;
by this [principle], the long vowel is established in cases such as *khaṭvātaka*.
For a cloud rains even upon water.

And here, the indicative proof (*jñāpaka*) is the rule *pravāhaṇasya ḍhe*, which prescribes the vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member in the formation *prāvāhaṇeyaḥ*—meaning "the descendant of Pravāhaṇa"—by means of the suffix *ḍhak* due to [the word] being listed in the *śubhrādi* group.
In that case, while the vṛddhi of the first member *pra-* is optional, there is invariably vṛddhi for the long vowel *ā* of the second member *vāhana*.
Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of the vṛddhi of the second member in the form *pravāhaṇeyaḥ*?

If it is argued that in the case of *pravāhaṇeyībhārya*, the purpose [of the rule] is the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "and [the feminine ending] of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) caused by *vṛddhi*, provided it does not denote a color or a transformation" (Pāṇini 6.3.35), we say no;
for that is already established by the rule "and [feminine endings denoting] a genus" (Pāṇini 6.3.41).
And its status as a genus is established by the principle: "A genus [is also denoted] by a family name (*gotra*) and by Vedic schools (*caraṇa*)."

In the rule *jāteśca*, because the term *amāninī* is understood from the preceding rule *svāṅgācca*, there is no prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) when the suffix *mānin* follows; thus, one says *pravāhaṇeyamāninī*. Consequently, in this case, the mention of the cause of *vṛddhi* (the rule *vṛddhinimittasya*) is for the purpose of prohibiting *puṃvadbhāva*. If that is so, how then was it explained by the author of the *Nyāsa*: "Since the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* is already established by *jāteśca*, [the mention of] *pravāhaṇasya* is for the purpose of prohibiting *puṃvadbhāva* by the rule *vṛddhinimittasya*"?
The rule *ṭha* (Pāṇini 4.2.115), which prescribes the suffix *ṭhak*, indicates that the rule *jāteśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.52) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Consequently, in the word *hāstikam*, the prohibition of the *paṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) by the rule *jāteśca* does not apply.
This is the reply.
In that case, it should be understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the individual (*vyakti*). || 90 ||
The embryonic stages, such as the *kalala* and so forth, come into being. || 91 ||

Just as the *garbha* (intermediate element) occurs in the middle, so too the feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) occur between the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the case endings (*svādi*). When the substitution of *kā-* is applied in the forms *kā*, *ke*, and *kāḥ*, the suffix *ṭāp* is added.

Because of the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*), when the case ending (*vibhakti*) is applied according to the rule *arvaṇastrasāvanañ* and the substitution [of *a*] has been made, the suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ugitaśca*.

Some say [the forms] are *arvatyau*, *arvatyaḥ*; others say that when the feminine suffixes are applied after the word *kroṣṭṛ*, by virtue of the rule "in the case of a feminine gender following the word *kroṣṭṛ*," there is the substitution of the form of the agentive suffix *-tṛ* (*tṛjvadbhāva*), resulting in *kroṣṭrībhyām*, *kroṣṭībhiḥ*.
And the evidence for this is that the statement "na yāsayoḥ" is intended to prohibit the substitution of *i* (the *ittva*);
for if words such as *garbha-vat-tāp* did not exist,
then when the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* had been applied, the forms *yakā* and *sakā* would not occur because of the absence of the suffix *tāp*.

And thus, because there would be no occurrence of *ittva* (the substitution of *i*) for a [root] ending in a consonant (*pratyayastha*), the rule *na yāsayoḥ* would be rendered meaningless. However, Śrī Puruṣottamadeva has explained that the statement prohibiting *ittva* for *yā* and *sā* is an *jñāpaka* (an indicator).

If *garbha-vṛddhi* were not applied, then when *tyadādyatva* (the substitution of *a* for the initial of *tyad*, etc. had been performed, [the form] would follow after the *sup* suffix; consequently, because the *yakāra* would not be followed by a *sakāra*, the rule *pratyayasthāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44) would not apply, and thus the rule *na yāsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.45) would become meaningless. However, Śrī Puruṣottamadeva has explained it as follows:
And there is an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the statement prohibiting *it*-ness (*ittva*) for the suffixes *yās* and *yāsī*.

If the feminine suffix *ṭāp* were not present as in *garbhavat*, then after the substitution of *yat* for the *tyadādi* stems, when followed by a case-ending (*sup*), in the forms *syāt* and *yakā sakā*, the rule "after a stem-final [consonant], *i* is substituted [for the *ā* of *āp*]" would have no occasion to apply at all, because the *āp* would not be preceded by a case-ending (*sup*).
Why, then, would there be a prohibition? || 91 ||
A technical rule applies to an injunction, not to a restatement.
Therefore, because the term *kaṅiti* in the rule *tena kaṅiti ca* is connected with "guṇa" and "vṛddhi," the paribhāṣā *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* does not apply.
Consequently, since the prohibition applies when a suffix marked by *k* or *ṅ* is the cause, the prohibition is established even in the case of the form *bhinna*.
This meaning is established by the principle of the primary and the secondary (*pradhānāpradhānanyāya*).
Furthermore, the evidence for this here is the rule *udīcām ātaḥ*.
In the rule *sthāne*, the mention of *sthāna* is for the purpose of conveying the sense of "in place of."
And this [rule] is not over-extensive because of the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth) in the rule *saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*;
otherwise, it would have been stated simply as *saṃkhyāvyayābhyām*.
And this is the meaning.

[The rule states: "After a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *ūdhas*, which follows either a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Now, if this were the case—namely, that it refers to a *bahuvrīhi* ending in the word *ūdhas* which follows a numeral or an indeclinable—then it would apply only here: *pañcaghaṭodhnī* ("having five pot-milks"), but not [in the following]. [Objection: But surely, if it were thus—"after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in the word *ūdhas* which follows a numeral or an indeclinable"—then it would apply only in this instance: *pañcaghaṭodhnī*; [but not elsewhere]. [Response: This is not so. For the word *ūdhas* is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*). And relative terms depend upon a correlative (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, when the word *ūdhas* is heard, there arises an expectation for its correlative, namely, "milk" (*payas*). Consequently, the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* is understood as "one whose milk consists of five pots," and not "one who possesses five pots. Thus, since the word *ūdhas* does not follow a numeral or an indeclinable in the sense required by the rule, the application of *ṅīp* is not established here. However, in the case of *pañcaghaṭodhnī*, the word *ūdhas* does indeed follow a numeral; therefore, the application of *ṅīp* is established. Hence, the mention of the word *ūdhas* in the rule is for the purpose of excluding cases like *pañcakhaṭvaḥ*. Alternatively, one might argue: "In the case of *pañcaghaṭodhnī*, the word *ūdhas* does not follow a numeral or an indeclinable, because the word *ghaṭa* intervenes. To this we reply: No, for the intervention of a word belonging to the same category (*jātīya*) does not constitute an intervention at all. Just as in the case of *pañcapācakaḥ* ("one who cooks five times"), where the intervention of the word *pācaka* (which belongs to the same category of agent nouns) does not prevent the formation of the desired form, so too here the intervention of the word *ghaṭa* (which belongs to the same category of common nouns) does not constitute an intervention. Therefore, the application of *ṅīp* is established. Thus, the mention of the word *ūdhas* is indeed for the purpose of excluding cases like *pañcakhaṭvaḥ*. Or rather, the mention of the word *ūdhas* is for the purpose of excluding cases like *dvimūrdhā* ("two-headed"). For if the rule were simply "after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in a word following a numeral or an indeclinable," then since the word *mūrdhan* follows a numeral in *dvimūrdhā*, the suffix *ṅīp* would undesirably apply. To prevent this, the word *ūdhas* is mentioned. Since the word *mūrdhan* is not *ūdhas*, the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied. Alternatively, the mention of the word *ūdhas* is for the purpose of excluding cases like *dvimūrdhā*. For in this case, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *ūdhas* that follows a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
It is said:
by virtue of proximity, the word *ūdhas* alone is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the numeral and the indeclinable, not the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself.
For instance, in the rule *saṃkhyāvyayābhyām*, the word *ūrdhva* alone is proximate [to the following term], not the other.
But even so, [the rule] would not apply to a three-word *bahuvrīhi*; therefore, an effort must be made for that purpose.
When a verbal root (prakṛti) is mentioned, that which has the suffix -ṇi added to it is also included.

Therefore, by the rule *heracaṅi*, even when the desiderative suffix (*san*) is applied to the causative form of the root *hinoti* (Pāṇini 7.3.56), the substitution of *ku* occurs, resulting in the form *jighāyiṣati*.

However, regarding the forms *abhiṣāvayati* and *pariṣāvayati*, the connection with the action belongs only to the root *sunoti*, not to the causative *sāvayati*; thus, the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule *upasargāt sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65) was stated in the *Vṛtti*, and not by this present paribhāṣā.
And the proof for this is the prohibition [contained] in the rule *heracaṅi*.

If, in the inclusion of the root-form (*prakṛtigrahaṇa*), there were no inclusion of what is additional to the causative suffix (*ṇi*), then— since the substitution of *k* for *h* is prescribed for the root *hinoti* alone when followed by a suffix conditioned by *abhyastam*— what occasion would there be for it to apply when the causative suffix is additionally present?
For what purpose is the prohibition "not in *acaṅ*" formulated?

Furthermore, this [rule] is not universally applicable; for it has been stated by Rakṣita that in the rule beginning with *bhā* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for roots such as *bhā* when they are in the causative (*ṇyanta*).
Consequently, in the word *arha*, there is no inclusion of the causative form of the root *arh*. Thus it was said by Rakṣita. || 93 ||
Furthermore, when a grammatical operation has already taken effect on a constituent part, that same operation does not apply again once that constituent has been finalized.

The term *aṅgavṛtti* means the occurrence (*vṛtti*) of the function (*kārya*) of a secondary element (*aṅga*). For that reason, there is no rule—that is, no prescription—regarding the recurrence of the function of a secondary element once it has been completed and is ready for application.
In the phrase "in the occurrence of the secondary element" (*aṅgavṛttau*), the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
The meaning is that there is no rule, no prescription, and thus no production of the recurrence of the function of the secondary element once again.
Therefore, when the substitution of *piba* is made in the form *pibati*, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel does not occur.
And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is indicated in the *Bhāṣya* at the rules "jñā-janor-jā" and "jyādādīyasaḥ.
For it is stated in the former instance:
"For what purpose is the substitution of *ja-* prescribed? Let the substitution of *ja-* alone be prescribed instead."
In that case as well, [the form] *jāyate* is indeed established by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*.

Furthermore, it has been stated later: "For what purpose is the substitution of *ā* for the suffix *iyas* following *jyā* prescribed? Let only the elision (*lopa*) of the original [suffix] be ordained.
Even if that were done, [the form] *jyāyān* would still be established by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*."

Therefore, since there is the absence of *jā* in the former case and the prescription of the long vowel *ā* in the other, both serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) that this is a *paribhāṣā*. However, the author of the *Nyāsa* says: "The prescription of a long-vowel substitute is for the sake of brevity in comprehension; for even when a short vowel is substituted, one understands [the rule] by means of the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*."
But surely, by the paribhāṣā "the operation of a subordinate element," this [suffix] would not apply?
This is not so; for it is stated that [the suffix applies] to that which is already established (*niṣṭhita*).
For once the substitution of *ja* has been applied, the stem (*aṅga*) is no longer established,
because it is no longer fit for usage.
It has already been stated that [the rule] *jyādādīyasaḥ* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this fact.

In the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, there is no recurrence (*ananuvṛtti*) of the mention of *kṅit*; and this non-recurrence is established because, in forms such as *uruyā*, the absence of lengthening is accounted for by their being Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Thus ends the third quarter of the Devika section in the Paribhāṣāvṛtti.
In a rule concerning what precedes, [a substitute] is not like the original (sthānivadbhāva).

Therefore, in the case of *papaktiḥ* and *yaṣṭiḥ*, when the substitution of *k* (*kutvam*) and the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatvam*)—which fall under the jurisdiction of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*—are to be applied, the elision of *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) does not behave as if it were the original element (*asthānivattvāt*), and thus the substitution of *k* and *ṣ* before consonants beginning with *jhal* is established.

Now, one might object: in the case of *pāpaktiḥ* and *yaṣṭiḥ*, once the elision of the entire cluster of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*) has been performed by the rule *yaṅoci ca*, the subsequent substitution of *k* and *ṣ* for *y* and *ṣ* (by the rule *halacorādeśe na sthānivat*) is already established.
This is not so.
Therefore, when the elision of the vowel *a* is performed by the rule *ato lopaḥ*, only the letter *ya* of the suffix *yaṅ* is elided by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca*. Why is this so?
Because in the rule *na padāntādi-sūtre*, the mention of the word *vare* is for the purpose of prohibiting the treatment as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in the case of the form *yāyāvara*.

For if there were elision of the entire complex (samudāyalopa), since the condition for the application of *sthānivadbhāva* would not be met, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* in the case of *vara* would be purposeless.
If this is so, then the rule *na dhātulopa ārddhadhātuke* ("there is no [application of *sthānivadbhāva*] when there is elision of a verbal root before an ārdhadhātuka suffix") would be redundant;
because forms such as *loluvaḥ* and *popuvaḥ* would already be established through *sthānivadbhāva* applied to the vowel *a* of the *yaṅ* suffix.

In that case, by the force of the rule regarding the elision of the *dhātu*, it is indicated that when an *ac* suffix follows, the elision applies to the entire [verbal root] as a whole. However, in other instances, it applies to each [letter] individually; thus, forms such as *sanīsraṃsaḥ* and *danīdhvaṃsakaḥ* are established.
Similarly, [the forms] *sanīsraṃsakaḥ* and *danīdhvaṃsakaḥ* are also derived.

If this is indeed the final conclusion regarding the rule *śīṅ* (Pāṇini 1.2.19), then the purpose of making *śīṅ* marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*) as stated by the author of the *Nyāsa*— namely, that it is so that the prohibition of *kit*-status may not apply in the case of *yaṅ*-elision, as in *śeśyitaḥ* and *śeśyitavān*— is inconsistent.
For even though the *niṣṭhā* suffixes are not *kit*, there would be no occurrence of *guṇa* due to the status of the *a* of the *yaṅ* being treated as *sthānivadbhāva*.
In that case, the explanation was given there by relying on the fact that the locative in *ārddhadhātuke* is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).

And if the elision of *ac* applies to the entire [stem], yet elsewhere there is no such restrictive rule— this is the meaning of the sentence— then by that, the elision applies both individually and to the aggregate as well.

Therefore, the intention of the author of the Nyāsa is that when there is the elision of the entire complex (samudāyalopa), the designation *ṅit* is applied in the rule *śeṣitaḥ* for the purpose of prohibiting the prohibition of *kit*.

And this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *nāglopiśāsvṛditām*. For there it is said: "In forms such as *acakathat*, because the substitute [of the penultimate vowel] is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the shortening will not occur after the causative suffix (*ṇic*); what then is the purpose of the prohibition 'not for those that elide a vowel' (*aglopinām na*)? To this it is replied: "It is for the sake of cases where the status of being treated as the original does not apply, such as *atyararājat*; for here the elision of the *ṭi*-suffix is not a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*), but rather a substitute for a consonant (*halac-ādeśa*). Thereupon it is further stated: "In that case, the prohibition 'not for those that elide a vowel' would indeed apply here."

For here, it is not only *a* that is elided; rather, another [vowel] may also be elided. Now, if the negation were based on that which is elided here, then the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would likewise apply to that which is elided. Having stated this, he concludes: "In that case, by teaching the prohibition 'not for those [roots] whose final vowel is elided,' the Teacher indicates that the status of being a substitute does not occur subsequently once it has begun. Therefore, it need not be stated that 'in the rules concerning what is not established in the preceding [section], there is no status as a substitute.'"
But others say:
"A substitute for a *hal* (consonant) or a *ca*-element is not like its original (*na sthānivat*).
For this very reason, it was stated by Rakṣita in the rule *nāglopiśāsvṛditām*:

Regarding the rule "not like the original" (*na sthānivat*) in the case of a substitute for *hal* (consonants): if this were not the case, then in the case of words such as *sthūla*, when the *yaṇ* and other elements are elided, the substitution of *av* would have to be explicitly stated—
as in *sthavīyān*.
Furthermore, many other faults have been stated;
therefore, [the rule] "it is not as if it were the original" (*na sthānivat*) does not apply when there is a substitution of *hal* (consonants) or *ac* (vowels).
However, in this case, by virtue of the inclusion of the term *aglopi*, it is accepted that even when there is the elision of a whole cluster, it is still considered *aglopi*.

This has been established in the *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā* [of Kaiyaṭa] on the grounds that the prohibition would be purposeless (*anarthakya*) in the case of *kevalāglōpa*. Now, one might object: "In forms such as *sthavīyān*, the substitution of *ava* (*avādeśaḥ*) ought to be stated;
for since the *ā* [of the suffix *iyasun*] would be subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution of *ava* would indeed necessarily occur."
It is said:

if the rule "in the case of a substitute for *hal* and *ac*, it is not like the original" (*na sthānivat*) were not present, the substitution of *ava* would not occur because the entire complex [of the suffix] would be treated as the original.
This is not so.
It is stated that the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* applies to the vowel (*ac*) and not to the entire aggregate.

It is replied: just as in this case, by the statement "that which is substituted in the place of both," a substitute for a vowel or a consonant (*aj-jhal-ādeśa*) receives the designation of a vowel-substitute (*aj-ādeśa*), so too it possesses the designation of a non-vowel-substitute (*anaj-ādeśa*).
Thus, it has been stated that when there is the designation *anaj*, then the designation *av* must be prescribed. Regarding what was said here—
that by the force of the mention of *aglopin* in this rule, even when there is the elision of the entire [stem], it is accepted as being *aglopin*,
because the prohibition would be purposeless in the case of the elision of only [the final consonant]— [This is the translation of the provided Sanskrit text.]

And this [rule] is a general indicator regarding the elision of *a* (aglopa); therefore, in the case of *adadṛṣat* from *dṛṣadam ākhyat*, even though there is an elision of *a* (*agan-aglope*), the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by the rule *aglopa iti pratiṣedhād dīrgho laghoḥ* does not occur.
Otherwise, the designation "elision of *a*" (*aglopa*) would not apply to *agan-aglope*;
for in the case of *acakathat*, where there is only the elision of *a*, the prohibition regarding elision of *a* would already have its purpose fulfilled.
And this is not established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), because that principle is prohibited in the case of a rule prescribing a long vowel.
And this [rule] is not eternal (*anitya*), because of the mention of "doubling" (*dvirvacana*) in the sūtra *na padāntādi*.

Therefore, in the case of *vetasvān*, since the elision of the vowel *a* is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the word ends in a consonant other than *s*; thus, there is an absence of the *ru*-substitution (the change to *r*).

Likewise, in the case of *kuṭādi*, because the substitute [of the vowel] is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the letter *ṛ* is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), and thus there is no application of the *jaś*-rule.
An objection is raised: "But since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included under the term 'preceding' (*pūrva*), the letter *ṭ* does not have the status of being at the end of a word.
It is replied: [True].
The inclusion of the word "parā" (further) is appropriate,
according to the maxim that a rule should be formulated as far as possible.
True.

In cases where a rule depends on what follows, as in *vṛkṣāt* (where the status of being a *pada* arises from the suffix *sup* because of the mention of "what follows"), the substitution of *jaś* in *kuṭādī* does not depend on the mention of "what follows.
For the substitution of *jaś* does not depend upon the vowel *ā*.
It is said in reply:
Although *jaś*-ness (*jaśtva*) depends upon the vowel *ā*, it is said in reply:

although the vowel *ā* is not the cause (*nimitta*) of *jaś*-ness, nevertheless, when there is the mention of "the following" (*para*), a word ending in the letter *ṭ* arises according to the rule *kuṭi*; thus, the mention of "the following" itself is the cause for *jaś*-ness.
[Objection: But even if another word is present, the substitution of *jaś* (i.e., *d*) does not occur for the letter *ṭ*, because it is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*).
For a word ending in *a* is what follows, and thus the rule for *sup*-suffixes applies.
[Reply: It is said in response:
When the inclusion of *par* is made, [one might argue that] the word ends in *ṭ* by way of partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*).
This is not so;
because of the principle of "treating the end as the beginning" (*antādivattva*), there is no partial modification.

Otherwise, even in the case of *vṛkṣam*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would be included in the preceding [element] by virtue of the inclusion of the original form, the long vowel would indeed occur by the rule *supi ca* through the mechanism of partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*). And thus, the principle *nāntādivat* (it is not like the end or the beginning when based on both) would be rendered useless. It is replied: [The principle *nāntādivat* is not useless. For if the single-substitute were considered as part of the preceding element, then in the case of *vṛkṣam*, since the substitute would be regarded as belonging to the preceding [element], the condition for the application of *supi ca* would be met, and the long vowel would necessarily result. Consequently, the rule *nāntādivat*—which states that a substitute is not treated as the end of the preceding element or the beginning of the following element when it depends on both—is necessary to prevent such an outcome. Thus, it is stated: [the principle is not redundant].

Where a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) relies on two things—one by way of being a whole (like *anta* and so forth) and the other by way of being a partial modification (*ekadeśavikāra*)—there the acceptance of partial modification applies, as in the case of *vṛkṣam*.

In the rule *kuṭādīnām*, the substitution of *jaś* does not rely on the subsequent form (*paramākāra*); therefore, it is correct that the letter *ṭakāra*, which undergoes partial modification, possesses the status of a word-final (*padānta*).

Now, one might object: even so, since this is a word-final operation (*padāntavidhi*), when the substitution of *jaś* is to be applied, the prohibition against treating a substitute as the original (*sthānivadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) regarding word-final operations would apply; thus, by the rule for *jaś*, the change must indeed occur.

It is said in reply: there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), for the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* depends upon the status of being a word-final (*padāntatva*), and the status of being a word-final depends upon the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*.

Even so, the substitution of a *jaś* sound by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo’nta* certainly occurs; yet there is no *sthānivadbhāva*, because that is prohibited by the specific injunction *na sthānivat* with respect to the application of the *jaś* rule.
It is said:

when *jaś*-substitution is to be applied to *jhal* sounds following a *repha* (the sound *r*) or an *apādīya* (a letter belonging to the *apṛkta* class) that occurs in conjunction with a *car* sound, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* is desired.
Thus, *dhastvasagniḥ* is cited as an example.
And this was stated by Rakṣita in the section on the *ṣāḍika* [suffixes] under the rule *ṭhājādāvṛddhaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ*. 95.
Even a general rule (*utsarga*) that has already arisen is set aside by an exception (*apavāda*) whose conditions are yet to arise;
the general rule applies only after having excluded the domain of the exception. || 97 ||

Therefore, in the case of *dadhati*, although the substitution of *jha* for *anta* (i.e., *jha* becoming *anti*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) because its cause has already arisen, it is superseded by the substitution of *at* according to the rule *ad abhyastāt*, which is triggered by a cause that will arise later.

And the evidence for this is the inclusion of the term *guṇa* in the rule *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ*, even though the substitution of the vowel *e* (the *guṇa* of *i*) was already established by the general rule of *guṇa*.

The purpose of that mention of *guṇa* is so that, by the force of the reference to *guṇa*, the specific paribhāṣā [P. 1.1.50] may apply, ensuring that the *guṇa* occurs in place of the first vowel (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*).

Otherwise, in the form *śete*, the letter *ṅ* would undergo the designation *it* (and be elided), and the vowel *e* would result; in that case, if [the elision] were *antaraṅga*, the mention of *guṇa* would be useless, because once the *ṅ* is elided, the substitution of *e* for the *i* would occur regardless.

For this very reason, having set aside the rule *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ*, the formulation *sārvadhātukamapit śīṅaḥ* was not adopted [as a substitute]. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, in forms such as *adhiśayyete*, because of the prohibition of the *ṅit*-designation, the substitution of *iy* by the rule *āto ṅitaḥ* would not occur;
for since the expression *aśīṅaḥ* is a specification in the ablative (*pañcamī*), the prohibition must apply to what follows immediately after the root *śīṅ*.

Furthermore, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "and not *śīṅ*," the root *ac* (the verbal base) ought to have the marker *ṅit* by virtue of its similarity [to *śīṅ*] and its being vowel-ending (*ajantatva*). However, this is not so, because the exclusion is not intended to include it. Alternatively, one may take "not *śīṅ*" as a separate action [of negation].
Therefore, this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the two technical rules (*paribhāṣā*).

Regarding the principle that even a general rule (*utsarga*) whose cause has already arisen is superseded by an exception (*apavāda*) whose cause is yet to arise, the commentator Rakṣita has stated that the inclusion of the vowel *ṛ* (in the form *ṛcchatṛtām*) serves as an indicator for this meaning.

If this [paribhāṣā] did not exist, then when the form *ṛ atus* is established, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the *ik* vowel would apply; subsequently, when reduplication occurs by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the lengthening of the initial vowel according to the rule *ata ādeḥ* would result in the forms *āratus* and *ārurus*, which are already established. [However, since the desired forms are *aratus* and *ararus*, the paribhāṣā must be accepted.]
But when this [substitution] is present, the *yaṇ* replacement does not occur;
for once reduplication has been performed, it is superseded by the long vowel substitution (*sarvaṇa-dīrgha*) which arises due to its cause.
And once the long vowel substitution has taken place, because the original base (*prakṛti*) is included [in the term *radh*], the form would be *radhur*.

In the view that [the root] *abhyasa* is included, there would be the elision of the *repha* (r), and with the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, the form would be *cātur*. However, if the root *ṛgatau* ("to go") is what is intended, then by means of *guṇa* substitution, the forms *āratur* and *ārur* are established.

And this is stated on the basis of resorting to the position that the rule *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* ("an internal operation is stronger than an external one") applies when they do not depend on the same cause (*avyāśrayatva*).

If, however, the rule *vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (an internal operation is stronger than one based on external phonemes) were to apply here, then the substitution of *urat* (the single substitute for *u* and *ṛ*) and so forth would occur, overriding the homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*).
For this very reason, it was stated by Rakṣita regarding the rule *uś ca*:
"Alternatively, the mention of *ṛ* there has been rejected, because [of this consequence]. || 97 ||
That which is substituted in place of *ṇau* (the causative suffix) is treated as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Whatever [operation], such as *vṛddhi* and so forth, has been performed when *ṇi* follows, that shall be treated as if it were in its original position (*sthānivat*) when a reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is to be made.
By this rule, in forms such as *śuśāvayiṣati* and *juhāvayiṣati*, the fact that the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) ends in the vowel *u* is established.
However, in the form *aśūśavat*, although the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *v* was performed after *ṇi*, it does not remain *sthānivat* during the reduplication.

This is because it is accepted that the substitute for *ajādi* (a vowel-initial element) which has been applied in the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇi*) retains its original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) during reduplication;
and this has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *dvirvacane'ci*.
And there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this in the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyaparaḥ*: the word *oḥ* serves as a qualifier for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*).

For by that rule, the substitution of *i* for the reduplication is prescribed when a labial (*pavarga*), a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*), or the letter *j* follows an *ac* vowel—as in forms such as *bibhāvayiṣati*.

If the operations performed upon the causative suffix (*ṇi*), such as the substitution of *vṛddhi* and so forth, were not treated as *sthānivat*, how could the substitution of the vowel *u* for the reduplication be prescribed?

Because the indicator (*jñāpaka*) belongs to the same class (*tulyajātīyatva*), other *puṅ* clusters similar to it—namely those followed by the vowel *a*—participate in the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Therefore, in the case of *acikīrtat*, [the rule] "not as the original" (*na sthānivat*) applies; this is how Rakṣita explains the rule *ur ṛt*.
However, this is not correct.

In the rule *stautiṇyoreva ṣaṇyabhyāsāt*, the example *siṣedhayiṣati* is given; here, by applying the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivattva*) through this [rule] when the letter *e* follows, the reduplication is established.

Likewise, in the case of *aujaḍhat*, the statement that reduplication occurs by means of this [rule] through the status of being "as if the original" would be incorrect. Similarly, regarding the rule *lopaḥ pibaterīccābhyāsasya*, the statement of the author of the Vṛtti—that in the form *apīpyat*, what was done in the causative suffix (*ṇau*) becomes "as if the original"—would be contradicted.
Therefore, this is a general technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).
It is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that such a rule does not apply everywhere; thus, there is a restriction in the case of *acikīrtat*.
And this [restriction] is necessarily required.
Otherwise, what would be the solution for the form *adhijigāpayiṣati*?
But another says:
"When a substitution beginning with a vowel (*ajādeśa*) is made for a portion of a stem (*aṅgaikadeśa*) in the context of the causative suffix *ṇi*, it is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*)."
Therefore, in the case of *adhijigāpayiṣati*, there is no application of the rule *sthānivat* (the substitute behaves like the original).
And this has been explained by Rakṣita in the commentary on the rule *ṇau ca saṃ-caṅoḥ*. Even so, in the case of *acikīrtat*, there remains precisely the same fault.
Exceptions regarding modifications due to repetition do not subvert general rules or injunctions. 99.

In cases of conflict between rules, those that are sublated do not sublate the sublaters—namely, those rules characterized by being subsequent, internal, or more powerful—even when they are based on repetition.

Therefore, in the case of *mīmāṃsate*, the shortening [of the reduplicated syllable] by the rule *sanyataḥ* is not sublated by the lengthening [of the root vowel] by the rule *mānbadhādibhyaḥ*. Likewise, in the case of *acikṣaṇat*, the shortening by the rule *sanyataḥ*, which has its own scope of application, is not sublated by the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] by the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ* in forms such as *acīkarat*.
And the proof for this is the inclusion of the term *akiṅ* (not ending in *ki*) in the rule *dīrgho’kitaḥ*.

For that [term] is employed so that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) does not occur in forms such as *grayamyate*; if there were a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) even among modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), then once the augment *nuk* had been applied, a long vowel would not occur simply because the stem would no longer end in *ac*, so what would be the purpose of including *akiṅ*? It was included for the sake of the aforementioned point.
It is an indicator. || 99 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter on the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) in the *Vṛtti*.
Thus ends the seventh chapter. || 7 ||
This [rule] is not considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to what precedes it, except in the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*).
When a reduplication is to be performed, the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (that which precedes is as if non-existent) does not apply.

Consequently, in forms such as *drogdhā*, *dogdhā*, *droḍhā*, and *droḍhā*, once the substitution of *gh* for *druha-* and the substitution of *ḍh* for *druha-* have been applied before a *jhal*-beginning suffix, the reduplication occurs according to the rule *sarvasya dve*.
Otherwise, by virtue of the *pūrvatrāsiddham* rule rendering the preceding operations non-existent, the reduplication would instead apply to the form *drohtā*.

Consequently, there would be an option regarding the substitution of *gh* for *d*, as in the case of *duh*. In that regard, it is not possible [to maintain] that when the substitution of *gh* applies to the root (*prakṛti*), it should also apply to the reduplicated form;
and thus, the substitution of *ḍh* might also occasionally occur.
And in this way, it would result in the undesirable consequence that one who harms is also the one who is harmed.
[Objection: Let the word *sarvasya* be recited after *asiddhapādam*, and let *dvepādaḥ* be recited [instead]; thus, there will be no lack of established proof (*asiddhatva*).
[Response: This is not so.

For if one were to read [the rule] thus, then in the case of *paṭhati-paṭhatitarām*, the reduplication would not occur because it would not precede the suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣapratyaya*). Furthermore, according to the statement "there is no 'subsequent-ness' (paratva) when the preceding rule is not established due to the absence of what follows," in the case of *grāmaṃ tv īkṣate*, the substitution of *tvā* and *mā* for the second person pronoun would be unestablished, and consequently, the *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *i* + *a*] would not take place.
And the proof for this is the mention of the word "sarvasya" (of all) in the rule *sarvasya dve*.
For that [word] ends in the suffix *a*, which has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
Therefore, the meaning is as follows:
The mention of "sarvakārya" (all operations) implies a repetition; the meaning is that after performing all operations, there is a repetition.
And this is logical only if non-ascertainment (*asiddhatva*) does not apply; thus, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Now, one might object: the mention of "sarvasya" (of all) is for the purpose of causing the doubling of every [element].
Otherwise, by the rule *parervarjane*, the doubling would apply to the final letter;
however, this is incorrect.
Since two [substitutes] are prescribed, and because they consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it is already established that they are replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*).
True;
in the case of *paryādi* and other such words ending in *hal*, the substitution of *iK* would apply to the final letter.
But surely there would be two substitutions of *iK*?
Consequently, because it consists of more than one *al* (phoneme), its status as a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatva*) is established.

Furthermore, the two *ikāra*s do not attain the status of being substitutes once they have undergone a single substitution (*ekādeśa*). Thus, due to having only one *al*, the substitute would apply only to the final [element].

However, there is no application of the rule for a single substitution while those two [elements] remain unapplied; and at the time of its application, because it consists of more than one *al*, it is a substitute for the whole. Therefore, there is no rule for the final element.

It might be argued as follows: "In that case, [the substitution] would apply to the two half-mātrās of the vowel (ac). Since two half-mātrās are prescribed for the word *pari*, and since the half-mātrā is not included by the mention of 'al', the condition of having more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) being absent, the rule stating 'of the whole' (*sarvasya*) would instead result in the substitution applying only to the final [phoneme]."
This is highly incorrect;
since it is impossible to pronounce two half-mātrās that are not joined together, the substitution cannot be made.
However, another says:

In the sūtra *sarvasya dve*, this statement of Kātyāyana is recited as a paribhāṣā: "That which is not established (*asiddha*) in what precedes does not cause reduplication (*advirvacana*). And this [paribhāṣā] is non-eternal (*anitya*).
Because of the statement "both [are used] when there is repetition," the form *praṇināya* is established. || 100 ||
Thus ends the first section, "The Doubling of Everything," in the commentary on the Paribhāṣās.
The teaching of the scriptures is impermanent. || 101 ||
In the case of *śākaṃ pacānasya*, the suffix *iṭ* does not occur;
likewise, in the case of *sāgaraṃ tartum icchati*, the suffix *iṭ* does not occur.

And the proof for this is that in the rule *ani loṭ*, the mention of *ni* together with the augment *an* is the indicator; for if the teaching regarding augments were mandatory, he would have formulated the rule simply as *niloṭ* without including the mention of *āṭ*.

Similarly, in the rule *yuvoranākau*, the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) in the *nyāsa* commentary indicates that the elision of *ghu* in the *leṭ* tense is optional. However, some say that the mention of *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* without the inclusion of the nasal augment (*num*) is the indicator.

But how can it be said that "the rule of the scripture (āgama-śāsana) prevails"? For since the single-substitute *ami* is included by the mention of the subsequent element (*paragrahaṇa*) in the rule *pūrvaparayoḥ ekaḥ*, one would expect the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) to occur on the basis of its being a word (*padatva*), by relying on the case-ending contained within it. It is replied: [The reply follows:]... [text continues] ...it is stated: "In the case of *āgama-śāsana*, the rule of the scripture prevails. This means that when there is a conflict between a rule concerning a grammatical operation (*kārya*) and a rule concerning the status of a word (*prasaṅga*), the rule concerning the operation prevails. However, this is not so in the present case. Why? Because here there is no conflict between two rules; rather, there is a conflict between a rule concerning the status of a word (*pada-prasaṅga*) and a rule concerning a specific grammatical operation (*kārya-prasaṅga*). And in such cases, the rule concerning the operation prevails. Therefore, the elision of the *n* does not take place. Furthermore, the mention of the subsequent element (*paragrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of including the substitute itself, and it does not serve to include the case-ending contained within it. Thus, there is no occurrence of the elision of the *n*. Moreover, the mention of the subsequent element is intended to indicate that the substitute is a single unit (*eka-saṃjñā*), and it does not serve to include the case-ending contained within it. Therefore, there is no occurrence of the elision of the *n*. Consequently, it is established that "in the case of *āgama-śāsana*, the rule of the scripture prevails.
